2

HTML – Structuring Your Web Pages

This chapter covers the basics of HTML ( HyperText Markup Language ). You’ll learn the key concepts about HTML and then use the AI to generate a simple page, and in doing so, learn about elements, tags, and attributes.

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to read, write, and understand HTML as a structured description of a web page, and confidently build simple, meaningful pages that form a solid foundation for everything that comes next.

In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:

  • What is HTML?
  • Building a basic web page
  • Working with forms and inputs
  • AI exercises
  • Other markup languages

    Suggested chatbot prompts with example responses for this chapter can be found at the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/prompts/ch02-html/readme.md

What is HTML?

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. That sounds scary, but the idea is simple.

HTML is not a programming language:

  • It does not make decisions
  • It does not run logic
  • It does not calculate anything

HTML describes the structure and meaning of content on a web page.

HTML is the page’s structure. It defines:

  • What text is a heading
  • What text is a paragraph
  • What counts as a list
  • Where do links point?
  • Which images belong on the page?
  • How tabular data is organized

CSS makes things look good. You will learn about CSS in Chapter 3 , CSS – Styling Your Web Pages . For this chapter, ignore how things look and focus on what they are and how they are structured.

JavaScript makes things interactive. The web pages that you create in this chapter will be static. In Chapter 5 , JavaScript – Making Web Pages Interactive , you will write JavaScript code to make them come alive.

HTML decides what things are. Without HTML, the web would just be a stream of unstructured text.

HTML is made of elements

HTML is built from tags to form elements . A tag is the actual markup syntax enclosed in angle brackets, such as <p> or </p> , which tells the browser how to interpret content. An element, on the other hand, is the complete structure that includes the opening tag, the content, and the closing tag.

For example, <p>Hello</p> is a paragraph element, made up of the opening <p> tag, the text Hello , and the closing </p> tag. Tags are the building blocks, while elements are the full constructs created from those tags.

Most elements look like this: 

<p>This is a paragraph.</p>
  • <p> means start a new paragraph
  • </p> means end of the paragraph
  • Everything in between is the content of the paragraph

In HTML, attributes provide additional information about an element and are placed inside the opening tag. They usually come in name–value pairs, such as class="intro" or href="https://example.com" , and they modify how the element behaves or is displayed.

For example, in <a href="https://example.com">Visit</a> , the href attribute tells the browser where the link should go. While the element defines the structure and meaning, attributes refine or configure that element’s behavior.

Two attributes appear constantly in HTML: id and class . An id identifies one unique element on a page. A class labels one or more elements as belonging to the same group. Later, CSS and JavaScript will use these heavily. For now, the important id idea is simple: id is for one specific element, while class can be shared.

Some elements are void elements , like <img> or <br> , which do not have closing tags or inner content. Others are container elements , such as <div> or <section> , which wrap content and can include other elements inside them.

A <div> is a generic container element with no inherent meaning. It’s useful for grouping content for styling, but it should not replace semantic elements like <section> , <nav> , or <p> when those are more appropriate.

It is also important to know that elements can be nested, meaning one element can sit inside another to create a hierarchy. Proper nesting is important because incorrect structure can lead to unexpected rendering or accessibility issues.

Good practice : Accessibility in web development means designing and structuring content so that it can be used by everyone, including people with disabilities such as visual, hearing, motor, or cognitive impairments. This includes using proper HTML structure, meaningful text alternatives like alt attributes for images, and clear navigation so assistive technologies such as screen readers can interpret the page correctly.

Another key idea is the distinction between block-level elements and inline elements . Block-level elements, like <p> and <h1> , typically start on a new line and take up the full width available, while inline elements, like <span> or <a> , flow within text without breaking the layout.

Modern HTML emphasizes semantic elements, such as <article> , <nav> , and <footer> , which describe the meaning of content rather than just its appearance. Using these correctly improves accessibility, search engine understanding, and overall code clarity.

You will reuse these ideas throughout the chapter.

Prompt : Please explain the difference between semantic HTML and non-semantic HTML with real-world examples and why it matters for accessibility.

Comments in HTML

HTML comments let you leave notes in the source code that are not shown on the page. They look like this: 

<!-- This is a comment -->

Comments are useful for reminders, temporary notes, or explaining examples in teaching code. They are not a way to hide sensitive information, because anyone can still view the page source.

The basic structure of a web page

Every HTML page follows the same overall pattern: 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>My first page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello world</h1>
    <p>This is my first web page.</p>
  </body>
</html>

Each part has a distinct role:

  • <!DOCTYPE html> tells the browser this is modern HTML , meaning standards-based HTML, specifically HTML5. If you omit it, browsers may fall back to quirks mode , which emulates legacy behavior from the early web to maintain compatibility with very old pages. That can lead to inconsistent layout, especially with CSS.
  • <html> wraps the entire document.
  • <head> contains metadata like the title, character encoding, and links to CSS for applying styles.
  • <body> contains everything the user can see.

Nothing visible on the page goes outside <body> . The page title is defined in <head> and usually appears in the browser tab.

Prompt : Please show me examples of good and bad HTML structure and explain what makes one better than the other.

Try it out!

Use your favorite text editor to create a file named myfirstpage.html . Copy the previous HTML into the file and save it. Then open the file in your preferred web browser. Compare the file in your text editor and browser side-by-side, as shown in Figure 2.1 :

Instead of a plain text editor and a web browser, you can also try out your work using VS Code and its Live Preview extension, as shown in Figure 2.2 and Figure 2.3 :

For the rest of this book, I recommend using VS Code with Live Preview, since it gives immediate feedback as you work and matches the workflow used in later chapters.

Prompt : Please show me the HTML for a basic web page with examples of headings, paragraphs, and lists, so that I can learn about how web pages are structured, with an explanation of all the elements.

Headings give content hierarchy

Headings define document structure. Their visual size is a styling decision. The font family and font size for each heading level will be applied using CSS later and do not have to match the level number!

HTML has six heading levels: 

<h1>Main page title</h1>
<h2>Section title</h2>
<h3>Subsection title</h3>
<h4>Sub-subsection title</h4>
<h5>Sub-sub-subsection title</h5>
<h6>Sub-sub-sub-subsection title</h6>

Key beginner rule:

  • <h1> is the most important heading on the page
  • <h2> is a section inside that page
  • <h3> is a subsection inside an <h2>

Treat headings as part of the page outline, not as a way to pick a bigger font.

Search engines, screen readers, and accessibility tools rely heavily on correct heading structure. Using headings purely for visual effect is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

Paragraphs hold readable text

Normal text belongs in paragraphs: 

<p>This is a paragraph of text.</p>

Browsers automatically add spacing between paragraphs.

You do not press Enter repeatedly like in Word. In fact, extra whitespace characters like carriage returns, tabs, and spaces are ignored when rendering HTML in a browser!

HTML is about meaning, not layout.

Links connect the web

Links are what connect pages into the web: 

<a href="https://example.com">Visit Example Website</a>

Here:

  • <a> stands for anchor
  • href is the destination
  • The text between the tags is what users click on

Links can point to:

  • Other websites
  • Other pages on the same site
  • Sections within the same page

Without links, HTML pages are just isolated documents.

Images add visual content

Images are embedded using the <img> element: 

<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A photo of a cat">

Note the following about the preceding code:

  • <img> has no closing tag
  • src is the image file location
  • alt describes the image in words

    <img> is a void element, which means it has no closing tag because it doesn’t wrap any other content or contain nested elements. Other void elements you’ll encounter include <br> (line break), <hr> (horizontal rule), and <input> for forms. While <img> does not need a closing tag, it does need certain attributes to be considered well-formed and accessible, like src and alt .

The alt text is important because it carries meaning when the image cannot. Screen readers rely on it. Search engines read it. If the image fails to load, the text still communicates meaning.

HTML treats images as content, not decoration. Decorative images, such as using emojis as custom bullets in lists, are usually handled in CSS.

Prompt : Please show me how to write accessible HTML for images, links, and forms.

Lists group related items

HTML supports two main list types.

Unordered lists use the <ul> tag: 

<ul>
  <li>Milk</li>
  <li>Bread</li>
  <li>Eggs</li>
</ul>

This means a list in which order does not matter.

Ordered lists use the <ol> tag: 

<ol>
  <li>Preheat the oven</li>
  <li>Mix ingredients</li>
  <li>Bake for 30 minutes</li>
</ol>

This means steps in a specific sequence .

Each list item lives inside <li> .

Tables structure data, not layout

Tables are for data, not page layout: 

<table>
  <tr>
    <th>Name</th>
    <th>Age</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Alex</td>
    <td>32</td>
  </tr>
</table>

Conceptually:

  • <table> wraps the data
  • <tr> is a table row
  • <th> is a table header cell
  • <td> is a table data cell

Tables are best when showing:

  • Prices
  • Schedules
  • Statistics
  • Comparisons

Using tables to position content for layout is an outdated practice and causes accessibility problems.

HTML elements nest inside one another

HTML elements form a tree structure.

Example: 

<body>
  <section>
    <h2>About me</h2>
    <p>I write books.</p>
  </section>
</body>

Here:

  • <section> lives inside <body>
  • <h2> and <p> live inside <section>

This nesting is how browsers understand relationships between content.

Prompt : Please give me examples of incorrectly nested HTML and explain why they break things.

Using <div> as a generic container

Sometimes you need to group several pieces of content together without adding any specific meaning. That is what the <div> element is for.

A <div> is a generic block-level container. It does not tell the browser or a screen reader what the content means. It simply groups content together.

For example: 

<div>
  <h2>About this book</h2>
  <p>This book teaches web development with AI as a learning partner.</p>
</div>

This can be useful when you want to style or script a group of elements later with CSS or JavaScript.

But <div> should not be your first choice when a semantic element fits better. If the content is a section of the page, use <section> . If it is navigation, use <nav> . If it is a paragraph, use <p> . If it is the page footer, use <footer> .

A good beginner rule is this: use <div> when you need a container, not when you need meaning. A page full of <div> elements can still work, but it tells humans and tools much less about the structure of the content. Semantic elements make your HTML easier to read, easier to maintain, and more accessible.

Prompt : Please show me three examples where <div> is appropriate and three where a semantic element would be better.

HTML describes meaning, not appearance

For beginners, this distinction makes the rest of the web technology stack easier to understand.

HTML answers questions like:

  • Is this a heading?
  • Is this a paragraph?
  • Is this navigation?
  • Is this a list of items?
  • Is this tabular data?

HTML does not answer:

  • Should this be blue?
  • Should this be centered?
  • Should this animate?

That separation is deliberate. It keeps the web flexible, accessible, and device-independent.

Good practice : Do not try to memorize every HTML tag. Start by asking what each piece of content is. Is it the main heading? A paragraph? A navigation link? A list of steps? A table of data? Once you can answer those questions, the tags become easier to choose, and AI-generated HTML becomes easier to review.

Prompt : What are ARIA attributes and when should beginners care about them?

What good structure gives you

When HTML is written properly:

  • Browsers can display it correctly on any screen size
  • Search engines understand the content
  • Screen readers can navigate the page
  • CSS and JavaScript become easier to apply later

A page can look fine in a browser while still having poor structure or accessibility.

Well-structured HTML is easier to maintain. Bad HTML creates maintenance problems almost immediately.

Prompt : How do search engines use HTML structure to understand a page?

HTML DOM (document object model)

The HTML DOM ( Document Object Model ) is how the browser represents an HTML page internally after it has been loaded. Instead of thinking of your page as plain text, the browser turns it into a tree of objects that it can understand, manipulate, and render.

Let’s see how it works with a simple HTML example: 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>My Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello</h1>
    <p>This is a paragraph.</p>
  </body>
</html>

When the browser reads the preceding code, it does not keep it as raw text. It parses the HTML and builds a tree structure, where each element becomes a node: 

Document
 └── html
      ├── head
      │    └── title
      │         └── "My Page"
      └── body
           ├── h1
           │    └── "Hello"
           └── p
                └── "This is a paragraph."

Here is how to think about this:

  • Document is the root of everything
  • Each HTML element becomes a node in the tree
  • Elements can have child nodes (like <body> containing <h1> and <p> )
  • Text inside elements also becomes nodes

This structure reflects the nesting you write in HTML. If you nest elements incorrectly, the DOM will also be incorrect, which can lead to confusing behavior.

What the browser actually does (step by step):

  1. It downloads the HTML file
  2. It reads it from top to bottom
  3. It parses each tag and creates nodes
  4. It builds the DOM tree in memory
  5. It uses that tree to render the page

The DOM is not just for display. CSS uses the DOM to decide what to style, and JavaScript uses the DOM to read and change the page dynamically after the page is initially rendered. For example, JavaScript can do things like:

  • Change text inside <h1>
  • Add new elements
  • Remove elements
  • Respond to user actions

HTML is the source document. The DOM is the browser’s live tree built from that document. Once the page is loaded, the browser works with the DOM, not your original HTML file. The DOM is the browser’s internal representation of your HTML as a tree of objects. If your HTML structure is clean and logical, the DOM will be easy to work with. This is why logical thinking about structure matters more than raw typing speed.

The beginner takeaway

If you remember only one thing from this chapter, it should be this:

HTML is about what content is, not how it looks.

Once you understand that distinction, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript make more sense as separate tools.

Prompt : Please show me 10 common beginner HTML mistakes and how to fix them.

Enough theory, let’s do something practical and build a more complete web page.

Building a basic web page

In this section, you’re going to make a tiny about me page, then watch it update instantly as you edit it.

Build a web page in VS code and preview it live

Create a project folder:

  1. Make a new folder on your computer called about-me-webpage
  2. Inside it, create another folder called images

Your folder structure will look like this: 

about-me-webpage/
  images/

Open the about-me-webpage folder in VS Code:

  1. Open VS Code.
  2. Go to File | Open Folder...
  3. Choose about-me-webpage.

    Opening the folder (not just a single file) is important because live preview tools behave better when VS Code knows what your project root is.

  1. If you see a warning about trusting the authors of files in this folder, check the box and click the Yes, I trust the authors button, as shown in Figure 2.4 :

Figure 2.4: Trusting the authors of files in this folder in VS Code

  1. In VS Code Explorer (left side), click New File , and name it index.html , as shown in Figure 2.5 :

Figure 2.5: VS Code Explorer and its New File button

  1. Add the following HTML to the empty file (this example includes everything you’ve learned with important elements highlighted). Paste this into index.html :

This HTML file is available from the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/Code/Chapter02/about-me-webpage/index.html 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" 
          content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <title>Mark's First Web Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Mark's First Web Page</h1>
    <p>
      Welcome! This page is a simple example of HTML structure: headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, and a table.
    </p>
    <h2>About this page</h2>
    <p>
      HTML tells the browser what each piece of content <em>is</em>.
      Styling comes later (that's CSS), and interactivity comes later (that's JavaScript).
    </p>
    <h2>Useful link</h2>
    <p>
      Here's a link to learn more about HTML:
      <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML">MDN Web Docs: HTML</a>.
    </p>
    <h2>Image</h2>
    <p>
      Below is an image. You can use a web image URL, or a local image file.
      The <strong>alt</strong> text describes the image for screen readers and when the image can't load.
    </p>
    <!-- Option A: Use a local image -->
    <!-- Save an image as images/profile.jpg and use this: -->
    <!-- <img src="images/profile.jpg" alt="A friendly profile photo"> -->
    <!-- Option B: Use a placeholder image from the web -->
    <img
      src="https://via.placeholder.com/640x240.png?text=My+First+Image"
      alt="A placeholder banner that says My First Image"
    >
    <h2>Lists</h2>
    <p>Unordered list (a list where the order doesn't matter):</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Headings organize the page</li>
      <li>Paragraphs hold normal text</li>
      <li>Links connect pages together</li>
    </ul>
    <p>Ordered list (a list of steps):</p>
    <ol>
      <li>Create a folder for your project</li>
      <li>Add an <code>index.html</code> file</li>
      <li>Open it with Live Preview</li>
    </ol>
    <h2>Table</h2>
    <p>
      Tables are for data. Here's a tiny "learning plan" table:
    </p>
    <table>
      <thead>
        <tr>
          <th>Topic</th>
          <th>What you'll practice</th>
          <th>Time (minutes)</th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr>
          <td>Headings</td>
          <td>Page outline and sections</td>
          <td>10</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
          <td>Links</td>
          <td>Link to another page</td>
          <td>10</td>
        </tr>
        <tr>
          <td>Images</td>
          <td>Add alt text</td>
          <td>10</td>
        </tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
    <h2>Next idea</h2>
    <p>
      Try editing the text above and watch the preview update instantly.
      When you're ready, you can add CSS to make it look nicer.
    </p>
  </body>
</html>

Note the following about the preceding code:

  • Document structure: <!DOCTYPE html> , <html> , <head> , <title> , <body>
  • Headings: <h1> , <h2>
  • Paragraphs: <p>
  • Links: <a href="...">
  • Images: <img src="..." alt="...">

If you see a broken image icon instead of the picture, it may be because the external image service is temporarily unavailable. Your HTML is still correct. Try switching to Option A which uses a local image file by saving any image to the correct path and filename images/profile.jpg and uncomment the local <img> element.

  • Lists: <ul> + <li> , and <ol> + <li>
  • Tables: <table> , <thead> , <tbody> , <tr> , <th> , <td>

    Good practice : The viewport meta tag is considered an standard part of any HTML document and is required for pages to render correctly on mobile devices. Without it, mobile browsers will render the page at a desktop-width viewport and then scale it down, making text unreadable. Tables should be divided into a heading row (a <thead> with a <tr> element and nested <th> header column elements) and data rows (a <tbody> with one or more <tr> elements with nested <td> datum column elements).

Generating bitmap images for web pages

Up to this point, you have been working with image files that already exist. In real projects, you often need images before you have a designer, a photo library, or final assets.

Image generation tools are useful for this purpose especially as placeholders.

Tools such as Google’s Nano Banana and ChatGPT Images can generate bitmap images from text descriptions. You can use them to create:

  • Placeholder images while building your layout
  • Hero images for landing pages
  • Illustrations for blog posts or product pages
  • Simple icons or visual accents

This gives you something to design around before the final artwork exists.

On April 21, 2026, OpenAI announced ChatGPT Images 2.0 with many improvements: https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-images-2-0/

The images generated by these tools are usually bitmap images, meaning they are made of pixels.

Common bitmap formats include:

  • JPEG is good for photos
  • PNG is good for transparency and sharp edges
  • WebP is a format with good compression

When you are building a page layout, you often just need something that looks reasonable.

For example, you might prompt an image generator with: 

Please create a simple hero image with a soft blue gradient background, abstract shapes, clean and minimal, suitable for a tech website.

The result does not need to be perfect. It just needs to fill the space to give the page visual structure and help you think about layout and spacing. This is much better than leaving empty space or using a broken image link.

A hero image is the large visual at the top of a page. It sets the tone for everything that follows.

For example, for a survey app landing page, you might generate something like: 

Please create a web app hero image showing a dashboard with charts and polls, clean UI, light background, friendly colors, no text.

A few practical tips for hero images:

  • Avoid putting important text in the image itself; use real HTML text instead
  • Keep the composition simple, so it works at different screen sizes
  • Prefer wide, horizontal images for hero sections

Generated images are useful but remember that generated images can sometimes include visual artifacts or odd details. Look at them critically before using them.

Bitmap images are not always the best choice. For diagrams, icons, and anything that needs to scale cleanly or animate, vector graphics are usually better.

In Chapter 4 , Drawing Scalable Graphics , you will learn about SVG, which is better than bitmaps for diagrams, charts, icons, animations, and dynamic graphics that change with data. In this book’s survey project, SVG will be especially useful for rendering charts and visualizing results.

Use generated images to support the page, not to distract from it. A useful image fits the content, the layout, and the purpose of the page.

Try these quick edits to prove it’s live

While the preview is open:

  • Change the <h1> and <title> text to something else
  • Add a new list item: <li>I can preview changes instantly</li>
  • Edit the table by changing a time value from 10 to 15

You’ve created a basic web page and used lots of different HTML elements. You could create a full website with read-only content but it would be static. One of the most common ways to make a website interactive is to provide forms for a visitor to fill in and then submit. These could be login forms for authenticating a visitor, or forms to create or edit data.

Let’s look at how you can create web pages with forms and various input elements.

Working with forms and inputs

So far, your page has been read-only . Forms are how a user types information into a page and sends it somewhere, like a contact form, login screen, newsletter signup, checkout, and so on.

At the center of this is the <form> element, which wraps your input controls (text boxes, dropdowns, buttons) and defines how the browser should submit the data.

In this section, you’re going to:

  1. Create a new page called contact.html with a contact form
  2. Link to it from your index.html About Me page

Create contact.html

In VS Code, create a new file in the same folder as index.html : contact.html .

Paste this in:

This HTML file is available from the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/Code/Chapter02/about-me-webpage/contact.html 

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>Contact Me</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Contact Me</h1>
    <p>
      Use this form to send me a message. For now, it doesn't actually send email.
      It demonstrates how forms collect data and submit it to a server.
    </p>
    <form action="/contact" method="post">
      <h2>Your details</h2>
      <p>
        <label for="fullName">Full name</label><br>
        <input type="text" id="fullName" name="fullName" required>
      </p>
      <p>
        <label for="email">Email address</label><br>
        <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
      </p>
      <p>
        <label for="phone">Phone (optional)</label><br>
        <input type="tel" id="phone" name="phone">
      </p>
      <h2>Your message</h2>
      <p>
        <label for="topic">Topic</label><br>
        <select id="topic" name="topic">
          <option value="question">Question</option>
          <option value="feedback">Feedback</option>
          <option value="business">Business inquiry</option>
        </select>
      </p>
      <p>
        <label for="message">Message</label><br>
        <textarea id="message" name="message" rows="6" cols="40" required></textarea>
      </p>
      <h2>Preferences</h2>
      <p>
        Preferred contact method:
        <br>
        <input type="radio" id="contactEmail" name="preferredContact" value="email" checked>
        <label for="contactEmail">Email</label>
        <br>
        <input type="radio" id="contactPhone" name="preferredContact" value="phone">
        <label for="contactPhone">Phone</label>
      </p>
      <p>
        <input type="checkbox" id="newsletter" name="newsletter" value="yes">
        <label for="newsletter">Send me occasional updates</label>
      </p>
      <p>
        <button type="submit">Send message</button>
        <button type="reset">Clear form</button>
      </p>
    </form>
    <p>
      <a href="index.html">Back to About Me</a>
    </p>
  </body>
</html>

A few things to notice:

  • The <form> has action="/contact" and method="post"
    • action is the URL the browser sends the form data to
    • method="post" sends the data in the request body; get (the default) appends it to the URL after ?
  • Every control that should be submitted has a name="..." . If you forget name, the value won’t be included in the submitted data.
  • Each text field is labeled using <label for="..."> that matches the input’s id . This improves both usability and accessibility.

Link to the contact form from index.html

Open your existing index.html and add a link somewhere sensible, for example, under your Useful link section or near the bottom.

For example: 

<h2>Contact</h2>
<p>
  Want to get in touch?
  <a href="contact.html">Go to my contact form</a>.
</p>

Because contact.html is in the same folder as index.html , a simple relative link like just the HTML filename works. Alternatively, you could specify an absolute link using a full URL: https://example.com/contact.html .

An absolute link is the full address of a resource, like a web page, that works regardless of the current page’s location. A relative link is a shorter address based on the current page’s location. If I am in Alaska and I want to send a letter to someone in Scotland, I would need to use their full, or absolute, address. If I wanted to send a letter to someone on my street, I could hand it to a neighbor and ask them to give it to “Bob at number 23.” This is their address relative to another address on the same street. To send it to someone in the same city, we might need to use their street name too. To send it to someone in the same state, we would need to include their city name as well. A resource like a web page has one absolute address, and many relative addresses depending on how close you already are to their location.

Try it out in live preview

Now we can see the results in Live Preview:

  1. Open index.html and start Live Preview , as shown in Figure 2.6 :

Figure 2.6: Live Preview of the link to the contact form

  1. Click the Go to my contact form link
  2. Fill in the form and click Send message

What you’ll likely see right now:

  • If you leave required fields empty, the browser will block submission and prompt you. (That’s HTML’s built-in validation.)
  • If it does submit, you might get a Cannot POST /contact -style message, or a 404 , or some not found response, as shown in Figure 2.7 :

Figure 2.7: A file not found message when you do not have a server to process a form

This error appears because your browser is trying to send the form data to a server at /contact , but no server is running to receive it yet. This is expected at this stage because you have only built the HTML page, not the server that processes the form.

You’ve just hit the boundary between frontend (HTML) and backend (server code) web development. You will learn how to process form submissions in Chapter 9 , Django – Web Development on the Backend .

</label>

You’ll see lots more input types out there, but if a beginner gets comfortable with this set, they can build most basic forms.

What “posting back to the web server” means

When the user clicks the Send button, the browser takes all the form controls that have a name and sends them as an HTTP request to the URL in the action.

There are two common ways to submit the data:

  • GET (default): the form data is appended to the URL after ? This is good for searches and filters where you want a shareable URL.
  • POST : the form data is sent in the request body. This is common for contact forms, logins, or anything that changes server state, like a form for editing customer or order data.

On the server side (you’ll do this later with Django), your web app would:

  1. Receive the request at something like /contact
  2. Read the submitted fields (name/value pairs)
  3. Validate them (for real, not just browser validation)
  4. Do something useful:
    • Store it in a database
    • Send an email
    • Create a support ticket
  5. Return a response page (like Thanks, message received! )

At this stage, you’re only building the HTML user interface. Server-side processing comes later.

Prompt : Please show what form data looks like when it is submitted from a browser including the difference between GET and POST with real HTTP examples.

14–16 correct : You’ve genuinely understood HTML structure. Move on.

10–13 correct : Solid understanding, but skim the chapter once more.

Below 10 : Re-read slowly. HTML will click if you focus on meaning, not syntax.

Create a custom quiz

Prompt : Please quiz me about the new tags introduced with HTML5. Focus mainly on understanding the concepts rather than memorizing exact syntax.

Mini-challenge: build a “Workshop Signup” website

You are creating a small website for a one-day workshop called Introduction to Web Development . The site has two pages:

  • A Workshop Info page that explains the event
  • A Signup page where users register their interest

You are only allowed to use HTML. No CSS. No JavaScript. Focus on structure and meaning.

Page 1: workshop.html (workshop info)

Create a file called workshop.html that includes the document structure:

  • <!DOCTYPE html>
  • <html> , <head> , <body>
  • A <title> that matches the page’s purpose

The requirements for the page content are:

  • Main heading: Use one <h1> for the workshop title.
  • Introduction paragraph: Describe what the workshop is about in plain text.
  • Image: Add an image banner for the workshop. Include meaningful alt text. You may use a placeholder image URL.
  • Agenda section: Use a <h2> heading.
  • Include an ordered list of workshop sessions (at least four items).
  • What you’ll learn section: Use an <h2> heading. Include an unordered list of skills or topics.
  • Schedule table: Use an <h2> heading. Include a <table> with columns for: Time, Topic, Format (Lecture, Hands-on, Break).
  • Add a link to the signup page: <a href="signup.html">Sign up for the workshop</a> .

Page 2: signup.html (workshop sign up)

Create a file called signup.html that includes the document structure:

  • Proper <head> and <body>
  • A clear page <title>

The requirements for the form are:

  • Your page must include a <form> element with method="post" and a realistic action value (for example /signup ).
  • Inside the form, include:
    • Personal details like full name (text input, required) and email address (email input, required).
    • Experience level as a set of radio buttons: Beginner, Some experience, Advanced. (All radio buttons must share the same name to be a group.)
    • Topics of interest with at least three checkboxes (for example HTML, CSS, Python, JavaScript).
    • Additional notes as a <textarea> for comments or questions.
    • Submit button.
  • Navigation with a link back to workshop.html.

Rules of the challenge

  • Every input that should be submitted must have a name
  • Every form control must have a <label> element
  • Headings must follow a logical order
  • Tables are for data only
  • Do not use <div> to replace meaningful elements you’ve already learned

If you want to push a little further:

  • Add required to appropriate inputs
  • Add a <select> dropdown for How did you hear about this workshop?
  • Add placeholder text to text inputs

Try submitting the form in Live Preview and observe what happens.

You’ve completed the challenge successfully if:

  • Both pages open correctly in Live Preview
  • The link from workshop.html to signup.html works
  • The form enforces required fields
  • Submitting the form produces a browser response (even if it errors)

    A solution to this mini-challenge can be found in the book’s GitHub repository at the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/code/chapter02/workshop-challenge/

What this challenge checks

This exercise proves you understand that:

  • HTML defines structure, not styling
  • Pages connect through links
  • Forms collect and submit data
  • Tables communicate structured information

While HTML specializes in web content, it is just one of several markup languages, and understanding related technologies like XML and SVG helps round out how structured data and graphics are represented on the web. Let’s learn about those languages next.

Other markup languages

HTML is the markup language most closely associated with the web, but it belongs to a wider family of languages that use tags to describe content. Understanding this family will help you see that HTML isn’t random or magical. It’s one practical solution that emerged from a longer history.

What “markup language” means

A markup language is a system for adding annotations to text so that a computer can understand what different parts of that text represent. In other words, markup answers questions like:

  • Is this text a heading or a paragraph?
  • Is this a list item or a table cell?
  • Is this content data, structure, or metadata?

Markup languages do not execute logic. They describe structure and meaning. That puts HTML in the same conceptual category as languages like XAML and SVG.

HTML is a domain-specific markup language designed for one job: describing documents meant to be viewed in a web browser.

HTML is intentionally forgiving. Browsers try very hard to display something sensible even if the markup is imperfect. That design choice is one of the reasons the web spread so quickly.

XML ( eXtensible Markup Language ) came later and took a different approach. Where HTML is opinionated and forgiving, XML is strict about syntax, extensible (you define your own tags), and focused on data, not presentation.

An example of XML is shown in the following code: 

<book>
  <title>Python Programming</title>
  <author>Mark</author>
  <pages>320</pages>
</book>

There are some key differences between XML and HTML:

  • Every tag must be closed either with a closing tag ( <book>...</book> ) or as a self-closing tag ( <br /> ) because, unlike HTML5, which allows unclosed void elements, XML will not allow them
  • Tags must be properly nested
  • There is no predefined set of tags
  • XML does not define how things should look

XML is commonly used for configuration files, data interchange, document formats, and APIs (especially historically).

Prompt : Please explain why HTML is forgiving but XML is strict, with examples.

SVG: markup for graphics

SVG ( Scalable Vector Graphics ) is another markup language, but for graphics instead of documents. SVG uses tags to describe shapes, paths, text, and transformations, as shown in the following code: 

<svg width="100" height="100">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" />
</svg>

There are important things to understand about SVG:

  • It is XML-based
  • It describes what the graphic is , not how to draw pixels
  • It scales cleanly at any resolution

SVG can be embedded directly inside HTML documents, which is why learning HTML structure makes SVG easier to understand later. You will learn about SVG in Chapter 4 , SVG – Drawing Scalable Graphics .

A very short history of markup languages

HTML was not the first markup language:

  1. Early document systems based on Standard Generalized Markup Language ( SGML ) inspired structured markup long before the web. It is the grandparent of most markup languages, including HTML, XML, and anything derived from them. SGML is a meta-language, not a markup language in the everyday sense. That means SGML does not define a fixed set of tags. Instead, it defines rules for creating your own markup languages.
  2. HTML was created to describe scientific documents with links. As browsers became more powerful, and became important for commerce and industry, HTML grew features. HTML is an SGML application.
  3. XML emerged to provide a strict, general-purpose markup format. XML is a simplified descendant of SGML.
  4. SVG emerged to describe graphics in a resolution-independent way. SVG inherits SGML ideas via XML.
  5. XAML ( Extensible Application Markup Language ) is a markup language created by Microsoft for defining user interfaces in desktop and cross-platform applications, rather than web pages. XAML is most commonly used with WPF ( Windows Presentation Foundation ), WinUI, .NET MAUI, and Avalonia.

They are not competitors. They are variations on the same idea: structured markup with meaning, applied to different domains.

Prompt : Where does XHTML fit in the history of markup languages?

Why beginners should care

HTML is not unique because it uses tags. It’s unique because it uses markup to describe documents meant for the web. Other markup languages exist for other jobs.

HTML just happens to be the one that holds the web together.

SGML is not something you learn to use. It is something you learn about. It’s the root of the markup family tree. Everything else makes more sense once you know where it came from.

References and resources

Let’s review the official HTML documentation and references.

MDN web docs (beginners should start here)

MDN Web Docs is the best HTML documentation on the internet for learning and day-to-day reference. It is maintained by Mozilla with contributions from browser vendors and the web community.

  • Homepage: https://developer.mozilla.org/
  • HTML overview: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML
  • HTML elements reference: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element
  • Forms and input elements: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Forms , https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/form , and https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/input

MDN is so good because it is written for humans, not lawyers, with uncomplicated examples, and it explains why, not just what. It is kept in sync with real browser behavior.

Good practice : If a beginner uses only one documentation site while learning HTML, it should be MDN.

W3C HTML specification (official but not beginner friendly)

The World Wide Web Consortium ( W3C ) publishes the official HTML specifications. This is the formal definition of how HTML works at a standards level.

  • HTML specification landing page: https://www.w3.org/TR/html/
  • Living HTML standard (WHATWG, see below): https://html.spec.whatwg.org/

The specification is written for browser implementers like the programmers at Microsoft, Google, and Apple, who build rendering engines. It is not written to teach HTML. It is dense, precise, and unforgiving.

This is reference material, not learning material. You don’t read it cover to cover. You look things up when you need exact behavior.

WHATWG HTML living standard

Most browsers now follow the WHATWG HTML Living Standard, which evolves continuously instead of being frozen into versions.

HTML Living Standard: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/

For current browser behavior, this is the main specification to check.

Again, this is not beginner reading. It’s for checking edge cases, resolving ambiguity, and understanding how browsers really behave.

How beginners should actually use these resources

A practical approach is to start with MDN, build a small example, and consult the specification only when needed:

  • Concepts
  • Examples
  • Best practices

Then get your hands dirty by building something:

  • Make mistakes
  • Break things
  • Fix them

Only then glance at the official specifications if:

  • Browser behavior seems odd
  • You need absolute precision
  • You’re curious how the machinery works

For learning HTML, use MDN Web Docs. It explains HTML the way humans think.

The W3C and WHATWG specifications define how browsers work, but they are not teaching material. Treat them as reference manuals, not tutorials.

Summary

In this chapter, you learned the following:

  • HTML describes the structure and meaning of content, not how it looks
  • An HTML document is built from elements, which are made of tags and content
  • Attributes provide additional information that configures how elements behave
  • Headings create a logical outline of a page and should reflect meaning, not appearance
  • Paragraphs, lists, links, images, and tables represent different types of content
  • Elements can be nested to form a hierarchical structure that browsers interpret as a tree
  • Block-level elements structure layout, while inline elements flow within text
  • Semantic HTML improves accessibility, search engine understanding, and maintainability
  • Forms allow users to input data and submit it to a server using GET or POST
  • Every form control must have a name to be included in submitted data
  • HTML is forgiving and designed for documents, unlike stricter markup languages like XML
  • SVG uses markup to describe scalable graphics and can be embedded in HTML
  • Good HTML creates a strong starting point for CSS styling and JavaScript interactivity

In the next chapter, you will learn about CSS, a language used to provide styling and layout to the content on a web page.
