7

SQL – Managing Data

Web pages can survive a bit of ugliness. Data models are less forgiving. Once your data is duplicated, inconsistent, or badly related, the whole application starts paying for it.

This chapter introduces SQL and relational databases using SQLite and a small sample database. The goal is not to turn you into a database administrator. It is to help you understand how structured data is stored, related, queried, and changed.

You will start with the basic ideas behind relational databases: tables, rows, columns, keys, relationships, NULL , and constraints. Then you will set up SQLite, inspect the sample database, and write real queries with SELECT , WHERE , ORDER BY , JOIN , GROUP BY , and HAVING . After that, you will modify data with INSERT , UPDATE , and DELETE , look at transactions, and finish with a practical introduction to indexes and performance.

By the end of this chapter, you should understand how relational databases store and connect related facts. Learning SQL syntax is important, but the bigger skill is learning to ask precise questions about data: what exists, how pieces relate, what must always be true, and what the application needs to answer.

In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:

  • Introduction to SQL and databases
  • Setting up SQLite and a sample database
  • Writing queries and joining tables
  • Modifying data
  • Improving performance with indexes

Suggested chatbot prompts with example responses for this chapter can be found at the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/prompts/ch07-sql/readme.md

Introduction to SQL and databases

We should start by answering the obvious question.

What is a database?

SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQL Server are database engines. SQL is the common language you use to talk to them. Each engine has its own extensions and quirks, but the core SQL concepts are shared.

A database is an organized system for storing data so it can be retrieved, updated, and kept consistent over time. In a relational database, data is stored in tables. Each table represents one kind of thing. For example, films, TV shows, actors, or episodes.

A table is made up of rows and columns . Each row represents a single record, such as one film or one person. Each column represents a single attribute of that record, such as a title, release year, or birth year. Every table has a primary key , which uniquely identifies each row. This is how the database keeps track of individual records without relying on names or other values that might change.

Relational databases are built around relationships between tables. Instead of duplicating data, tables reference each other using foreign keys . For example, an episode row does not repeat the show’s name and release year. Instead, it stores a reference to the show’s primary key. This keeps data consistent and avoids subtle bugs where the same fact exists in multiple places with slightly different values.

SQL is a language for asking for data and shaping the result. SQL stands for Structured Query Language , but the word query is a little too narrow. SQL is used not only to read data, but also to insert it, update it, delete it, and define the structure of the database itself. Subsets of SQL include the following:

  • Data Definition Language (DDL) : This is used to define or modify the structure of your database. These commands deal with the containers (tables, views, indexes) rather than the actual data inside them. Key Commands: CREATE , ALTER , DROP , TRUNCATE . Analogy: Building the shelves in a library.
  • Data Manipulation Language (DML) : This is the subset you likely use most often. It is used to add, modify, or delete the actual data records (rows) within the tables. Key commands: INSERT , UPDATE , DELETE . Analogy: Putting books onto the shelves or changing their covers.
  • Data Query Language (DQL) : This is focused entirely on retrieving data. While some people group SELECT under DML, it is technically its own category because it doesn’t manipulate the data, it only fetches it. Key command: SELECT . Analogy: Reading a book from the shelf.

There are more sub-languages like Data Control Language ( DCL ), used for security and permissions with key commands like GRANT and REVOKE , and Transaction Control Language ( TCL ) that allows you to group multiple changes into a single transaction that either succeeds or fails as a whole. TCL has key commands like COMMIT and ROLLBACK . But I don’t want to overwhelm you too soon!

Core SQL is not a programming language in the usual sense. The core SQL language has no loops, no if statements in the way Python or JavaScript does, and no concept of step-by-step control flow. You do not tell the database how to find the data. You describe the result you want, and the database engine decides the most efficient way to get there. That is why SQL is called declarative rather than procedural. You declare the outcome, not the procedure. You describe the result you want, not the steps to get there.

Good practice : Although SQL is primarily a declarative language, most real-world database systems also include procedural extensions. Procedural SQL exists because real applications sometimes need logic to do batch processing, data validation, and enforcement beyond simple constraints, and complex transformations during migrations or ETL processes. Procedural SQL keywords include: DECLARE , SET , IF , and WHILE . Use SQL the way it was intended: describe the result you want and let the database engine handle the details. Procedural features exist for edge cases, not as the default approach.

Prompt : I have been told that SQL has no loops, no if -statements in the way Python or JavaScript does, and no concept of step-by-step control flow. But I’ve seen that T-SQL does have those keywords. Why? Do all SQL dialects actually have flow control statements?

SQL dialects

While the ISO/ANSI SQL standard provides a blueprint for how SQL should work, almost every database company adds its own flavor or dialect. These dialects exist because different databases were built for different needs.

Here are a few important dialects and how they differ:

  • T-SQL (Transact-SQL) is used by Microsoft SQL Server. T-SQL is SQL Server’s procedural extension to SQL. It adds variables, control-flow statements, error handling, and stored procedure support, so database code can include more application-like logic. It focuses on high-performance business logic and deep integration with the Windows ecosystem.
  • PL/SQL (Procedural Language/SQL) is used by Oracle Database. This dialect is widely considered the most sophisticated. It is heavily influenced by Ada (a strict programming language used in defense and aviation). It is built for massive, mission-critical enterprise systems where data integrity is the top priority.
  • PostgreSQL (PL/pgSQL) is used by PostgreSQL. PostgreSQL is often favored by people who care about standards and advanced SQL features.

    Prompt : How closely do modern databases actually follow the ISO SQL standard? Explain why SQL dialects diverged and why full portability is difficult in practice.

Why are there so many dialects of SQL? It’s like how English has different accents and slang in London, New York, and Sydney. The core vocabulary is the same, but vendors also add features that make their systems more distinctive and less portable. Additionally, a database designed to run on a phone, such as SQLite, does not need the massive procedural overhead of an enterprise engine like Oracle. Also, many SQL dialects were invented before the official SQL standards were fully established.

How SQL is used to query data

Querying data means asking the database questions. SQL queries usually start with SELECT . A SELECT statement specifies:

  • Which columns you want
  • Which table or tables the data comes from
  • Which rows should be included
  • How the results should be sorted or grouped

For example, a simple query might say: Give me the names and release years of all films released after 2000, sorted by year. The SQL would look something like the following code: 

SELECT title, year FROM films WHERE year > 2000 ORDER BY year

You are not telling the database how to scan the table, which index to use, or how to order operations. You are only describing the result set.

When a database receives a SQL query, it goes through several steps internally. It parses the SQL text, checks that the tables and columns exist, checks permissions, and then builds a query plan. The query plan is the strategy the database chooses to answer the query. Two identical queries can run very differently depending on indexes, data size, and the database engine, but the SQL you write does not change.

SQL is also used to modify data. INSERT adds new rows. UPDATE changes existing rows. DELETE removes rows. These statements follow the same declarative idea. You describe which data should be affected and what the new values should be, and the database handles the mechanics safely and consistently.

For example, to delete all films released before the year 2000, use the following code: 

DELETE FROM films WHERE year < 2000

Why this separation matters

Because SQL describes the result rather than the step-by-step procedure, the same query can be used against a tiny table or a much larger one. Whether it performs well then depends on the schema, indexes, and the database engine’s query plan. Poorly designed tables lead to awkward queries and performance problems, no matter how good your SQL looks.

SQL is a good place to repeat a theme from this book: typing the command is only part of the job. The harder part is deciding what the data should look like before the query exists. Which facts belong together? Which facts should never be repeated? Which values are optional? Which rules should the database enforce even if the application makes a mistake? Get those decisions wrong and every query becomes awkward. Get them right and most of the SQL becomes ordA database is the system that stores and protects your data. SQL is the language you use to ask questions of that system and to change what it contains. Learning SQL means getting used to thinking in sets and relationships, not lines of code executed one after another.

A database is the system that stores and protects your data. SQL is the language you use to ask questions of that system and to change what it contains. Learning SQL means getting used to thinking in sets and relationships, not lines of code executed one after another.

SQL data types

SQL data types define what kind of values a column can store and how the database interprets, compares, and stores those values. Choosing appropriate data types helps keep data valid and queries predictable.

Data types control:

  • Which values are allowed
  • How comparisons and sorting behave
  • How indexes work
  • How arithmetic and functions are applied

A poorly chosen data type can lead to confusing bugs, incorrect comparisons, and unnecessary complexity later.

Most relational databases group data types into a few broad categories.

Numeric types

These store numbers and allow arithmetic. Common examples include:

  • INTEGER or INT : Whole numbers
  • REAL , FLOAT , DOUBLE : Approximate decimal numbers
  • NUMERIC or DECIMAL : Exact decimal numbers, often used for money

    Good practice : Use integer types for counts, IDs, and years. Use exact decimal types for values where precision matters, such as money. Avoid floating-point types for currency.

Text types

These store strings of characters. Common examples include:

  • TEXT : Prioritizes flexibility
  • VARCHAR(n) : Expresses an expectation about maximum length ( n )
  • CHAR(n) : Fixed storage size ( n )

For most application data, TEXT is sufficient unless you have a strong reason to enforce a length limit.

Date and time types

These store dates and timestamps. Common examples include:

  • DATE
  • TIME
  • TIMESTAMP

Use date and time types instead of storing dates as text. They allow correct sorting, comparison, and date-based calculations.

Boolean types

These store true or false values. Common examples include:

  • BOOLEAN
  • INTEGER used as 0 or 1 in some systems

Use a Boolean type when available rather than an integer. It makes the meaning clear and avoids inconsistent conventions like mixing 0 , 1 , true , and false .

Binary types

These store raw binary data. Examples include:

  • BLOB
  • BYTEA

Binary types are used for files, images, or opaque data. They are rarely involved in filtering or joining and are often better stored outside the database unless transactional consistency is required.

SQLite and type affinity

SQLite is more flexible than most databases. It uses a system called type affinity , meaning columns have a preferred type, but the database does not strictly enforce it.

For example, a column declared as INTEGER can still store text. SQLite will try to convert values when possible, but it will not reject mismatched types in many cases.

This flexibility is convenient for learning and prototyping, but it means developer discipline matters more. Using appropriate types and constraints is still important, even if SQLite does not force them.

PostgreSQL and SQL Server, by contrast, enforce data types much more strictly.

Data types show what kind of data belongs in a column. They tell the database and future readers of your schema what kind of data belongs in each column. Choosing clear, appropriate types early makes queries simpler, prevents invalid data, and reduces surprises as your database grows.

Normalization is the next idea, and it is where many beginners first get stuck.

Database schema design

Database schema design is about deciding what data you store, how you structure it, and how pieces of data relate to each other. A well-designed schema makes queries simpler, data more consistent, and applications easier to change over time. A poorly designed one leads to duplication, bugs, and increasingly complex SQL.

Prompt : How do you safely change a database schema once real data exists? Please explain migrations and why they exist even when ALTER TABLE is available. Please include examples of schema design mistakes that are painful to fix later.

A table represents one kind of thing

In a relational database, each table models a single concept. Examples are a user, a film, an episode, or an order. A table should answer one clear question: What is one row in this table? If you cannot explain that in a short sentence, the table is probably doing too much.

A row represents one instance of that thing

Each row is a single record. One user, one film, one episode. Rows should be independent of each other. The database does not care about row order, and your design should not rely on it. Every row must be uniquely identifiable, which is why tables have a primary key. This is usually an integer ID or GUID that never changes, even if the data in the row does.

A column represents one attribute

Columns hold individual facts about the thing the table represents. A column should contain one value of one type. For example, a release year, an email address, or a duration in minutes. Mixing multiple facts into one column, such as storing a comma-separated list of actors in a single text field, makes querying harder and breaks the relational model.

What goes where

Good schema design starts by separating entities from attributes .

If a value describes the thing itself, it belongs in the table for that thing. A film’s title and release year belong in the titles table. If a value describes a relationship between two things, it usually belongs in a separate table. A character name belongs to the relationship between an actor and a film, not to the actor or the film alone.

A useful rule of thumb is this: if a value would have to be repeated for multiple rows, stop and ask whether it should be stored somewhere else and referenced instead. Repeating the same data across multiple rows or tables seems harmless at first, especially in small examples. In real systems, it causes three classic classes of bugs known as anomalies:

  • An insertion anomaly happens when you cannot add a piece of data without also adding unrelated data. For example, if a table mixes films and actors, you might not be able to add a new actor unless they are already linked to a film.
  • An update anomaly occurs when the same value is stored in multiple places and must be changed everywhere. If you update it in one row but miss another, your data becomes inconsistent.
  • A deletion anomaly happens when removing one piece of data accidentally deletes something else you wanted to keep. For instance, deleting the last film an actor appeared in might also remove the only record of that actor.

Normalization exists largely to prevent these problems. Normalization is a systematic way of structuring tables to reduce redundancy and dependency issues, typically by splitting data into related tables and linking them with keys.

You can learn more about the standard normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) and how they eliminate these anomalies at the following links: https://www.guru99.com/database-normalization.html and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database_normalization

Normalization: storing facts once

Normalization is the process of organizing data so that each fact is stored in exactly one place to provide a single source of truth. In practice, this usually means:

  • Creating separate tables for separate concepts
  • Using primary keys to identify rows
  • Using foreign keys to reference related data
  • Removing repeated or derived values

For example, instead of storing a person’s name in every episode they appear in, you store the person once in a person table and reference them from an appearance or credit table. If the person’s name changes, there is exactly one row to update.

Beginners often worry that splitting data into more tables makes querying harder. In reality, the opposite is true over time. Well-designed schemas lead to predictable joins and simpler logic. Poor schemas lead to string parsing, duplicated filters, and fragile assumptions.

Joins exist precisely to recombine normalized data at query time. That is the trade-off relational databases make: store data cleanly and consistently, then reconstruct the views you need using SQL.

Schema design decisions are hard to undo once data exists. Adding a new column is easy. Untangling duplicated data across millions of rows is not. That is why spending time on tables, rows, columns, and relationships early on pays off disproportionately later.

Good database schema design is about respecting what tables, rows, and columns are meant to represent, and resisting the temptation to repeat data for short-term convenience.

Prompt : Please explain normalization vs denormalization with a realistic example and show when denormalization is justified.

Primary and foreign keys

Primary keys and foreign keys are what give a relational database its identity and structure. They answer two fundamental questions: Who is this row? and How does this row relate to others?

Primary keys are for identity

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. It is the database’s notion of identity. No two rows in the same table can share the same primary key value, and a primary key cannot be NULL (meaning unknown or not applicable , which will be explained in more detail in a later section).

In practice, a primary key is usually a single column, often an auto-incrementing integer or a GUID. The actual value rarely matters to humans. What matters is that it is stable and unique. Titles can change, names can be corrected, and emails can be updated, but the primary key stays the same. This is why primary keys should never encode meaning or business logic.

For example, a person’s name is a poor primary key. Names are not unique and they change. An internal person_id is a good primary key because it exists solely to identify the row.

Primary keys also serve as the target for relationships. Other tables point to them to say, This row refers to that row .

In SQLite, declaring a column as INTEGER PRIMARY KEY gives it a special role. The column becomes an alias for the internal rowid , and when you insert a row without providing a value, SQLite automatically assigns a unique integer. In practice, this behaves like an auto-incrementing ID, typically increasing by one each time a new row is added.

It is worth knowing that SQLite also supports an explicit AUTOINCREMENT keyword, but this is rarely needed. Without it, SQLite will usually pick the next highest unused value, which is fast and efficient. With AUTOINCREMENT , SQLite guarantees that it will never reuse a previously issued value, even if rows are deleted, but this comes with a small performance and storage cost. For most applications, INTEGER PRIMARY KEY on its own is the better choice.

Other database systems provide similar features, but with different syntax and behavior. In MySQL, you use the AUTO_INCREMENT attribute to achieve the same effect. In PostgreSQL, older code often uses SERIAL , while modern versions recommend GENERATED AS IDENTITY , which is more flexible and standards compliant. Although the goal is the same across all systems, which is to generate unique numeric identifiers automatically, the exact rules and guarantees can vary slightly, especially around gaps in sequences and reuse of deleted values.

Foreign keys are for relationships

A foreign key is a column in one table that references the primary key of another table. It represents a relationship between two entities.

For example, an episode belongs to a series. The episode table might contain a series_id column that references the primary key of the series table. That series_id is a foreign key.

Foreign keys let the database enforce rules about relationships. With a foreign key in place, the database can prevent:

  • Inserting a row that refers to a non-existent parent
  • Deleting a parent row that still has dependent rows
  • Creating orphaned records that no longer make sense

This enforcement is a major advantage of relational databases over ad-hoc data storage.

One-to-many relationships

The most common relationship is one-to-many. One series has many episodes. One customer has many orders. One author has many books.

In a one-to-many relationship, the foreign key lives on the many side. Each episode row stores the series_id it belongs to. The series table does not need to know how many episodes it has. That information can always be derived by querying the episodes table.

Figure 7.1 shows a classic one-to-many relationship between the people table and the emails table. On the left, the people table stores one row per person, identified by a unique id . On the right, the emails table stores email addresses. Each email row includes a person_id , which links it back to the person it belongs to. The key idea is that one person can have many email addresses, but each email address belongs to only one person:

Figure 7.1: One-to-many relationship

You can see this in the sample data:

  • John Doe (id = 1) has two email addresses: john_doe@gmail.com and jdoe@work.com . Both rows in the emails table have person_id = 1 .
  • Jane Doe (id = 2) has one email: janed@msn.com
  • Mika Jones (id = 3) also has one email: m_jones@gmail.com

So, the relationship works like this:

  • people.id is the primary key
  • emails.person_id is a foreign key
  • The foreign key allows multiple rows in emails to point to the same row in people

The 1---M notation in the diagram reinforces this: one row in people maps to many rows in emails. The duplication lives on the “many” side. The person_id value repeats in the emails table, and that repetition is what creates the relationship.

One-to-one relationship

Figure 7.2 shows a one-to-one relationship between the people table and the notes table.

Each person can have at most one note, and each note belongs to exactly one person. The relationship is shown as 1---1 , meaning there is no duplication on either side.

Figure 7.2: One-to-one relationship

Looking at the data:

  • John Doe (id = 1) is linked to a single note: “Client since 2021” (note id = 1)
  • Jane Doe (id = 2) has no note in this example
  • Mika Jones (id = 3) is linked to: “Met at conference” (note id = 3)

Even though not every person has a note, the rule still holds. No person has more than one note, and no note is shared between people.

In a real schema, this is usually enforced by placing a unique foreign key in the notes table, for example: 

person_id INTEGER UNIQUE

That UNIQUE constraint is what turns a one-to-many structure into a true one-to-one relationship. The foreign key still lives on one side (for example, the notes table), but the uniqueness constraint prevents duplicates, so the relationship cannot expand into many.

Many-to-many relationships

Sometimes both sides can have many related rows. A film can have many actors, and an actor can appear in many films. This cannot be represented with a single foreign key.

Instead, you create a junction table , sometimes called a link table or join table. This table contains at least two foreign keys, one pointing to each side of the relationship. Each row represents one relationship instance.

For example, a credits table might contain film_id and person_id as foreign keys, plus extra columns such as character_name or role .

Figure 7.3 shows a many-to-many relationship between people and addresses , implemented using an intermediate table called people_addresses .

At a conceptual level:

  • A person can have multiple addresses (home, work, and so on)
  • An address can belong to multiple people (a shared household or workplace)

That means neither table can hold a simple foreign key without causing duplication or breaking the model. Instead, the relationship is handled through the people_addresses table.

Figure 7.3: Many-to-many relationship

How the data connects:

  • people.id identifies each person
  • addresses.id identifies each address
  • people_addresses links them using pairs of IDs

Looking at the sample rows:

  • John Doe (id = 1) resides at address 1: 742 Evergreen Terrace
  • Jane Doe (id = 2) is linked to address 1 and address 2 so she shares the home address with John and works at address 2 (100 Main Street)
  • Mika Jones (id = 3) works at address 2 with Jane

A many-to-many relationship cannot be represented directly with a single foreign key. To support many on both sides, you need a separate table that:

  • Stores combinations of related rows
  • Allows multiple entries per person and per address
  • Keeps the schema normalized and avoids duplication

The intermediate table turns one complex many-to-many relationship into two simple one-to-many relationships:

  • people is related to people_addresses
  • addresses is related to people_addresses

This is the standard and correct way to model many-to-many relationships in relational databases.

Referential integrity and cascading rules

Foreign keys are usually defined with rules that say what happens when the referenced row changes. Common options include:

  • RESTRICT or NO ACTION : prevent deletion if related rows exist
  • CASCADE : automatically delete or update related rows
  • SET NULL : keep the row but clear the foreign key

Choosing these rules is a design decision. Cascading deletes can be convenient, but they can also remove large amounts of data very quickly if used carelessly.

NULL values

NULL is one of the most misunderstood concepts in SQL, and many subtle bugs come from treating it like an ordinary value. In SQL, NULL does not mean zero, an empty string, or false. It means unknown or not applicable .

A NULL does not represent data that exists but happens to be blank. It represents the absence of a value. This distinction matters because SQL must account for uncertainty when comparing or filtering data.

Comparisons involving NULL do not behave the way most programmers expect. For example, the following expression is not true : 

universe = NULL

But it is also not false ! It is unknown . This is why SQL has special syntax for checking for NULL : 

universe IS NULL
universe IS NOT NULL

Any time you want to test for missing data, you must use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL .

Three-valued logic

SQL uses three-valued logic, not two-valued logic. A condition can evaluate to: TRUE , FALSE , or UNKNOWN . Any comparison involving NULL produces UNKNOWN , not TRUE or FALSE . For example: 

NULL = 'Star Trek'   evaluates to UNKNOWN
NULL <> 'Star Trek'  evaluates to UNKNOWN
NULL = NULL          evaluates to UNKNOWN

This has a practical consequence: the WHERE clause keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE . Rows where the condition is FALSE or UNKNOWN are excluded. This explains why queries sometimes lose rows unexpectedly when NULL values are involved.

NULL values can also affect joins in subtle ways. Join conditions that rely on equality will not match rows where the join key is NULL , because NULL never equals anything, including another NULL .

This is one reason why foreign key columns are often defined as NOT NULL unless there is a strong modeling reason to allow NULL .

Most NULL bugs come from forgetting that SQL has three truth states, not two, and that UNKNOWN is treated as exclude this row in filters.

.

Prompt : Please show me some common bugs caused by misunderstanding NULL and how to avoid them

Constraints

Constraints are rules enforced by the database to protect the integrity of your data. They act as a safety net that prevents invalid, inconsistent, or nonsensical values from ever being stored. Instead of relying on application code to do the right thing , constraints make the database itself responsible for guarding its own correctness.

Common constraints are shown in Table 7.1 :

Constraint

Description

NOT NULL

Ensures that a column must always have a value. It prevents rows from being inserted or updated with missing data in fields that are required for the record to make sense. For example, a title name, an email address, or a release year usually cannot be NULL . Allowing NULL values in these columns forces every query and every application layer to constantly check for missing values. If a value is genuinely optional, allow NULL . If it is not, say so explicitly in the schema.

UNIQUE

Ensures that no two rows share the same value in a column, or in a combination of columns. It enforces logical uniqueness rather than identity. This is different from a primary key, which enforces row identity. For example, you might allow only one user account per email address, or only one episode number per season. In those cases, the values must be unique within a defined scope. They are especially important in multi-user systems, where two requests can arrive at nearly the same time.

CHECK

Restricts the range or format of values that can be stored in a column. It encodes simple business rules directly into the database. Examples include a release year must be greater than or equal to 1888, a rating must be between 1 and 5, and a status must be one of a fixed set of values. They are not meant to replace complex validation logic, but they are very effective for guarding basic invariants.

FOREIGN KEY

Enforces relationships between tables. It ensures that a value in one table refers to a valid row in another table. For example, an episode cannot reference a season that does not exist, and a credit cannot reference a person that is not in the person table. Foreign keys can also define what happens when related data changes. Common behaviors include preventing deletion, cascading deletes, or setting the reference to NULL .

Table 7.1: Common constraints

Each constraint type solves a different class of problem, but they work best together. NOT NULL ensures required data exists. UNIQUE ensures it is not duplicated. CHECK ensures it makes sense. FOREIGN KEY ensures it relates correctly to other data.

Without constraints, a database is just a passive storage system that accepts whatever it is given. With constraints, the database actively defends the assumptions your application is built on. This reduces bugs, simplifies queries, and makes long-term maintenance significantly easier. Constraints are about preventing bad data.

SQL naming conventions for database objects

Sticking to a consistent naming convention for your database objects will make it easier to maintain. Since most SQL dialects are case-insensitive but preserve case in display, a few conventions have become common to ensure your code remains readable and portable across different systems.

The most widely recommended convention, especially for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite, is lower_snake_case . For example:

  • Table names: user_accounts , order_items , product_categories
  • Column names: first_name , created_at , email

Why? Many SQL engines convert everything to lowercase internally. Using lower_snake_case ensures that your code looks the same in your editor as it does in the database logs.

Some guidelines for naming tables:

  • Tables represent collections of things so use collective or plural names. For example, use a users table instead of a user table. A table is a container for many records.
  • Avoid prefixes. Don’t name tables tbl_users . Database tools already know it’s a table.
  • Be descriptive. If a table stores a relationship between users and groups, name it user_groups rather than mapping_table_1 .
  • Avoid SQL keywords. A table named order would conflict with ORDER BY , a table named group would conflict with GROUP BY , and USER is a keyword in PostgreSQL.

    Good practice : Check your database’s reserved words list when choosing table names. When in doubt, use more descriptive names like user_accounts or customer_orders .

Some guidelines for naming columns:

  • For the column designated as the primary key (row unique identifier), there are two competing schools of thought. You can use the simple id , so every table has a column simply named id . But when joining users and orders, you end up with two columns named id , which can be confusing. Or you can use a prefix like user_id so the primary key column name includes the table name.
  • Prefix Boolean column names with is_ , has_ , or can_ to clarify that the value is true or false . For example, is_active , has_discount , and can_post .
  • For dates and times, include a suffix to indicate if it is a date or a full timestamp. For example, created_at (timestamp), birth_date (date only).

Here are some names to always avoid:

  • Never name a table User , Order , or Group . These are reserved keywords in some dialects of SQL and will require you to use annoying quotes like "User" or square brackets like [User] every time you write a query.
  • Never use spaces in table or column names like Order Date because it will require you to use extra quotes like "Order Date" or square brackets like [Order Date] every time you write a query. Use underscores like order_date .
  • Avoid abbreviations like cust_addr_id . Use customer_address_id . Space is cheap. Time spent decoding abbreviations is not.

    Good practice : Using UPPERCASE for SQL keywords is the most widely accepted convention in the industry. While SQL is case-insensitive (meaning select works the same as SELECT ), writing keywords in uppercase improves visual parsing.

Now, let’s make sure that you have SQLite installed and then set up an example database.

Setting up SQLite and a sample database

SQLite is a small, fast, cross-platform, self-contained Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) that is available in the public domain. It’s the most common RDBMS for mobile platforms such as iOS (iPhone and iPad) and Android. SQLite is the most used database engine in the world, and there are more than one trillion SQLite databases in active use. You can read more about this at https://www.sqlite.org/mostdeployed.html .

I am using SQLite here because it is cross-platform, easy to install, and more than enough for learning core SQL and database design.

Now let’s install SQLite on your computer.

Setting up SQLite CLI tools for Windows

On Windows, we need to download SQLite CLI tools and add the folder for SQLite to the system path so it will be found when we enter commands at a command prompt or terminal:

  1. Start your favorite browser and navigate to https://www.sqlite.org/download.html .
  2. Scroll down the page to the Precompiled Binaries for Windows section.
  3. Click sqlite-tools-win-x64-3510200.zip (the file will probably have a higher version number by the time you read this), as shown in Figure 7.4 :

Figure 7.4: Downloading SQLite for Windows on Intel x64

  1. Extract the ZIP file into a folder named C:\Sqlite . Make sure that the three extracted files, including sqlite3.exe , are directly inside the C:\Sqlite folder, or the executable will not be found later when you try to use it.
  2. In the Windows Start menu, navigate to Settings .
  3. Search for environment and choose Edit the system environment variables . On non-English versions of Windows, please search for the equivalent word in your local language to find the setting.
  4. Click the Environment Variables button.
  5. In System variables , select Path in the list, and then click Edit… .
  6. If C:\Sqlite is not already in the path, then click New , enter C:\Sqlite , and press Enter .
  7. Click OK , then OK , then OK again, and then close Settings .

  8. To confirm that the path to SQLite has been configured correctly, at any command prompt or terminal, enter the following command to start SQLite: 

    sqlite3

  9. Note the result, as shown in the following output: 

    SQLite version 3.51.2 2026-01-09 17:27:48
Enter ".help" for usage hints.
Connected to a transient in-memory database.
Use ".open FILENAME" to reopen on a persistent database.
sqlite>
  10. To exit the SQLite command prompt, do the following:
    • On Windows, press Ctrl + C twice.
    • On macOS, press Ctrl + D .

Setting up SQLite for macOS and Linux

On macOS, SQLite is included in the /usr/bin/ directory as a command-line application named sqlite3 .

On Linux, you can get set up with SQLite using the following command: 

sudo apt-get install sqlite3

SQLite can be downloaded and installed for other OSs from the following link:

https://www.sqlite.org/download.html .
