Writing queries and joining tables

This section focuses on reading data from one or more tables. Writing queries is about asking the database clear questions and getting back predictable, useful results. We will use the Media database you have already created.

Tools for running queries

SQLite has good tooling on every major platform, and you do not need much to get started. Below are the most practical cross-platform options, what they are good at, and when you would use each one.

SQLite command-line tool

The sqlite3 CLI is the reference tool that ships with SQLite itself. It runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows, and it behaves consistently everywhere.

It is worth using because:

  • Zero abstraction between you and SQL
  • Excellent for learning, debugging, and scripting
  • Good for running schema files and seed scripts
  • Makes it very clear what SQL is doing, without UI noise

Typical usage looks like the following command: 

sqlite3 media.db

Then, at the SQLite prompt sqlite> , you enter SQL statements and special commands like .tables (to list all the tables in the database) or like .schema to view schema/structure. For example, enter the following command: 

.tables

You should see a list of the six tables, as shown in the following output: 

credits   episodes  people    roles     seasons   titles

Now show the schema, aka the structure of the titles table, as shown in the following command: 

.schema titles

You should see how the titles table was created, including column names and data types, the primary key, and constraints, as shown in the following output: 

CREATE TABLE titles (
  title_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name         TEXT    NOT NULL,
  kind         TEXT    NOT NULL CHECK (kind IN ('film','series')),
  release_year INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (release_year >= 1888),
  universe     TEXT    NULL,
  UNIQUE(name, release_year)
);

You can also enter just .schema without a table name to see the schemas of all the tables in the database.

Now enter a simple SQL query to return all columns of all rows in the titles table, as shown in the following command: 

SELECT * FROM titles;

You should see the following results: 

1|Star Trek: The Next Generation|series|1987|Star Trek
2|Star Trek|film|2009|Star Trek
3|The Office|series|2005|The Office
4|The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring|film|2001|Middle-earth
5|The Matrix|film|1999|The Matrix

Warning! If you see the SQLite prompt change to ...> then it indicates that you have not completed the SQL statement with a semi-colon so SQLite expects you to continue entering more of SQL. Just enter the ; and it will then run!

This CLI makes the mechanics visible: SQL is text sent to a database engine, and the engine returns rows or an error. For learning, that directness is useful.

SQLiteStudio

SQLiteStudio is a full graphical database browser and editor. It runs on all major platforms and is very beginner-friendly. It is useful early on because you can see the tables, rows, columns, and relationships while you write SQL.

Its main downside is that it can encourage clicking instead of writing SQL if overused. For learning SQL, you want to stay mostly in the query editor, not the table grid.

Let’s explore some SQLiteStudio capabilities:

  1. Start SQLiteStudio .
  2. Navigate to Tools | Open SQL Editor .

  3. In the Query tab editor, enter an example query, as shown in the following code, and then in the toolbar, click the Execute query button, as shown in Figure 7.9 : 

    SELECT * FROM titles;

Figure 7.9: Running a SQL query using SQLiteStudio

SQLiteStudio is not as fussy as the SQLite CLI about terminating every SQL statement with a semi-colon. If you forget it, the query will still run.

VS Code and the SQLite extension

VS Code works well as a lightweight database client when paired with the right extension. Popular extensions allow you to open a SQLite database file directly, browse tables and schemas, run SQL queries inside the editor, and keep SQL files under version control.

This works well when SQL lives alongside application code, migrations, or exercises. It also mirrors how developers actually work in real projects.

The strengths include everything in one editor, SQL scripts saved as files, not ad-hoc queries, easy to rerun and modify queries, and it’s a good fit if you later introduce Django or another backend.

Now let’s make sure you can execute SQL statements using VS Code:

  1. If you haven’t installed the SQLite extension already, start VS Code, navigate to Extensions , search for sqlite , and then click Install on the SQLite extension ( alexcvzz.vscode-sqlite ).
  2. In VS Code, navigate to View | Command Palette... , search for Sqlite: New Query and select it.

  3. In the query editor, enter an example query, as shown in the following code: 

    SELECT * FROM titles;
  4. Right-click in the query editor, select Run Query , select Choose database from file , and then browse to select the Media.db file. (You will only need to do this the first time you run the query so it connects to the database.)
  5. The results will be shown in a second window pane, as shown in Figure 7.10 :

Figure 7.10: Running a SQL query using the SQLite extension for VS Code

Next, we will introduce each important SQL keyword in turn. For any code examples, run them in your preferred tool: the SQLite CLI, SQLiteStudio, or VS Code and its SQLite extension. I recommend trying a mix of all three to see the pros and cons and which you prefer.

SELECT: the shape of a query

Every read query starts with SELECT . A SELECT statement answers four basic questions:

  • What columns do I want? You can list the column names that you want, or use * to mean all of them.
  • Where does the data come from? You must specify which table(s) you want to query.
  • Which rows should be included? You can optionally filter which rows should be included using a WHERE clause.
  • How should the results be ordered or grouped? You can optionally sort the results using an ORDER BY clause.

A minimal query looks like this: 

SELECT name, release_year
FROM titles;

The preceding code asks the database to return two columns from every row in the titles table. The database does not guarantee the order of rows unless you explicitly ask for one.

Good practice : Start each SQL keyword on a new line to make the query easier to scan and understand.

Filtering rows with WHERE

Most queries care about only some rows. The WHERE clause filters the result set, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT name, release_year
FROM titles
WHERE kind = 'film';

This returns only films, excluding TV series. The database evaluates the condition for every row and keeps only those that match.

You can combine conditions using AND and OR , as shown in the following code: 

SELECT name, release_year
FROM titles
WHERE kind = 'film'
  AND release_year >= 2000;

This reads naturally: films released from 2000 onwards.

Sorting results with ORDER BY

If you care about order, you must say so explicitly, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT name, release_year
FROM titles
ORDER BY release_year;

By default, ordering is ascending. You can reverse it, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT name, release_year
FROM titles
ORDER BY release_year DESC;

You can also sort by multiple columns, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT name, kind, release_year
FROM titles
ORDER BY kind, release_year DESC;

This groups films and series together and sorts each group by year.

Limiting the number of rows in the results

When exploring data, it is often useful to limit how many rows you see, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT name, release_year
FROM titles
ORDER BY release_year DESC
LIMIT 3;

This returns only the three most recent titles. This is especially useful with large tables.

Good practice : If a query uses LIMIT and the result matters, it should almost always have an ORDER BY because without ORDER BY, LIMIT does not mean “the first N rows” in any meaningful sense. LIMIT 3 does not mean the first three titles you inserted or the oldest or the newest . It means any three rows .

Selecting calculated values

SQL can return expressions, not just stored columns, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT name,
       release_year,
       release_year + 10 AS ten_year_anniversary
FROM titles;

This does not modify the data. It simply shapes the output. Calculated columns are part of the result set, not the table.

Joining tables: bringing related data together

SQL becomes more useful when you combine data from multiple tables.

For example, episodes belong to seasons, and seasons belong to titles. To list episodes for a specific series, you join those tables together, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT t.name AS series_name,
       s.season_no,
       e.episode_no,
       e.name AS episode_name
FROM titles t
JOIN seasons s  ON s.title_id = t.title_id
JOIN episodes e ON e.season_id = s.season_id
WHERE t.name = 'Star Trek: The Next Generation'
ORDER BY s.season_no, e.episode_no;

Each JOIN keyword connects tables using primary keys and foreign keys. You are not merging tables blindly. You are following relationships defined in the schema.

titles t and seasons s are examples of a table alias. It is shorthand that gives a table a temporary name for the duration of the query. t is an alias for the titles table. For the rest of the query, t and titles mean the same thing.

When queries involve joins, repeating full table names quickly becomes annoying. Also, when multiple tables have columns with the same name, aliases are required to disambiguate.

For example, both titles and seasons contain a title_id column. Without aliases, the database cannot know which one you mean, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT title_id
FROM titles
JOIN seasons ON seasons.title_id = titles.title_id;

The preceding code is ambiguous and will fail.

We can clarify what we mean with table aliases, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT t.title_id
FROM titles t
JOIN seasons s ON s.title_id = t.title_id;

Now the query is unambiguous.

Querying many-to-many relationships

Actors and titles have a many-to-many relationship through the credit table. This table is where the relationship lives.

To list the acting cast of a film we need to join four tables ( credits , titles , people , and roles ), as shown in the following code: 

SELECT t.name AS title,
       p.full_name,
       c.character_name
FROM credits c
JOIN titles  t ON t.title_id = c.title_id
JOIN people  p ON p.person_id = c.person_id
JOIN roles   r ON r.role_id = c.role_id
WHERE t.name = 'The Matrix'
  AND r.role_name = 'actor'
ORDER BY p.full_name;

This query shows why junction tables matter. The character name belongs to the relationship between a person and a title, not to either table on its own.

Types of joins

Joins are how SQL recombines related data stored in separate tables. Each JOIN type answers a slightly different question about how rows from two tables should be matched. The differences matter, because they control which rows appear in the result and which are excluded.

INNER JOIN

An INNER JOIN returns only rows where a match exists in both tables. This is the most commonly used join and is often what people mean when they just say JOIN . In fact, you can just use JOIN instead of the full syntax INNER JOIN , as shown in the following code: 

SELECT t.name, s.season_no
FROM titles t
JOIN season s ON s.title_id = t.title_id;

This returns only titles that actually have seasons. If a title has no seasons, it does not appear at all. Think of INNER JOIN as only where both sides agree .

Prompt : Please show me some examples where moving a condition from WHERE to ON changes the meaning of a LEFT JOIN .

LEFT JOIN (LEFT OUTER JOIN)

A LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, and matching rows from the right table. If there is no match, the right-side columns are returned as NULL : 

SELECT t.name, s.season_no
FROM titles t
LEFT JOIN seasons s ON s.title_id = t.title_id;

This returns every title, even films or series with no seasons. For those rows, season_no will be NULL . LEFT JOIN is used when the left table represents the thing you care about, and the right table is optional.

Good practice : A very common mistake is putting conditions on the right table in the WHERE clause, which turns a LEFT JOIN back into an INNER JOIN . Conditions that apply to the joined table should usually go in the ON clause instead.

RIGHT JOIN (RIGHT OUTER JOIN)

A RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image of a LEFT JOIN . It returns all rows from the right table, and matching rows from the left table: 

SELECT t.name, s.season_no
FROM titles t
RIGHT JOIN seasons s ON s.title_id = t.title_id;

In practice, RIGHT JOIN is rarely needed. The same result can almost always be expressed more clearly by swapping table order and using LEFT JOIN instead. Many teams avoid RIGHT JOIN entirely for readability.

Warning! RIGHT JOIN was added to SQLite in version 3.39.0 back in 2022. If you’re using an older SQLite version or certain tools that bundle older versions, RIGHT JOIN may not work. You can always rewrite a RIGHT JOIN as a LEFT JOIN by swapping the table order.

FULL JOIN (FULL OUTER JOIN)

A FULL JOIN returns:

  • Rows that match on both sides
  • Rows that exist only in the left table
  • Rows that exist only in the right table

Where no match exists, columns from the missing side are NULL . 

SELECT t.name, s.season_no
FROM titles t
FULL JOIN seasons s ON s.title_id = t.title_id;

This is useful for reconciliation and comparison queries, such as finding records that exist in one table but not the other.

Warning! SQLite does not support FULL JOIN directly. In SQLite, it must be simulated with a UNION of LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN logic.

CROSS JOIN

A CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product of two tables. Every row from the first table is paired with every row from the second table. 

SELECT t.name, r.role_name
FROM titles t
CROSS JOIN roles r;

If there are 5 titles and 3 roles, the result has 15 rows.

CROSS JOIN is rarely used accidentally, because the result size grows very quickly. When it is used deliberately, it is usually for generating combinations, test data, or reference matrices.

SELF JOIN

A SELF JOIN is not a separate join type, but a pattern. It is any join where a table is joined to itself using aliases. 

SELECT t1.name, t2.name
FROM titles t1
JOIN titles t2
  ON t1.universe = t2.universe
  AND t1.title_id <> t2.title_id;

This compares rows within the same table. Self joins are common in hierarchies, comparisons, and graph-like relationships.

Prompt : Please explain JOIN s visually using Venn diagrams and explain where those diagrams break down.

To summarize, JOIN s reshape existing data by aligning rows across tables. Understanding which rows survive the join is far more important than memorizing syntax.

Now let’s look at grouping and aggregates like COUNT and SUM .

Aggregates: asking summary questions

SQL is very good at answering questions about groups of rows. Some commonly used functions include the following:

  • COALESCE(expression1, expression2, ...) : returns the first non- NULL value from a list of expressions. You give it two or more values or expressions, and it picks the first one that is not NULL . COALESCE(universe, 'Standalone') means, if universe has a value, use it. If it is NULL, use ‘Standalone’ instead .
  • COUNT(*) : Returns the number of rows in the result set or in each group. It counts rows, not values, and it includes rows even if some columns contain NULL .

    Prompt : Please explain why COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) produce different results with examples.

For example, how many titles exist per universe? We can use grouping with some functions, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT COALESCE(universe, 'Standalone') AS universe,
       COUNT(*) AS title_count
FROM titles
GROUP BY COALESCE(universe, 'Standalone')
ORDER BY title_count DESC;

GROUP BY collects rows into groups. Aggregate functions like COUNT , AVG , MIN , and MAX operate on each group.

Another example: how many episodes does each series have? We can combine joining and grouping, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT t.name,
       COUNT(e.episode_id) AS episode_count
FROM titles t
JOIN seasons s  ON s.title_id = t.title_id
JOIN episodes e ON e.season_id = s.season_id
WHERE t.kind = 'series'
GROUP BY t.title_id
ORDER BY episode_count DESC;

The rule to remember is that when you use GROUP BY , every selected column must either be grouped or aggregated.

Prompt : Why does NULL behave differently from other values in comparisons and aggregates?

Filtering groups with HAVING

WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters after grouping. Let’s see an example that uses both, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT t.name,
       COUNT(*) AS cast_size
FROM credits c
JOIN titles t ON t.title_id = c.title_id
JOIN roles  r ON r.role_id = c.role_id
WHERE r.role_name = 'actor'
GROUP BY t.title_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY cast_size DESC;

This returns only titles with two or more credited actors.

Prompt : Please show me some examples where HAVING is required and WHERE cannot be used.

A useful order for designing queries

When writing a query, design it in this order:

  1. Start with the table and its columns that represent what you care most about with SELECT and FROM
  2. Join outward to other tables to bring in related data with JOIN
  3. Filter rows with WHERE
  4. Group if you need summaries with GROUP BY
  5. Filter groups with HAVING
  6. Sort the final result with ORDER BY

SQL queries read top to bottom, but they make sense when designed inside out.

Syntax check: quick quiz

These questions catch mistakes beginners often make:

  1. Which clause controls which rows are included in a result set?

A) SELECT B) WHERE C) ORDER BY D) GROUP BY

  1. Which clause guarantees the order of rows returned by a query?

A) WHERE B) LIMIT C) ORDER BY D) JOIN

  1. What does the following query return? 

    SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM titles
WHERE kind = 'series';

A) A list of TV series

B) The number of rows in the table

C) The number of TV series

D) One row per TV series

  1. Which statement is true about GROUP BY ?

A) It filters rows before aggregation

B) It sorts the result set

C) Every selected column must be aggregated or grouped

D) It can replace JOIN

  1. What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING ?

A) WHERE filters columns, HAVING filters rows

B) WHERE runs after GROUP BY

C) WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after grouping

D) They are interchangeable

  1. Which JOIN returns only rows that have matching values on both sides?

A) LEFT JOIN B) RIGHT JOIN C) FULL JOIN D) INNER JOIN

  1. Why is the following query invalid? 

    SELECT name, COUNT(*)
FROM titles;

A) COUNT cannot be used with SELECT

B) name must be part of a GROUP BY clause

C) titles cannot be counted

D) COUNT(*) requires a WHERE clause

Query exercises: write the SQL

For the exercises in Table 7.2 , you should write the SQL yourself. Solutions should be runnable against the Media database schema used in this chapter.

Name

Description

Exercise 1: simple filtering

Write a query that lists the names and release years of all films, sorted from oldest to newest.

Exercise 2: limiting results

Write a query that returns the three most recent titles, regardless of whether they are films or series.

Exercise 3: joining tables

Write a query that lists all episodes for Star Trek: The Next Generation , showing the season number, episode number, and episode name, in broadcast order.

Exercise 4: many-to-many relationships

Write a query that lists all actors who appear in The Matrix , along with the character they played.

Exercise 5: aggregation

Write a query that shows how many titles exist in each universe. Treat titles with no universe as “Standalone”.

Exercise 6: grouping and HAVING

Write a query that returns only titles that have two or more credited actors, along with the actor count.

Exercise 7: understanding joins

Write a query that lists all people in the database and the titles they are associated with. Include people even if they have only one credit.

Exercise 8: thinking in sets

Write a query that finds all people who appear in more than one title.

Table 7.2: Query exercises

A warning about SQL injection attacks

At this point, you are writing SQL by hand and running it directly against a database. That is safe because you control the input.

In real applications, SQL queries are often built using user input, such as form fields, query strings, or API parameters. If you insert that input directly into a SQL string, you create a serious security vulnerability called SQL injection.

For example, this kind of code is dangerous: 

SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '<user_input>';

If <user_input> is not handled safely, an attacker can change the meaning of the query. Instead of filtering rows, they can bypass checks or even modify data.

The rules to remember are simple:

  • Never build SQL by concatenating user input into strings
  • Always use parameterized queries (also called prepared statements)

You will see how to do this properly in Chapter 9 , Django – Web Development on the Backend , where SQL is generated and executed by application code.

Good practice : If a value comes from a user, it must never be inserted directly into a SQL string.

Now that you have practiced reading, let’s move on to modifying it. That means inserting new rows, updating existing rows, and deleting rows.

Modifying data

This section focuses on changing data. Until now, queries have been read-only. INSERT , UPDATE , and DELETE are the statements that modify what is stored in the database.

A good way to think about it is this: read queries are questions, write queries are decisions.

Start by making a backup copy of Media.db so that you can quickly reset if you make a mess of this section. Simply copy the file and name the copied file Media_backup.db or similar. (If you forget to make a backup then you can also just recreate the Media.db using the Media.sql script.)

For each subsection, run the SQL and note its effect on the data by running the following query on a table before and after each modification SQL statement, as shown in the following code: 

SELECT * FROM <table_name>;

INSERT: adding new rows

INSERT creates new rows in a table. At a minimum, you must specify the table and the values for the required columns. Columns that allow NULL do not have to be supplied with values.

Inserting one row

The safest and most readable form explicitly names the columns, as shown in the following code: 

INSERT INTO titles (name, kind, release_year, universe)
VALUES ('Arrival', 'film', 2016, NULL);

The preceding code says exactly what is being inserted and where. If the table later gains a new column, this statement will still behave correctly. In SQLite, a column declared as title_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is a special case because it becomes an alias for the internal rowid , and SQLite will automatically generate a value if you don’t supply one.

Avoid relying on implicit column order, as shown in the following code: 

INSERT INTO titles
VALUES ('Arrival', 'film', 2016, NULL);

This works only as long as the table definition never changes. That assumption rarely survives real projects.

Inserting multiple rows

You can insert more than one row at a time, as shown in the following code: 

INSERT INTO roles (role_name)
VALUES ('producer'),
       ('composer');

This is clearer and more efficient than issuing multiple separate INSERT statements.

Inserting the result of a query

INSERT does not have to use literal values. You can insert the result of a query, as shown in the following code: 

INSERT INTO credits (title_id, person_id, role_id, character_name)
SELECT t.title_id, p.person_id, r.role_id, 'Linguist'
FROM titles t, people p, roles r
WHERE t.name = 'Arrival'
  AND p.full_name = 'Amy Adams'
  AND r.role_name = 'actor';

This pattern is common when linking existing data together. It also avoids hard-coding IDs, which makes scripts safer and more portable.

UPDATE: changing existing rows

UPDATE modifies one or more existing rows. The WHERE clause is the most important part of an UPDATE statement because it prevents you from accidentally updating ALL rows in the table!

Updating a single column of a single row

For example, to ensure you only update the film named Arrival and not all the other films in the titles table, as shown in the following code: 

UPDATE titles
SET universe = 'Standalone Sci-Fi'
WHERE name = 'Arrival';

This updates only the intended row. Without a WHERE clause, every row in the table is updated. This is where you will be especially glad you have database backups!

The following is valid SQL and a common source of accidental damage. A good habit is to always write the WHERE clause first, then add the SET clause: 

UPDATE titles
SET universe = 'Standalone Sci-Fi';

Good practice : Always include a WHERE clause in UPDATE and DELETE statements.

Updating multiple columns

You can update several columns at once, as shown in the following code: 

UPDATE episodes
SET length_min = 45,
    air_date = '1991-09-30'
WHERE name = 'Darmok';

Each affected row is updated as a single operation.

Updating with conditions and joins

Some databases allow UPDATE statements that reference other tables. Conceptually, you are still updating one table, but using related data to decide how. A subquery is a SELECT statement nested inside another SQL statement. The inner query runs first and its results are used by the outer query.

For example, updating all episodes for a specific series, as shown in the following code: 

UPDATE episodes
SET length_min = 50
WHERE season_id IN (
  SELECT s.season_id
  FROM seasons s
  JOIN titles t ON t.title_id = s.title_id
  WHERE t.name = 'Star Trek: The Next Generation'
);

This reads as, update episodes whose season belongs to this series . The subquery finds all season_id values for a specific series, and the outer UPDATE uses those IDs to target the right episodes.

DELETE: removing rows

Be extremely careful with the DELETE statement. There is no undo.

Deleting just the rows you want to

DELETE removes rows from a table that match the WHERE clause, as shown in the following code: 

DELETE FROM titles
WHERE name = 'Arrival';

The preceding code deletes only the matching row.

Warning! The following code deletes all rows in the table! The table structure remains, but the data is gone: DELETE FROM titles; There is no undo unless you’ve wrapped this statement in a transaction (you will learn about transactions in the next section). Always triple-check for a WHERE clause before running a DELETE statement.

Deleting with foreign keys

Foreign key constraints matter when deleting. If other tables reference the row you are deleting, the database may block the deletion, automatically delete dependent rows, or set foreign key values to NULL .

The behavior depends on how the foreign key was defined. This is deliberate protection, not an inconvenience.

Comparing deleting with dropping a table

DELETE removes rows but leaves the table structure intact. DROP removes the entire table, as shown in the following code: 

DROP TABLE titles;

DROP is a schema change, not a data change. It is irreversible and should be treated with caution.

Now, let’s see how we can add a sort of undo capability when we are modifying data.

Transactions

Transactions are how a database draws a hard line between this change happened and this change did not happen . They exist to prevent a system from ending up in a broken, half-updated state when something goes wrong.

Real database operations rarely involve a single statement. Even a simple user action can translate into multiple inserts, updates, or deletes. If one step succeeds and another fails, the database can be left in an inconsistent state.

Imagine adding a new order:

  1. Insert the order
  2. Insert the order items
  3. Update inventory counts

If the order is inserted but updating inventory fails, did the operation work? From the user’s point of view, no. From the database’s point of view, half the changes were applied.

What a transaction is

A transaction is a group of database operations treated as a single unit of work. The database guarantees that either all the operations succeed together, or none of them take effect at all.

You explicitly control this with the following commands:

  • BEGIN (or START TRANSACTION )
  • COMMIT
  • ROLLBACK

Until a transaction is committed, its changes are provisional. If something goes wrong, a rollback restores the database to exactly the state it was in before the transaction started.

Prompt : How do SQLite and PostgreSQL differ in transaction and locking behavior?

Atomicity in plain language

Transactions are often described using the ACID properties. The most important one for beginners is atomicity. Atomicity means all or nothing .

Either the entire transaction commits, or the database behaves as if it never happened. There is no in-between state that other users can see.

Prompt : Please explain the ACID properties in detail for a beginner with code examples using real-world failures like power loss or server crashes.

Why transactions matter even more with constraints

Constraints and transactions work together. If any statement inside a transaction violates a constraint, the database can abort the transaction. This prevents invalid data from leaking into the system.

For example, if one insert succeeds but a later insert violates a foreign key constraint, the entire transaction can be rolled back. The database does not leave behind partial results that break relationships.

Transactions are also about multiple users working at the same time. Without transactions, two users updating related data simultaneously can interfere with each other in unpredictable ways. Transactions define clear boundaries where changes begin and end, allowing the database to manage locking and isolation safely.

Good practice : Any time you have more than one statement that must succeed or fail together, you should be using a transaction. This includes creating related rows across multiple tables, updating totals or derived values, deleting data with dependent rows, and migrations and data fixes.

Single-statement operations are often implicitly transactional, but relying on that behavior is fragile and varies by database.

Prompt : What is isolation level, and why does it matter even for simple applications? Please explain lost updates, dirty reads, and phantom reads with simple examples.

Now that you know how to insert, update, and delete rows in tables, and how to manage multiple changes so they either all happen, or none of it happens, let’s look at how to work with indexes.

Improving performance with indexes

You can write perfectly correct SQL that is painfully slow if the database has no efficient way to find the data. Indexes exist to solve that problem, and query plans explain how the database uses them.

What an index is

An index is a separate data structure that allows the database to find rows quickly without scanning an entire table. Conceptually, it is like the index in the back of a book. Instead of reading every page to find a name, you jump directly to the relevant pages.

In a database, an index stores selected column values in a structure optimized for lookup, along with references to the actual table rows. Most relational databases use variations of B-trees for indexes, which keep data sorted and allow fast searches, insertions, and range scans.

An important point is that an index is not the table itself. It is an additional structure that must be kept in sync with the table’s data.

Why indexes make reads faster

Without an index, the database has no choice but to perform a full table scan . That means checking every row to see whether it matches your query. This is acceptable for small tables, but it becomes slow very quickly as the table grows.

With an index, the database can jump directly to the relevant rows. For example:

  • Filtering with WHERE on indexed columns becomes much faster
  • Joining tables on indexed keys becomes cheaper
  • Sorting and grouping can often reuse the index order

Indexes are especially effective for selective queries, where only a small fraction of rows match the condition.

Prompt : Please explain how a database chooses between a table scan and an index scan.

Why indexes slow down writes

Every time you INSERT , UPDATE , or DELETE a row, the database must update not only the table, but also every index that involves the affected columns.

If a table has many indexes, each write operation has more work to do:

  • New index entries must be created
  • Existing entries may need to be reordered
  • Deleted rows must be removed from indexes

This is why write-heavy workloads often have fewer indexes, while read-heavy workloads tend to have more. Indexes trade write speed and storage space for faster reads.

Prompt : Please show me some examples where adding an index makes a query slower, not faster.

How to choose effective indexes

A practical way to think about indexes is to start from your queries, not your tables. Ask:

  • Which columns appear frequently in WHERE clauses?
  • Which columns are used to join tables?
  • Which columns are used to sort or group results?

These are prime candidates for indexes.

Also consider selectivity. Indexes are most useful when they significantly reduce the number of rows the database needs to examine. Indexing a column with only a few possible values, such as a Boolean flag, often provides little benefit on its own.

Prompt : Please explain index selectivity and why indexing Boolean columns is often useless.

Composite indexes , which cover multiple columns, can make specific queries much faster, but column order matters. An index on (kind, release_year) helps queries that filter by kind , or by kind and release_year together, but not queries that filter only by release_year .

When not to index

Not every column should be indexed. Indexes cost storage and slow down writes. Tables that are small, rarely queried, or frequently updated may not benefit from additional indexes.

A common beginner mistake is adding indexes just in case. A better approach is to add them in response to real queries and real performance problems.

Indexes do not make SQL faster in general. They make specific access patterns faster. Query plans are how the database explains which access pattern it chose and why.

Prompt : Please explain why ORDER BY can sometimes be satisfied by an index and sometimes cannot.

How to identify performance issues

Identifying performance issues in SQL is about understanding where time is being spent and why. Slow queries are rarely caused by SQL syntax itself. They are usually the result of how data is structured, how much data is involved, and how the database chooses to access it.

Start with symptoms, not guesses

Common signs of performance problems include:

  • Queries that feel fast with small datasets but slow dramatically as data grows
  • Reports or pages that hang or time out under load
  • Queries that seem fine in development but struggle in production

The first mistake many developers make is trying to optimize blindly. Performance work should always start with observation.

Measure before you change

Before changing anything, establish what slow actually means. Run the query on realistic data and note how long it takes, how many rows it returns, and whether the time is consistent or varies wildly.

If a query returns thousands of rows when you expect tens, the problem is often logical, not technical.

Use EXPLAIN to see what the database is doing

Most databases provide EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE to show how a query will be executed. At a high level, look for:

  • Full table scans on large tables
  • Joins that process far more rows than expected
  • Indexes not being used where you expected them to be
  • Large differences between estimated row counts and actual row counts

You do not need to understand every detail of the plan. Even spotting a table scan versus an index scan is enough to explain many slow queries.

Check filtering and joins first

Performance problems often come from:

  • Missing or incorrect WHERE conditions
  • Joins that multiply rows unexpectedly
  • Filtering after joining instead of before

A useful technique is to remove joins one by one and see how the query’s behavior changes. This helps isolate where row counts explode.

Look at indexes last, not first

Indexes matter, but they are not a magic fix. Before adding an index, ask:

  • Does the query filter or join on this column?
  • Does the filter significantly reduce the number of rows?
  • Is the data type and comparison correct?

Adding indexes to compensate for poor query logic usually leads to more complexity and slower writes without solving the real issue.

Performance issues are best approached systematically. Start by understanding what the query is doing, inspect the execution plan, verify row counts at each step, and only then consider indexing or refactoring.

Prompt : Please show me how to debug a slow SQL query step by step.

Practice, references, and resources

In this section, you will be tested on what you’ve learned in this chapter and be provided with useful links to reference materials and resources.

Check your understanding

Answer the following questions:

  1. What does it mean that SQL is a declarative language?
  2. What is the difference between a table, a row, and a column?
  3. Why are primary keys important?
  4. What is a foreign key, and what problem does it solve?
  5. Why is normalization important in database design?
  6. What is the purpose of the WHERE clause in a SELECT query?
  7. What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN ?
  8. What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING ?
  9. Why is it dangerous to run UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause?
  10. What is a transaction, and why is it important?

Links

SQL is standardized, but every database has extensions and edge cases. When in doubt, always check the official documentation for the database you are actually using. Trust vendor documentation first, blogs second, and copy-pasted snippets last.

Below are reliable, official SQL reference guides and documentation sites. They are maintained by the database vendors or core project teams and reflect actual behavior instead of myths propagated on sites like LinkedIn.

Cross-database and standards-oriented references

These are useful for readers who want a broader or more neutral view of SQL.

ISO SQL standard overview: https://www.iso.org/standard/76583.html

W3Schools SQL reference (non-official, but approachable and searchable): https://www.w3schools.com/sql/

MDN SQL overview: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/SQL

SQLite

SQLite is extremely well documented, and its docs are unusually readable.

Official SQLite documentation home: https://www.sqlite.org/docs.html

SQL language reference that is good for learning about SQLite-specific behavior and extensions: https://www.sqlite.org/lang.html

SELECT statement reference: https://www.sqlite.org/lang_select.html

Data types and type affinity which is important for understanding SQLite’s flexibility: https://www.sqlite.org/datatype3.html

SQLite command-line tool documentation: https://www.sqlite.org/cli.html

PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL has one of the most comprehensive and rigorous SQL documentations available. It is verbose, but extremely precise.

PostgreSQL official documentation home: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/

PostgreSQL SQL command reference (alphabetical): https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-commands.html

Indexes and performance concepts: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes.html

SQL Server (T-SQL)

Microsoft SQL Server uses Transact-SQL (T-SQL), which extends standard SQL with procedural features.

SQL Server documentation home: https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/sql-server/

T-SQL language reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/t-sql/language-reference

Transactions and locking: https://learn.microsoft.com/sql/t-sql/language-elements/transactions-transact-sql

Summary

In this chapter, you learned that SQL is not mainly about clever syntax. It is about describing the data you want and relying on the database engine to work out how to retrieve or change it safely. That is why relational databases care so much about schema design, keys, constraints, and transactions. Good SQL starts with a good model.

You worked through the core pieces that make relational systems usable: tables, rows, columns, primary keys, foreign keys, normalization, NULL, and constraints. You then used those ideas in practice with SQLite, writing queries that filter, sort, join, group, and summarize data. You also saw how to change data safely and why transactions and indexes matter once a system becomes real rather than toy-sized.

Databases are unforgiving when the model is wrong. A confused schema leads to awkward queries, brittle joins, and performance work based on guesswork. A sound schema does not make every query easy, but it removes a lot of unnecessary difficulty. Start with the data model, then write the query that fits it.

Specifically, you learned:

  • What SQL is and is not, including the idea that SQL is declarative and set-based rather than step-by-step
  • How tables, rows, and columns model real-world concepts, and why repeating data leads to bugs and inconsistencies
  • How primary keys give rows identity and foreign keys define and enforce relationships between tables
  • How constraints such as NOT NULL , UNIQUE , CHECK , and foreign keys prevent invalid data from entering the database
  • How to run SQL queries cross-platform using tools like SQLiteStudio, VS Code, and the SQLite command-line tool
  • How to write SELECT queries to retrieve data, filter rows, sort results, and limit output predictably
  • How to combine related data using different types of JOIN , and how to tell which rows appear in the result
  • How to summarize data using GROUP BY , aggregate functions like COUNT and AVG , and filtering with HAVING
  • How to insert new data, update existing data, and delete rows safely using INSERT , UPDATE , and DELETE
  • Why transactions matter, and how they prevent databases from ending up in a “half-worked” state
  • What indexes are, how they speed up reads while slowing writes, and how query plans explain database behavior

In the next chapter, you will learn about Python, a high-level, general-purpose programming language known for its readable syntax and large standard library, widely used for web development, data analysis, automation, and scripting. That is a good transition, because Python gives you a general-purpose language for building application logic, while this chapter has focused on the data layer that logic depends on.

Python – Programming on the Backend

Python is the language you will use for the backend side of this book, so this chapter is about getting comfortable with the parts of Python that matter most in real work. This chapter does not try to cover every corner of Python. It gives you enough fluency to read Python code, run it, change it, and understand what it is doing.

You will begin by installing Python and making sure it runs properly from the command line and inside VS Code. Then you will work through the basics: variables, values, conditions, loops, functions, and the built-in data structures that Python relies on heavily. After that, you will look at strings, debugging, exceptions, modules, packages, virtual environments, and file input and output (I/O). The chapter ends with a small command-line task tracker that pulls those ideas together into one working program.

Python syntax is only the starting point. You also need to see how Python programs are organized, how data moves through them, how they fail, and how to keep them understandable as they grow.

By the end of this chapter, you should understand Python’s core syntax, know how to use its built-in data structures, and be able to write small but useful Python programs.

In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:

  • Introducing Python
  • Syntax and basics
  • Data structures
  • Strings in more depth
  • Functions and classes
  • Errors and debugging basics
  • Modules, imports, and packages
  • Virtual environments
  • File input and output
  • A small, cohesive mini-project

Suggested chatbot prompts with example responses for this chapter can be found at the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/prompts/ch08-python/readme.md

Introducing Python

Python is a general-purpose language built around a simple idea: code should be readable.

It was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991, which makes it older than Java, JavaScript, and even the web as we know it today. It feels modern because its design favors clarity over cleverness. That focus on readability is on purpose. Python assumes code will be read more often than it is written.

Clean syntax using indentation

One of the first things people notice about Python is how little visual noise there is. Python avoids excessive punctuation and boilerplate. Instead of braces or keywords to mark blocks of code, Python uses indentation. That means the structure of your program is visible at a glance:

  • When something is nested, it is indented.
  • When it ends, the indentation stops.

This forces consistency, but it also removes an entire category of errors that beginners often struggle with in other languages.

The official Python design philosophy, known as The Zen of Python , explicitly states that readability counts and that simple is better than complex. You can read it at the following link: https://peps.python.org/pep-0020/

Prompt : Why does Python use indentation instead of braces, and what trade-offs does this design make? How does Python’s readability philosophy affect long-term maintenance of code? Please compare Python’s design philosophy with JavaScript and C# in practical terms.

Professional Python

Python is often described as beginner-friendly, and that is true, but it leaves out something important. Python is not a beginner language that you leave behind later. It is used professionally across a wide range of industries, including web development, automation, scientific computing, data analysis, machine learning, game development, and system administration.

Companies such as Google, Netflix, and Spotify use Python extensively in production systems. That combination explains much of Python’s appeal: it is easy to start with, but it does not trap you in beginner territory.

Prompt : What coding habits separate beginner Python developers from professionals?

A rich standard library

Another important aspect of Python is that it comes with a rich standard library. When you install Python, you already have access to tools for working with files, dates and times, text processing, networking, mathematics, and more. This is often summarized as “batteries included”.

For beginners, this means you can do useful things quickly without installing extra packages. For experienced developers, it means fewer external dependencies and a more predictable development environment.

Python is interpreted, not compiled

Python is also an interpreted language, which affects how you work with it. You write Python code in plain text files, and the Python interpreter executes that code directly. There is no separate compilation step that turns your code into a standalone executable file, as happens in languages like C or C++, before you can run your program.

This gives you a quick feedback loop. You write a small piece of code, run it, see what happens, and adjust. That tight loop is especially valuable when learning, because experimentation becomes cheap and mistakes are easy to recover from.

A vast ecosystem

Python has a very large ecosystem. There are millions of Python developers worldwide, and an enormous amount of documentation, tutorials, libraries, and community support. If you encounter a problem, it is very likely that someone else has encountered it before and written about it. That support matters. Learning a language also means learning where to look things up, how to read documentation, and how to build confidence one small fix at a time. Python usually makes that learning process easier because it introduces complexity gradually.

Installing Python

Before diving into Python’s syntax, you need a working Python installation. Python may already be installed on your computer, depending on your operating system:

  • On Windows, Python is not reliably installed by default. Some newer Windows versions include a stub that launches the Microsoft Store, which often confuses beginners. The safest approach is to explicitly check.
  • On macOS, Python is usually installed, but historically it was Python 2, which is no longer supported. Recent macOS versions may include Python 3, but you should still verify the version.
  • On Linux, Python 3 is almost always installed because many system tools depend on it. Even so, checking is still necessary.

You can read the Python 2 end-of-life notice at the following link: https://www.python.org/doc/sunset-python-2/

Checking Python is done from the command line, because it is often run at the command line. Open a terminal or command prompt and run the following command: 

python --version

If that does not work, try explicitly running Python 3, as shown in the following command: 

python3 --version

You should see something like the following output: 

Python 3.14.2

If so, then Python is installed correctly and you are ready to proceed.

What if Python is missing?

If you see an error such as command not found or a message pushing you to the Microsoft Store, then Python is either missing or not configured properly.

Warning! Python 3 is required for this book. Python 2 reached end of life in January 2020 and should not be used for new projects.

To manually install Python, for all platforms, the official source of truth is the Python website, maintained by the Python Software Foundation. You can download Python from the following link:

https://www.python.org/downloads/

Warning! For Windows, download the official installer from python.org , not the Microsoft Store, and during installation, make sure Add Python to PATH is checked. That checkbox is the single most common source of beginner frustration. If Python is not on the PATH, typing python will not work from the command line.

For macOS, downloading the macOS installer from python.org is the simplest option. Advanced users may prefer Homebrew, but beginners should not start there.

For Linux, Python 3 is usually already installed. If not, installation is done through the system package manager, such as apt , dnf , or pacman , depending on the distribution.

After installation, repeat the version check command to confirm success.

Python releases and lifecycle

Python releases go through five phases, as described in the following points:

  1. Early development (feature phase) : Before the first beta, the next full release can accept new features, bug fixes, and security fixes.
  2. Pre-release (beta phase) : After the first beta, no new features can go in, but feature fixes (including significant changes to new features), bug fixes, and security fixes are accepted for the upcoming feature release.
  3. Stable maintenance (bugfix phase) : Once a version has been fully released, bug fixes and security fixes are accepted. New binaries are built and released roughly every two months. This phase is also called maintenance mode or stable release.
  4. Security-only support : After two years (18 months for versions before 3.13), only security fixes are accepted and no more binaries are released. New source-only versions can be released as needed.
  5. End-of-life : Five years after a release, support ends. The release cycle is frozen; no further changes are allowed.

The descriptions come from the official Python release lifecycle page in the Python Developer Guide at the following link: https://devguide.python.org/versions/

At the time of writing in April 2026, as shown in Figure 8.1 and explained in the following points:

  • Python versions 2.6 to 3.9 have all reached their end-of-life and are therefore not supported
  • Python versions 3.10 to 3.12 are all in their security phases meaning that although they are supported, they only get security fixes
  • Python versions 3.13 and 3.14 are in their bugfix phase meaning they are actively supported with new binaries that you can download and install every two months

Figure 8.1: Python versions and their support phases

Good practice : Set bimonthly reminders in your calendar to check what the latest version of Python is and keep your installations updated.

Trying out the Python interactive shell

As a quick sanity check, let’s try out the Python interactive shell.

At a command prompt or terminal, enter the following command: 

python

Or: 

python3

You should see the >>> prompt, which means that Python is running and ready. Try performing a simple calculation, as shown in the following command and output: 

>>> 2+2
4

To exit the Python interactive shell, enter the following command: 

>>> exit()

You can also press Ctrl + D on macOS and Linux, or Ctrl + Z then Enter on Windows.

A working Python installation is the first thing you need. Once Python runs reliably from the command line, the rest of the chapter can focus on learning the language itself, not fighting the environment.

In the rest of this chapter, you will move from understanding what Python is to actually using it. You will start with the basic rules and syntax that define how Python code works, and then you will explore Python’s core data structures.

Syntax and basics

Python’s syntax is purposely small. There are fewer rules to memorize than in most languages, but the rules that do exist matter a lot. This section focuses on the core building blocks you will use in almost every Python program: indentation, statements, variables, basic types, expressions, comments, and simple input and output.

Writing Python code files and running them

Python code is usually written in plain text files with a .py extension. Each file is a Python program, also called a script. VS Code is just an editor, but the Python extension connects it to the Python interpreter installed on the system.

Create a Chapter08 folder, with a subfolder named python-basics . Open the python-basics folder in VS Code using File | Open Folder .

Opening a folder, rather than a single file, matters because VS Code uses the folder as the working context for running code and managing settings.

Next, in the python-basics folder, create a new file called hello.py .

Good practice : File names should be lowercase, use underscores instead of spaces, and avoid special characters. This convention is not enforced by Python, but it is widely followed and prevents subtle problems later.

In hello.py , write the simplest Python script, as shown in Figure 8.2 and in the following code: 

print("Hello, Python")

Figure 8.2: Writing Python code files in VS Code

You can (1) select the Python interpreter version by clicking in the status bar, and (2) run the code file by clicking the Run Python File button in the top-right of the code editor, as shown in Figure 8.2 .

This file is not a project or an application. It is just a simple script. A sequence of instructions that Python will execute from top to bottom.

In VS Code, open the terminal with Terminal | New Terminal . This terminal opens in the folder you selected earlier. This is important because Python will look for files in the current directory.

In Terminal , enter the following command: 

python hello.py

If that does not work, use: 

python3 hello.py

The difference depends on how Python was installed, and both are normal. The result should appear immediately in the terminal, as shown in the following output: 

Hello, Python

Figure 8.3: Viewing the output of running the Python code file in VS Code Terminal

VS Code did not run Python itself. It asked the operating system to run the Python interpreter, passed it the file name, and displayed the output. Remembering that chain will help later when debugging.

Running Python files with the UI

When a Python file is open, there is a ▶ button in the top-right corner of the code editor. Clicking it runs the current file using the selected Python interpreter and shows the output in the terminal. This button is doing the same thing as typing the command manually. It is not a different execution mode. If something fails here, it would also fail in the terminal.

In the bottom-right corner of VS Code, the Python version is shown in the status bar. If you click it, you can select which Python interpreter to use when you have multiple versions installed at the same time.

Python does not automatically re-run code when you save. The loop is always:

  1. Edit the code file
  2. Save the changes to the code file
  3. Run the code file again

Modify the program slightly, as shown in the following code: 

name = input("What is your name? ")
print("Hello,", name)

Run it again and show how input flows through the terminal, as shown in Figure 8.4 :

Figure 8.4: Getting input from the user

Errors are normal and expected. If Python encounters something it cannot understand, it stops and prints a traceback. For now, the most important skill is reading the last line of the error message, which usually explains what went wrong and on which line.

You’ve now learned the basics of how to write Python code in .py files, how to edit those files in VS Code, and then run them using the Python interpreter via the terminal or the Run Python File button.

Now let’s look more closely at how Python code is written.

The importance of indentation

The most important rule to understand first is indentation . In Python, indentation is not cosmetic. It defines structure. Blocks of code that belong together are indented by the same amount, usually four spaces. There are no braces to mark where a block starts or ends. When the indentation level increases, you are inside a block. When it decreases, you have left that block.

For example, indentation determines if a statement is inside a block or not, as shown in the following code: 

if True:
    print("This line is inside the block")
    print("So is this one")
print("This line is outside the block")

The colon at the end of the if line tells Python that a block follows. The indentation tells Python which lines belong to that block. Mixing tabs and spaces is a common beginner mistake.

Good practice : The rule to adopt early is simple: always use spaces and always use the same number of spaces. For most code examples for languages like JavaScript or C#, I use two spaces to save horizontal space in my print books. In this book’s Python examples, I use the traditional four spaces because indentation matters so much.

Python comments

Python supports comments , which are notes for humans that Python ignores. Comments start with a # , as shown in the following code: 

# This is a comment
count = 10  # This comment is inline

Comments are useful for explaining why something is done, not what the code already clearly says. If the code is hard to explain without comments, that is often a sign the code itself should be simplified.

Python statements and variables

Python programs are made up of statements . A statement is a complete instruction that Python can execute. Some statements perform actions, like calling a function. Others define things, like variables or functions. Unlike some languages, Python usually uses one statement per line, which makes code easier to read and comprehend.

Next come variables . A variable is a name that refers to a value. In Python, you do not declare a variable’s type explicitly. The type is inferred from the value you assign, as shown in the following code: 

age = 42
name = "Mark"
pi = 3.14159

In the preceding code, age refers to an integer, name refers to a string, and pi refers to a floating-point number. Like JavaScript, Python is dynamically typed , which means the same variable name can later refer to a different type of value. That flexibility is useful, but it makes clear names and consistent use more important.

Prompt : Please explain dynamic typing in Python with examples of both its strengths and pitfalls.

Python data types

Python has a small set of built-in basic types that you will use constantly. The most common ones are integers ( int ), floating-point numbers ( float ), strings ( str ), and booleans ( bool ), as shown in the following code: 

count = 10        # int
price = 9.99      # float
title = "Python"  # str
is_active = True  # bool

Strings in Python are enclosed in either single quotes or double quotes. Both are equivalent. Choose one style and be consistent. Strings can be combined using the + operator and repeated using * , as shown in the following code: 

greeting = "Hello"
name = "World"
message = greeting + " " + name
print(message * 3)       # prints Hello WorldHello WorldHello World

Python expressions

Python supports expressions , which are combinations of values and operators that produce a result. Arithmetic expressions behave mostly as you would expect, as shown in the following code: 

total = 10 + 3
difference = 10 - 3
product = 10 * 3
quotient = 10 / 3
modulus = 10 % 3
print(total, difference, product, quotient, modulus)

The / operator always produces a floating-point result. If you want integer division, use // , as shown in the following code: 

result = 7 // 2   # result is 3

Python comparisons

Comparisons produce Boolean values. These are used heavily in decision-making, as shown in the following code: 

x = 5
x > 3      # True
x == 5     # True
x != 10    # True

Note that == checks for equality. A single = is used only for assignment. Confusing these is a classic beginner error.

Conditional statements

To make decisions, Python uses conditional statements , most commonly if , elif , and else , as shown in the following code: 

temperature = 18
if temperature > 20:
    print("It's warm")
elif temperature > 10:
    print("It's mild")
else:
    print("It's cold")

Only one branch runs. The first condition that evaluates to True wins. This structure reads top to bottom and closely mirrors how people explain decisions in plain language.

Comparison and logical operators

Conditions are built using comparison operators like:

  • == equal to
  • != not equal to
  • < , <= , > , >=

Logical operators combine conditions:

  • and requires both conditions to be true
  • or requires at least one condition to be true
  • not negates a condition 
if rating >= 8 and rating <= 10:
    print("Positive")

Truthiness in Python

Python allows non-boolean values to be used in conditions. This is known as truthiness. For example:

  • Empty lists, empty strings, and zero evaluate to false
  • Non-empty collections and non-zero numbers evaluate to true
  • None evaluates to false 
if titles:
    print("There are titles to process")

This checks whether the list named titles is non-empty, without explicitly comparing lengths.

Structural pattern matching with match

Since Python 3.10, Python has structural pattern matching , introduced with the match statement. This fills the same role as a switch statement in JavaScript, but it is more flexible.

For example: 

status = 404
match status:
    case 200:
        print("OK")
    case 404:
        print("Not found")
    case 500:
        print("Server error")
    case _:
        print("Unknown status")

In this simplest form, match behaves very much like a traditional switch . The underscore ( _ ) is the default case.

Python’s match is more flexible than a simple switch because it is based on pattern matching, not just value matching. It can match literal values, data structures, object attributes, type patterns, and combinations of patterns with guards. For example: 

command = ("play", "Arrival")
match command:
    case ("play", title):
        print(f"Playing {title}")
    case ("stop", _):
        print("Stopping playback")

This is more flexible than a classic switch statement.

("play", "Arrival") is an example of a tuple. You will learn about tuples in the next section, Data structures .

Now let’s move on to looping.

Looping statements

Looping statements let a Python program repeat work efficiently instead of writing the same code over and over. Python’s looping model is simple, but it is built around a simple idea: you usually loop over things, not over numeric indexes.

The for loop

The for loop is the most commonly used loop in Python. It iterates over an iterable, like a list, tuple, string, dictionary, range, or any object that can produce values one at a time: 

titles = ["Arrival", "The Matrix", "Star Trek"]
for title in titles:
    print(title)

This reads naturally: for each title in titles . You are not managing counters or indexes. Python handles iteration for you.

Looping with range

When you do need a sequence of numbers, range provides it: 

for i in range(3):
    print(i)

This produces 0 , 1 , and 2 . range is commonly used when repeating an action a fixed number of times or when working with indexes.

The while loop

A while loop repeats as long as a condition remains true : 

count = 0
while count < 3:
    print(count)
    count += 1

Unlike for , while loops require you to manage state explicitly. They are useful when you do not know in advance how many iterations are needed, but they are easier to misuse if the condition never becomes false .

Controlling loops with break and continue

break exits the loop immediately: 

for title in titles:
    if title == "The Matrix":
        break
    print(title)

continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next one: 

for title in titles:
    if title.startswith("The"):
        continue
    print(title)

Both should be used sparingly. If a loop needs many breaks and continues, it often signals that the logic should be simplified or moved into a function.

Python loops are simple by design. The power comes from iterating over meaningful values instead of low-level mechanics, which keeps code readable as programs grow.

Prompt : Please explain enumerate , range , and zip with practical examples.

Python input and output

Finally, let’s review basic input and output, which let programs interact with the outside world. The most common output function is print , as shown in the following code: 

print("Hello, Python")

To get input from the user, Python provides the input function. It always returns a string, as shown in the following code: 

name = input("What is your name? ")
print("Hello,", name)

If you need a number like an integer, then you must convert the input explicitly using the int or float functions, as shown in the following code: 

age = int(input("How old are you? "))

This explicitness is intentional. Python prefers clarity over guessing what you meant.

At this point, you should understand how Python code is structured, how values are stored in variables, how basic types work, and how simple logic and interaction are expressed. These fundamentals will appear in every example that follows.

In the next section, data structures will build directly on these ideas and show how Python handles collections of information rather than single values. These data structures let you model real-world information directly in code, instead of juggling isolated values one at a time.

Data structures

So far, you have worked with single values stored in variables. That is useful, but real programs almost always deal with collections of data: a list of names, a set of options, a mapping from usernames to email addresses, or a sequence of values that changes over time.

Python’s built-in data structures are one of the main reasons the language feels productive so quickly. They let you model real-world information directly, without ceremony.

Python’s core built-in data structures are lists , tuples , dictionaries , and sets . You will use lists and dictionaries constantly, tuples occasionally, and sets when the problem fits.

We will start with lists, because they are the most familiar and the most flexible.

Lists

A list is an ordered collection of values. You create a list using square brackets, with items separated by commas, as shown in the following code: 

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
names = ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"]

Lists can hold values of different types, although mixing types without a good reason is usually a bad idea, as shown in the following code: 

mixed = [1, "two", 3.0]

Good practice : Python allows mixed types in a list by design, but doing so makes your code harder to understand, more error-prone, and less maintainable due to loss of predictability. When a list contains a single, consistent type, you can make assumptions about what operations are valid. For example, if a list contains only integers, you can safely add, compare, or sort them without extra checks. For most beginner-level and production code, a simple rule is that a list should contain items of the same kind, even if Python does not enforce it.

You access items in a list using an index. Python uses zero-based indexing, which means the first item is at position 0: 

names[0]   # "Alice"
names[1]   # "Bob"

You can also use negative indexes to count from the end: 

names[-1]  # "Charlie"

Lists are mutable, which means you can change them after creation. You can replace items, add new ones, or remove existing ones, as shown in the following code: 

names.append("Diana")
names[1] = "Robert"

This mutability is why lists are often used to represent things that grow, shrink, or change over time.

Tuples

A tuple looks like a list, but it uses parentheses aka round brackets instead of square brackets, as shown in the following code: 

coordinates = (51.5074, -0.1278)

Tuples are ordered collections like lists, but they are immutable. Once created, you cannot change their contents. This makes tuples useful for data that should not change, such as coordinates, configuration values, or fixed records.

To read an item from a tuple, you use the same syntax as with a list, as shown in the following code: 

coordinates[0]  # 51.5074

If you try to assign a new value, Python will raise an error. This is a feature, not a limitation. It lets you express what the code should do clearly.

Prompt : Please explain why tuples exist when lists already work.

Dictionaries

The most important and distinctive data structure in Python is the dictionary . A dictionary stores key–value pairs like "age": 42 , as shown in the following code: 

user = {
    "name": "Mark",
    "age": 42,
    "is_admin": True
}

Instead of accessing values by position, you access them by key. Keys are usually strings, and values can be anything. You retrieve values using the key name, as shown in the following code: 

user["name"]      # "Mark"
user["age"]       # 42

You can add or update entries by assignment, as shown in the following code: 

user["email"] = "mark@example.com"
user["age"] = 43

Dictionaries are helpful because they map naturally to how we think about structured data. JSON, which is used everywhere on the web, maps almost directly to Python dictionaries and lists. If you understand dictionaries well, many web and data tasks suddenly become much easier.

Prompt : When should I choose a list versus a dictionary in real programs?

Sets

Then there are sets. A set is an unordered collection of unique values. You create a set using curly braces, like a dictionary but without key–value pairs, as shown in the following code: 

tags = {"python", "web", "data"}

Sets automatically remove duplicates, as shown in the following code: 

numbers = {1, 2, 2, 3}
# numbers is {1, 2, 3}

Sets are useful when you care about membership rather than order. For example, checking whether a value exists in a collection is fast and expressive with sets, as shown in the following code: 

"python" in tags   # True

Across all these data structures, you will often use loops to process items one by one. The most common loop in Python is the for loop, as shown in the following code: 

for name in names:
    print(name)

This reads almost like English. Python handles the indexing internally, which reduces errors and makes the code clearer.

Prompt : Please explain how Python’s for loop works internally compared to index-based loops.

You will also frequently check conditions while working with collections, as shown in the following code: 

if "email" in user:
    print("Email is set")

Prompt : Please explain sets with real-world use cases beyond removing duplicates.

Collections summary

At this stage, you do not need to memorize every method or operation. Focus on the role each structure plays:

  • Lists are ordered and changeable
  • Tuples are ordered and fixed
  • Dictionaries map keys to values
  • Sets store unique items with no guaranteed order

These four structures cover an enormous amount of everyday programming. As your programs grow, you will combine them freely: lists of dictionaries, dictionaries containing lists, sets derived from lists, and so on.

Prompt : Please show me some practical examples of nesting lists and dictionaries together.

In later chapters, you will see these same data structures appear everywhere: handling form data, processing files, working with databases, and exchanging data with web APIs. If you are comfortable with them here, everything that follows becomes easier to understand.

Prompt : Please explain common mistakes beginners make with mutable lists and dictionaries.

Now we’ve looked at collections, let’s go deeper into string values.

Strings in more depth

Strings appear everywhere in Python programs. User input, file contents, URLs, JSON data, HTML, error messages, and configuration values are all strings. Because they are so common, Python provides a rich set of features for working with them. Understanding strings well pays off immediately, especially in web and data-related code.

A string in Python is an immutable sequence of characters. Immutable means that once a string is created, it cannot be changed in place. Any operation that appears to modify a string is actually creating a new one, as shown in the following code: 

text = "hello"
text.upper()
print(text)

This prints hello , not HELLO , because upper() returns a new string and leaves the original unchanged. To change the original text, you must assign the result of calling the upper() function to the text variable, as shown in the following code: 

text = text.upper()
print(text)

Now text refers to the new string. This immutability is a design choice that makes strings safer and more predictable.

Creating strings

Python provides several ways to create strings. You have already seen single-quoted and double-quoted strings, as shown in the following code: 

name = "Alice"
city = 'London'

Both forms are equivalent. Use whichever makes the string easier to read, especially when it contains quotation marks.

For multi-line text, Python supports triple-quoted strings , as shown in the following code: 

message = """Hello,
This is a multi-line string.
Goodbye."""

These are useful for long messages, documentation, or embedded text blocks.

F-strings

One of the most important Python features is f-strings . F-strings provide a clear and readable way to embed values directly into strings, as shown in the following code: 

name = "Alice"
age = 30
message = f"{name} is {age} years old"
print(message)

The f prefix tells Python to evaluate expressions inside curly braces. This approach is clearer and less error-prone than string concatenation, especially as strings become more complex.

F-strings can include expressions, not just variable names, as shown in the following code: 

price = 9.99
quantity = 3
total = f"Total: {price * quantity}"

String methods

Python strings come with many built-in methods for common tasks. You do not need to memorize them all, but a few are worth learning early.

The lower() and upper() methods change case: 

text = "Python"
text.lower()   # "python"
text.upper()   # "PYTHON"

The strip() method removes whitespace from the start and end of a string: 

raw = "  hello  "
clean = raw.strip()

This is especially useful when dealing with user input.

The split() method breaks a string into a list of substrings: 

csv = "red,green,blue"
colors = csv.split(",")

The opposite operation is join() , which combines a list of strings into a single string, as shown in the following code: 

colors = ["red", "green", "blue"]
result = ",".join(colors)

Indexing and slicing strings

Strings can be indexed and sliced, just like lists: 

word = "Python"
word[0]      # "P"
word[1:4]    # "yth"
word[-1]     # "n"

Slicing creates new strings and never modifies the original.

Substrings

Another common task is checking whether a string contains a value or starts or ends in a particular way, as shown in the following code: 

email = "user@example.com"
"@" in email
email.startswith("user")
email.endswith(".com")

These operations read cleanly and avoid fragile manual parsing.

User input starts as a string

It is also important to understand that input from the user always starts as a string: 

age = input("How old are you? ")

If you need a number, you must convert it explicitly, as shown in the following code: 

age = int(age)

Failing to do this is one of the most common beginner mistakes and a frequent source of TypeError and ValueError exceptions.

Strings are immutable

At this point, you should think of strings as immutable building blocks. You create them, transform them, combine them, and pass them around, but you never alter them in place. Python’s string tools are designed to make these transformations readable and safe.

As you move into file handling, web development, and APIs, strings will dominate your code. Being comfortable with f-strings and a handful of core string methods will make that work feel straightforward rather than fiddly.

Now that we know how to handle string values in depth, let’s see how you can break down a large, complex project into small functional units. This makes it easier to manage lots of code, and makes it easier to test and debug.

Functions and classes

As your programs grow beyond a few lines, repeating the same logic over and over quickly becomes painful. Functions solve this problem. A function is a named block of code that performs a specific task. Once defined, you can call it as many times as you like. This makes programs easier to read and easier to change.

Prompt : How do functions help programs scale beyond a few hundred lines? Please explain why small functions are easier to test and debug.

Defining functions

In Python, functions are defined using the def keyword, followed by the function name, a pair of parentheses, and a colon. The function body is indented, like any other block, as shown in the following code: 

def greet():
    print("Hello, Python")

This code defines a function called greet . Nothing happens yet. Defining a function does not run it. To execute the code inside the function, you must call it by name, as shown in the following code:
