greet()

When Python reaches this line, it jumps into the function, runs the indented block, and then returns to where it left off.

Function parameters

Most useful functions accept parameters . Parameters are variables that receive values from the caller. They let the function work with different data each time it is called, as shown in the following code: 

def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)
greet("Alice")
greet("Bob")

In the preceding code, name is a parameter. When you call greet("Alice") , the value "Alice" is passed into the function and assigned to name .

Returning values from functions

Functions can also return values using the return statement. Returning a value sends data back to the caller and ends the function immediately, as shown in the following code: 

def add(a, b):
    return a + b
result = add(3, 4)
print(result)

Functions do not only perform actions. They can compute a result and hand it back to the caller.

A function can have multiple return statements, but only one will run per call, as shown in the following code: 

def check_age(age):
    if age >= 18:
        return "Adult"
    else:
        return "Minor"

As soon as return executes, the function exits.

Local variables and scope

Variables defined inside a function are local to that function. This means they exist only while the function is running and cannot be accessed from outside, as shown in the following code: 

def example():
    x = 10
    print(x)
example()
# print(x)  # This would cause an error

This concept is called scope . Local variables help prevent accidental interference between different parts of a program. If everything were global, even small programs would become fragile very quickly.

Functions can call other functions, including ones you have written yourself, as shown in the following code: 

def square(n):
    return n * n
def print_square(n):
    result = square(n)
    print(result)
print_square(5)

This kind of composition is normal in Python. Small functions that do one thing well are easier to test and easier to reuse than large functions that try to do everything at once.

Default parameter values

It is also worth noting that Python allows default parameter values , as shown in the following code: 

def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    print(greeting, name)
greet("Alice")
greet("Bob", "Hi")

Defaults make functions flexible without making them complicated.

Grouping data and behavior with classes

So far, your Python code has been organized around variables and functions.

That works well for small scripts. But as programs grow, you often need a way to group related data and behavior together. That is what classes are for.

A class lets you define a new kind of object that has:

  • Data (called attributes)
  • Behavior (called methods)

Here is a basic class: 

class Task:
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title
        self.completed = False
    def mark_complete(self):
        self.completed = True

This class is a template for creating task objects.

Now you can create and use a task: 

task = Task("Write Chapter 8")
print(task.title)        # Write Chapter 8
print(task.completed)    # False
task.mark_complete()
print(task.completed)    # True

The __init__ method

The __init__ method runs when you create a new object: 

task = Task("Write Chapter 8")

It is used to set up the initial state of the object:

  • self refers to the current object
  • self.title and self.completed are attributes stored on that object

The __init__ method defines what data each instance of the class starts with. self is the object you are working with.

When you write: 

task.mark_complete()

Python turns that into: 

Task.mark_complete(task)

So self is the instance being passed in. You do not need to name it self , but you should. It is a strong convention and every Python developer expects it.

Making objects printable

By default, printing an object is not very helpful: 

print(task)

You might see something like: 

<__main__.Task object at 0x...>

You can improve this by defining a special method: 

def __str__(self) -> str:
    status = "✓" if self.completed else "✗"
    return f"{status} {self.title}"

Now: 

print(task)

produces: 

✗ Write Chapter 8

Let’s break down the method:

  • __str__ is a special method name that Python calls when converting an object to a string
  • self is the instance
  • -> str is a type hint that says this method returns a string

So, whenever you see def __str__(self) -> str: in a class, it means, When Python needs a string representation of this object, call this method and expect a string back .

You will see this pattern often in real Python code, especially in frameworks like Django.

Methods are functions inside a class

A method is a function defined inside a class: 

def mark_complete(self):
    self.completed = True

The only difference is that it operates on an instance ( self ).

This means everything you learned about functions still applies, including parameters, return values, and control flow. The difference is that methods usually work with the object’s internal data.

Adding more structure

You can expand the class naturally: 

class Task:
    def __init__(self, title, priority="medium"):
        self.title = title
        self.completed = False
        self.priority = priority
    def mark_complete(self):
        self.completed = True
    def is_high_priority(self):
        return self.priority == "high"
    def __str__(self) -> str:
        status = "✓" if self.completed else "✗"
        return f"{status} [{self.priority}] {self.title}"

Now the object has multiple attributes, multiple methods, and a clear string representation.

Why classes matter for Django

You do not need classes for simple scripts.

But Django uses classes everywhere.

For example:

  • Database models are classes
  • Views are often classes
  • Forms are classes

A Django model might look like this: 

class Task(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    completed = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    def __str__(self):
        return self.title

If you understand attributes, methods, __init__ , and __str__ then this code is not mysterious and scary. It is just a class with some framework-specific behavior.

Good practice : Use classes when you are modeling something with state (like a task, user, or order), you want to group related data and behavior, or you want multiple instances of the same kind of object. Avoid classes when a simple function or dictionary is enough or adding a class would make the code harder to follow.

Python’s optional type hints

Type hints are optional annotations that describe the expected types of variables, parameters, and return values. They help with clarity and tooling, but they do not change how Python runs.

Type hints let you document purpose directly in the code: 

def total_runtime(minutes: list[int]) -> int:
    return sum(minutes)

The preceding code says:

  • minutes parameter is expected to be a list of integers
  • total_runtime function is expected to return an integer

The code still runs exactly the same with or without the hints. Python does not enforce them at runtime. They are for humans and tools, not for the interpreter.

Type hints were added to address real problems in larger Python codebases. A function signature with type hints tells the reader how it is meant to be used without reading the implementation.

Code editors like VS Code can use type hints to:

  • Provide more accurate autocomplete
  • Highlight likely mistakes before you run the code
  • Improve navigation and refactoring

Static type checkers can analyze your code and warn you about type mismatches that would otherwise only show up at runtime.

Type hints do not turn Python into a statically typed language. They are optional, gradual, and non-enforced by default. You can add type hints only where they help, mix typed and untyped code freely, and ignore them entirely if you choose.

This is called gradual typing . It lets teams add type information over time without rewriting everything.

Type hints are most valuable at boundaries:

  • Function parameters and return values
  • Public APIs
  • Complex data structures
  • Code that is reused by others

They are less useful for short-lived variables inside small functions, where the type is obvious.

Type hints are not required to learn Python. Beginners can write clean, correct code without them. However, understanding what they are and why they exist prepares readers for modern Python codebases, documentation, and frameworks like Django for web development.

Prompt : Please show me some examples where type hints prevent bugs without changing runtime behavior.

Decorators

Sooner or later, you will see Python code like this: 

@something
def my_function():
    ...

That @something syntax is a decorator .

Decorators can look strange at first, but the core idea is simple: a decorator is a way to wrap one function with another function. This lets you add behavior without changing the original function body.

In other words, a decorator says, before or after this function runs, do some extra work .

This matters because Python treats functions as values. A function can be passed into another function, returned from a function, or replaced by another function.

Here is a very small example without using the @ syntax yet: 

def say_hello():
    print("Hello")
def wrapper(func):
    def inner():
        print("Before the function runs")
        func()
        print("After the function runs")
    return inner
say_hello = wrapper(say_hello)
say_hello()

This prints: 

Before the function runs
Hello
After the function runs

What happened?

  1. wrapper takes a function as input
  2. it defines a new function called inner
  3. inner runs some extra code, then calls the original function
  4. wrapper returns the new function
  5. say_hello is replaced with that wrapped version

That is the essence of a decorator.

The @ syntax

Python provides a cleaner way to write the same idea: 

def wrapper(func):
    def inner():
        print("Before the function runs")
        func()
        print("After the function runs")
    return inner
@wrapper
def say_hello():
    print("Hello")
say_hello()

This does the same thing as: 

say_hello = wrapper(say_hello)

The @wrapper line is a more readable shortcut.

Why decorators exist

Decorators are useful when you want to add behavior to many functions in a consistent way. Common uses include logging, timing, access control, caching, and validation.

For example, instead of adding “print a log message” inside ten different functions, you can write one decorator and apply it to all ten. This keeps the core function focused on its real job.

Here is a simple decorator that logs when a function is called: 

def log_call(func):
    def inner():
        print(f"Calling {func.__name__}")
        func()
    return inner
@log_call
def greet():
    print("Hi")
greet()

This prints: 

Calling greet
Hi

The function greet still does its own job. The decorator adds extra behavior around it.

Decorators and function parameters

One complication is that real functions often take arguments. A decorator must usually accept those too.

Here is a version that handles any positional and keyword arguments: 

def log_call(func):
    def inner(*args, **kwargs):
        print(f"Calling {func.__name__}")
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return inner
@log_call
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}")
greet("Alice")

You do not need to master *args and **kwargs yet. For now, know that they allow the wrapper to pass through whatever arguments the original function expects.

Why beginners should care

You do not need decorators for everyday beginner Python scripts.

But you do need to recognize them, because they appear often in real Python codebases and web frameworks. Django uses decorators for tasks such as requiring login or restricting HTTP methods. Other libraries use them for caching, validation, and configuration.

At this stage, do not rush to write decorators. Make sure you can recognize what they do.

  • A decorator wraps a function
  • The @name syntax is shorthand
  • Decorators add behavior without changing the original function body

    Good practice : When first learning Python, use decorators sparingly. Read them often, recognize what they do, and only write your own when the benefit is obvious.

If a decorator hides simple logic that would be clearer written normally, it is probably making the code worse, not better.

That leads us neatly on to other guidance for writing functions.

Guidance for writing functions

At this stage, you should focus on writing clear, simple functions:

  • Give them descriptive names
  • Make them do one thing
  • Pass data in using parameters
  • Get results out using return values

Functions are the point where Python code starts to scale. Almost everything you do next, working with files, handling user input, processing data, or building web applications, will rely heavily on functions.

But before we go any deeper, let’s get into handling errors and implementing strategies to debug problems.

Errors and debugging basics

Errors are a normal part of writing code. Every programmer, regardless of experience, sees error messages constantly. The difference between a beginner and an experienced developer is not how often errors happen, but how quickly they can understand and fix them. This section is about building that skill early.

When Python encounters a problem that it cannot recover from, it stops executing your program and prints an error message to the terminal. This message usually includes a traceback . A traceback is a report of what Python was doing when the error occurred.

Here is a simple example: 

print(message)

If message has not been defined, Python will respond with something like the following: 

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "example.py", line 1, in <module>
    print(message)
NameError: name 'message' is not defined

The preceding output may look intimidating, but it follows a predictable structure. The most important rule is this: read the last line first . The final line tells you the type of error and usually explains the problem in plain language. In this case, Python is telling you that you tried to use a variable that does not exist.

The lines above the final message show where the error happened. They include the file name and line number. In small programs, this is often enough to locate and fix the issue immediately.

Common errors

There are a few error types that beginners encounter frequently. Learning to recognize them early will save a lot of time.

A SyntaxError means Python could not understand the structure of your code. This often happens because of a missing colon, unmatched parentheses, or incorrect indentation, as shown in the following code: 

if x > 5
    print("Too big")

Here, the missing colon at the end of the if statement causes a syntax error before the program even runs.

An IndentationError is specific to Python and occurs when indentation is inconsistent or invalid, as shown in the following code: 

if True:
print("Hello")

Python expects the indented block after the colon. Errors like this are common when copying and pasting code or mixing tabs and spaces.

A TypeError happens when you use a value in a way that does not make sense for its type, as shown in the following code: 

age = "30"
age + 5

Python cannot add a string and an integer, so it raises a TypeError . The error message usually explains exactly what types were involved.

A ValueError occurs when a value is the right type but has an invalid value: 

age = int("thirty")

Here, Python knows how to convert strings to integers, but “thirty” is not a valid number.

But what if your code runs without throwing an error and still gives results that you do not expect? That’s where debugging skills become vital.

Debugging

Debugging starts with forming a simple hypothesis: what did I expect to happen, and what actually happened? Then you test that hypothesis by inspecting the program’s state.

One of the simplest and most effective debugging tools is still the print function, as shown in the following code: 

print(age)
print(type(age))

Printing values at key points in your program helps you confirm whether variables contain what you think they do. This approach is not elegant, but it is honest and effective, especially for beginners.

Make incremental changes

Another important habit is making small changes and re-running the program often. If you change ten things at once and something breaks, you do not know which change caused the problem. If you change one thing and re-run, the cause is obvious.

VS Code also provides basic debugging support through breakpoints and variable inspection, but you do not need to master the debugger yet. Understanding error messages and using simple print statements will take you surprisingly far.

Prompt : Please create a Python code file with a problem that needs debugging so that I can practice my debugging skills.

One final idea to internalize is that error messages are part of Python’s documentation. They are written by humans and are meant to be read. When Python says something is not defined, incompatible, or invalid, it is almost always telling the truth. Your job is to connect that message to the code you wrote.

AI coding assistants can also help when debugging. You can paste an error message or traceback and ask for an explanation or suggested fix. This can be useful, especially when you are stuck. However, treat AI as a guide rather than an authority. Always read the error yourself first and try to understand what it is telling you before relying on a generated explanation.

If you can stay calm, read the last line, check the line number, and test small changes, debugging becomes a repeatable process instead of a source of frustration. That skill will serve you far longer than memorizing syntax rules.

Handling runtime errors safely

try / except blocks are how Python handles runtime errors safely. They let you protect parts of your program that might fail and decide what should happen instead of letting the program crash.

A try block contains code that might fail. When something goes wrong, Python does not continue. It raises an exception, which means it stops normal execution and signals that an error has occurred.

If an exception occurs, Python stops executing the try block immediately and looks for a matching except block to handle the problem: 

try:
    age = int(input("How old are you? "))
except ValueError:
    print("Please enter a number.")

In the preceding code, if the age conversion succeeds, the except block is skipped. If it fails because the user enters something that cannot be converted to a number and the int function raises a ValueError , the program prints a friendly message instead of crashing.

User input is one of the most common sources of errors. Users type unexpected values, press Enter , or paste nonsense. We can handle this common issue easily: 

try:
    quantity = int(input("Quantity: "))
    price = float(input("Price: "))
    total = quantity * price
    print(f"Total: {total}")
except ValueError:
    print("Invalid input. Please enter numbers only.")

Here, both conversions are protected. If either fails, the program handles it gracefully.

File operations fail for reasons outside your control: missing files, permissions, or disk issues. Again, we can handle these situations: 

try:
    with open("config.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        text = file.read()
except OSError:
    print("Could not read configuration file.")

Without the try / except , the program would crash even though the error is not necessarily fatal.

Catching specific exception types is important. This avoids hiding unrelated bugs. Good practice is to specify which error type you expect: 

try:
    result = 10 / value
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Cannot divide by zero.")

Other errors will still stop the program. Specific exceptions make error handling clearer and safer.

Good error handling anticipates what can go wrong, catches only what it understands, and leaves everything else visible so problems can be fixed properly.

Prompt : How should I decide whether to catch an exception or let it crash?

Now we will move on to structuring your code, which is especially important when you work on large Python projects.

Modules, imports, and packages

As programs grow, putting all your code into a single file quickly becomes unmanageable. Python solves this problem with modules . A module is simply a Python file. Any .py file can be used as a module, and modules let you organize code and reuse it across multiple programs.

Importing standard modules

At the most basic level, you make a module available in your current code file by importing the module , as shown in the following code: 

import math

The preceding code tells Python to load another module and make its contents available to your program. In this case, math is part of Python’s standard library, which means it ships with Python itself.

Once imported, you access names inside a module using dot notation, as shown in the following code: 

import math
result = math.sqrt(16)
print(result)

Here, math.sqrt refers to the sqrt function defined inside the math module. This explicit naming is intentional. It avoids confusion about where functions come from and makes code easier to read.

Python also allows you to import specific names from a module: 

from math import sqrt
result = sqrt(16)

This is shorter, but it comes with a trade-off. When you import names directly, it can be harder to tell where they originated, especially in larger programs. For beginners, using import module_name and dot notation is usually clearer.

Defining your own modules

Modules are not limited to the standard library. You can import your own Python files as well. Suppose you have two files in the same folder:

Here is a file named helpers.py : 

def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

Here is a file named main.py : 

import helpers
helpers.greet("Alice")

When Python runs main.py , it looks for a file called helpers.py in the same directory and loads it as a module. This allows you to separate related code into logical units without any special configuration.

It is important to understand that when a module is imported, Python executes the code at the top level of that file once. This can lead to surprising behavior if a module contains code that runs immediately.

For example: 

print("Loading helpers module")

If this line is at the top of helpers.py , it will run as soon as the module is imported. This is why modules usually contain only function definitions and constants, and not any executable logic.

Prompt : Please explain how Python decides where to look when importing a module.

Preventing execution in modules

There is a common Python pattern to control this behavior: 

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("This file is being run directly")

When a file is run directly, __name__ is set to "__main__" . When it is imported, __name__ is set to the module’s name instead. This allows a file to behave both as a script and as an importable module.

Prompt : Why does Python execute module-level code on import? Please explain __name__ == '__main__' in more depth with real examples.

What’s important for beginners about modules

At this stage, you do not need to memorize Python’s full import system. What matters is understanding:

  • A module is a .py file
  • Importing a module makes its functions and constants available
  • Python executes a module once when it is first imported
  • Code meant for reuse should live inside functions

Modules are how Python scales from small scripts to real applications. They are also how you access the standard library and, later, third-party packages.

Prompt : Please show me some common mistakes with circular imports and how to avoid them.

Packages and how they relate to modules

At some point, you will want to use code that does not come with Python itself. Python solves this through packages . Understanding what a package is, how to install one, and how it relates to modules will remove a lot of mystery from Python development:

  • A module is a single Python file. If you have a file called utils.py that contains utility function definitions, that file is a module.
  • A package is a collection of one or more modules, usually organized into folders. Packages often provide a cohesive set of related functionality. For example, a package might include modules for HTTP requests, data parsing, and error handling, all grouped under one name.

From the developer’s point of view, both modules and packages are accessed using import . Python does not care whether the name you import comes from a single file or a whole directory structure.

For example, you might import two modules from the standard library, as shown in the following code: 

import math
import json

This works the same way for third-party packages once they are installed.

Installing packages

Python packages are installed using a tool called pip , which stands for Python package installer . Pip downloads packages from the Python Package Index, commonly called PyPI, which is the central repository for Python packages maintained by the community.

Installing a package is done from the command line, usually inside an activated virtual environment, as shown in the following command: 

pip install requests

This command downloads the requests package and installs it into the active Python environment. Later in this chapter, you will learn about virtual environments. One of their benefits is that, if you are using a virtual environment, the package is installed only there, which avoids polluting your system with packages.

Once installed, you can import it into your code like a standard library module, as shown in the following code: 

import requests
response = requests.get("https://example.com")
print(response.status_code)

Installing a package does not magically change Python’s syntax or behavior. It simply makes additional modules available for import.

How packages work

Behind the scenes, Python searches a list of directories, known as sys.path , to find modules and packages. When you install a package with pip , it places files into one of these directories inside your environment. When you write import requests , Python looks through those locations until it finds a matching package.

You do not need to inspect sys.path or understand Python’s full import algorithm at this stage. The important idea is that installation affects availability, not usage. Importing is how you actually use the code.

Package versions

It is also common to install a specific version of a package, as shown in the following command: 

pip install requests==2.31.0

This matters because packages evolve. Code written against one version may not behave the same way against another. Virtual environments exist largely to manage this reality.

As projects grow, developers usually record installed packages in a file called requirements.txt : 

requests==2.31.0

This file is not magic. It is simply a list of packages and versions. You can install all the packages listed, as shown in the following code: 

pip install -r requirements.txt

The preceding command tells pip to install everything listed. This makes it easy to recreate the same environment on another machine or in a deployment system.

Prompt : Please explain requirements.txt vs tools like pip-tools or poetry

One final point that often trips up beginners: installing a package and importing it are separate steps. If you try to import a package that is not installed in the active environment, Python will raise a ModuleNotFoundError . When this happens, the fix is almost always to install the package into the environment you are currently using.

If you remember only one rule from this section, make it this:

  • Pip installs packages into an environment
  • Import uses those installed packages in your code

Once that distinction is clear, Python’s packaging story becomes far less confusing and much more predictable.

We’ve mentioned virtual environments a few times while talking about packages. Let’s look at them next.

Virtual environments

Sooner or later, every Python developer runs into a confusing situation: one project works, another suddenly breaks, and the error message mentions a package version you do not remember installing.

The problem

Virtual environments exist to prevent exactly this problem. They are not an advanced feature, but they are something you should understand conceptually early, even if you do not use them heavily yet.

By default, when you install a Python package, it is installed into a shared location associated with your Python interpreter. If all your projects share the same interpreter and the same installed packages, you can easily end up with conflicts. One project might need version 1 of a library, another might need version 2, and only one of them can win. This is not hypothetical. It happens a lot in real-world Python work.

Prompt : Please explain the difference between system Python and virtual environments.

The solution

A virtual environment is a self-contained Python environment that lives inside a project. It has its own Python interpreter and its own set of installed packages, isolated from everything else on your system. When you activate a virtual environment, Python commands and package installs apply only to that environment.

The basic rule is simple:

  • One project equals one virtual environment
  • Each environment has its own dependencies
  • Projects do not interfere with each other

Python includes built-in support for virtual environments through the venv module, so no extra tools are required.

Prompt : Please show me what goes wrong when multiple projects share one environment.

Creating a virtual environment

Creating a virtual environment is usually done from the command line, inside your project folder, as shown in the following command: 

python -m venv .venv

This creates a folder called .venv containing a copy of the Python interpreter and supporting files. The name .venv is a convention. The leading dot makes the folder less visually noisy, and many tools recognize it automatically.

Good practice : The dot prefix for the folder name is a convention. You can name the folder anything. Using venv is the older and still very common convention. Many tutorials and official examples use venv , so it aligns well with most learning materials. The downside is that the folder appears alongside your source code in alphabetical order, which some people find visually noisy, especially in larger projects.

Using .venv follows the Unix convention that directories starting with a dot are hidden by default on macOS and Linux. This keeps the project root visually cleaner and reinforces the idea that the virtual environment is an implementation detail rather than application code. Tools such as VS Code, Poetry, and some Python linters and formatters explicitly look for .venv and will auto-detect it without extra configuration. The trade-off is that hidden directories can be confusing for beginners. For professional projects, especially those using Python tooling and aiming for a tidy project root, .venv is increasingly popular.

Once created, the environment must be activated. Activating an environment is different depending on your OS:

  • On Windows, enter the following command: 

    .venv\Scripts\activate

  • On macOS and Linux, enter the following command: 

    source .venv/bin/activate

After activation, the terminal prompt usually changes to show the environment name. This is your visual cue that the environment is active. From this point on, running python or pip refers to the virtual environment, not the system-wide Python.

When you install packages inside an active environment, they are isolated to that project: 

pip install requests

Another project, with a different environment, will not see that package unless it installs it explicitly.

VS Code and virtual environments

VS Code integrates well with virtual environments. When a .venv folder exists, the Python extension will usually detect it and offer to use it automatically. You can also select it manually using the Python interpreter selector in the bottom-right corner of the editor. Once selected, running Python files from VS Code uses the virtual environment interpreter behind the scenes.

Prompt : Please explain how VS Code detects and uses virtual environments.

At this stage, you do not need to know the advanced features. What matters is understanding why virtual environments exist and recognizing them when you see them.

You will often encounter files like requirements.txt or commands like: 

pip install -r requirements.txt

These are simply ways to describe and reproduce the packages installed in a virtual environment. They make it possible for someone else, or a deployment system, to recreate the same setup reliably.

Good practice : Do not install project dependencies into your system Python once you start using virtual environments regularly. Mixing approaches leads to confusion very quickly.

In short, virtual environments allow many projects to coexist on the same machine without conflict. You do not need to use them for every tiny experiment, but for anything that matters or lasts longer than a single session, they are the correct default. Understanding this now will save you hours of frustration later.

Now let’s look at how to read and write to the filesystem. This is where your Python projects “remember” previous work they’ve done.

File input and output

So far, most of your Python programs have lived entirely in memory. When the program ends, all its data disappears. File input and output, usually shortened to file I/O, is how programs read data from disk and write data back so it can be reused later.

At the most basic level, working with files involves three steps:

  1. Open a file.
  2. Read from it or write to it.
  3. Close it.

Python hides much of this ceremony for you, but the underlying model is still the same.

Writing text to a file

The simplest way to write text to a file is to open it in write mode. If the file does not exist, Python creates it. If it does exist, Python overwrites it.

For example, to open or create a new file named example.txt , and write a short message to it, as shown in the following code: 

with open("example.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Hello, file")

Note the following about the preceding code:

  • The with statement is important. It ensures the file is properly closed even if something goes wrong. You should treat with as the default way to work with files. The with statement isn’t only for files, it’s used for database connections, network requests, and any context manager, which is any object that can set up and tear down resources automatically.
  • The "w" mode means write. There are other modes, but these are the most common:
    • "w" write, replacing the file
    • "a" append, adding to the end of the file
    • "r" read, which is the default

If you want to add content instead of replacing it, use append mode, as shown in the following code: 

with open("example.txt", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("\nAnother line")

Reading text from a file

Reading works the same way, but with the read mode, as shown in the following code: 

with open("example.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    contents = file.read()
print(contents)

This reads the entire file into a single string. For small files like configuration files, logs, or simple data files, this is perfectly reasonable.

You can also read line by line, which is useful for larger files, as shown in the following code: 

with open("example.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.strip())

Each line includes a trailing newline character, which is why strip() is often used.

Files are just big strings

One important idea to internalize is that text files are just strings on disk. When you read a file, you get a string. When you write to a file, you are writing a string. Everything you learned in the strings section applies directly here.

That is why formats like CSV, JSON, and even HTML are approachable in Python. They are text first, structure second.

Prompt : Please explain why files are treated as strings in Python.

Using JSON for structured data

It is common to use JSON instead of inventing your own file format. JSON is a text-based format designed to represent structured data, and it maps cleanly onto Python’s data structures:

  • JSON objects map to Python dictionaries
  • JSON arrays map to Python lists
  • Strings, numbers, Booleans, and null map naturally

Instead of manually writing strings to a file, you can use the json module from the standard library, as shown in the following code: 

import json
text = json.dumps(data, indent=2)

This converts Python data structures into a formatted string. Writing that string to disk is normal file I/O.

Reading JSON works in reverse, as shown in the following code: 

data = json.loads(text)

The file itself is still plain text. JSON simply gives that text a predictable structure.

Paths and file locations

In small scripts, file names like "tasks.json" work because Python looks in the current working directory. In real programs, paths can get more complex. A commonly used module for handling paths is pathlib , as shown in the following code: 

from pathlib import Path
DATA_FILE = Path("tasks.json")

Path objects make file operations clearer and safer than manipulating strings manually, as shown in the following code: 

DATA_FILE.exists()
DATA_FILE.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
DATA_FILE.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")

These are convenience methods built on top of normal file I/O. They still follow the same rules, but with less boilerplate.

Common file I/O errors

File operations can fail for reasons outside your program’s control:

  • The file does not exist.
  • The file is locked or unreadable.
  • The disk is full.
  • The contents are not in the format you expect.

That is why file I/O is often wrapped in try and except blocks, as shown in the following code: 

try:
    text = DATA_FILE.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
except OSError:
    print("Could not read file")

The preceding code prevents your program from crashing and lets you decide how to recover.

File I/O summary

File I/O is what gives a programming project permanence. Without it, tasks vanish when the program exits. With it, your program maintains state across runs.

The most important takeaway from this section is not the specific functions. It is this pattern:

  • Convert in-memory data to text.
  • Write that text to disk.
  • Read it back later.
  • Convert it back into Python data structures.

That pattern appears everywhere in Python development: configuration files, logs, caches, databases, and web APIs. If you understand file I/O at this level, nothing about saving and loading data later will feel mysterious.

Prompt : Please show me some common file I/O mistakes and how to avoid data loss.

Now let’s build a complete mini-project using everything you’ve learned in this chapter.

A small, cohesive mini-project

In the final section of this chapter, we will build a small, cohesive mini-project: a Command-line Task Tracker.

This mini-project ties together everything you have learned so far: variables, conditionals, loops, data structures, functions, modules/imports, strings (including f-strings), file I/O, and basic error handling.

You will build a small command-line task tracker that can:

  1. Add a task
  2. List tasks
  3. Mark a task as done
  4. Delete a task
  5. Save and load tasks from a JSON file so they persist between runs

You will keep the data model simple: a list of dictionaries. Each task will look like this: 

{"title": "Buy milk", "done": False}

Writing the code

Create a new file in VS Code called task_tracker.py and paste the following code. Read it top-to-bottom first, then run it, then tweak it.

You can download this entire file from the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/Code/Chapter08/python-basics/task_tracker.py

Good practice : If your code uses type hints, especially with classes or larger projects, add from __future__ import annotations at the top of the file and forget about it. It removes edge cases without adding complexity. For modern Python (3.10+), it is generally a good default to include this import at the top of your files if you are using type hints. It makes annotations more flexible and avoids subtle issues as your code grows. In newer Python versions (3.13+), this behavior is becoming the default, so this import will eventually no longer be necessary. 

from __future__ import annotations
import json
from pathlib import Path
DATA_FILE = Path("tasks.json")
def load_tasks() -> list[dict]:
    """Load tasks from disk. If the file doesn't exist yet, return an empty list."""
    if not DATA_FILE.exists():
        return []
    try:
        text = DATA_FILE.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        data = json.loads(text)
        # Defensive check: ensure it's a list of dicts.
        if not isinstance(data, list):
            return []
        cleaned: list[dict] = []
        for item in data:
            if isinstance(item, dict) and "title" in item and "done" in item:
                cleaned.append({"title": str(item["title"]), "done": bool(item["done"])})
        return cleaned
    except (OSError, json.JSONDecodeError):
        # File can't be read or contains invalid JSON.
        return []
def save_tasks(tasks: list[dict]) -> None:
    """Save tasks to disk as JSON."""
    try:
        text = json.dumps(tasks, indent=2)
        DATA_FILE.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
    except OSError:
        print("Warning: could not save tasks to disk.")
def add_task(tasks: list[dict]) -> None:
    title = input("Task title: ").strip()
    if not title:
        print("Task title cannot be empty.")
        return
    tasks.append({"title": title, "done": False})
    save_tasks(tasks)
    print(f'Added: "{title}"')
def list_tasks(tasks: list[dict]) -> None:
    if not tasks:
        print("No tasks yet. Add one with: add")
        return
    for i, task in enumerate(tasks, start=1):
        status = "✓" if task["done"] else " "
        print(f"{i:>2}. [{status}] {task['title']}")
def mark_done(tasks: list[dict]) -> None:
    if not tasks:
        print("No tasks to mark as done.")
        return
    raw = input("Task number to mark done: ").strip()
    try:
        index = int(raw) - 1
    except ValueError:
        print("Please enter a valid number.")
        return
    if index < 0 or index >= len(tasks):
        print("That task number is out of range.")
        return
    tasks[index]["done"] = True
    save_tasks(tasks)
    print(f'Marked done: "{tasks[index]["title"]}"')
def delete_task(tasks: list[dict]) -> None:
    if not tasks:
        print("No tasks to delete.")
        return
    raw = input("Task number to delete: ").strip()
    try:
        index = int(raw) - 1
    except ValueError:
        print("Please enter a valid number.")
        return
    if index < 0 or index >= len(tasks):
        print("That task number is out of range.")
        return
    removed = tasks.pop(index)
    save_tasks(tasks)
    print(f'Deleted: "{removed["title"]}"')
def print_help() -> None:
    print("Commands:")
    print("  add     Add a new task")
    print("  list    List all tasks")
    print("  done    Mark a task as done")
    print("  delete  Delete a task")
    print("  help    Show this help")
    print("  quit    Exit the program")
def main() -> None:
    tasks = load_tasks()
    print("Task Tracker")
    print_help()
    while True:
        command = input("\n> ").strip().lower()
        if command == "add":
            add_task(tasks)
        elif command == "list":
            list_tasks(tasks)
        elif command == "done":
            mark_done(tasks)
        elif command == "delete":
            delete_task(tasks)
        elif command == "help":
            print_help()
        elif command in {"quit", "exit"}:
            print("Goodbye.")
            break
        elif command == "":
            continue
        else:
            print("Unknown command. Type: help")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Trying the project

Run the code file and try this quick session:

  2. add : “Make tea”
  3. list
  4. done : 2
  5. list
  6. Quit and run it again. Your tasks should still be there, because they were saved to tasks.json .

What this mini-project reinforces

This mini-project applied the following knowledge:

  • Data structures: a list of dictionaries is a very common Python pattern
  • Functions: each command is implemented as a function that operates on the shared tasks list
  • Modules/imports: you used json and pathlib from the standard library
  • Strings: strip() , lower() , f-strings, and clean printing
  • Errors and debugging: try / except prevents the program from crashing on invalid input or a bad JSON file

Django – Web Development on the Backend

This chapter introduces Django, a practical, opinionated web framework for building real applications without writing every piece of routing, forms, authentication, and database code yourself. You will see how Django fits into the broader web stack you have already learned, especially HTML, CSS, SQL, and Python, and why it includes common web features such as routing, forms, authentication, database migrations, and an admin interface instead of expecting you to assemble them yourself. You do not need to memorize every Django class, function, setting, and command. Focus on how Django structures a web project and why its conventions exist.

You will start by setting up a minimal Django project named Scribble for managing blog posts, and run it locally, then move through the core building blocks that make Django work, including the Model-View-Template ( MVT ) pattern:

  • Models for cleanly mapping Python code to relational database tables
  • Views for handling requests and passing data from the server to the browser
  • Templates for rendering dynamic HTML without messily mixing logic and presentation

Along the way, you will explore the Django admin interface, which demonstrates how much functionality Django gives you for free once your models are defined.

By the end of the chapter, you should feel comfortable navigating a Django project and understand how its major parts cooperate to form a working web application. You will have a working Django project, a clear understanding of how models, views, and templates fit together, practical experience defining data and rendering dynamic pages, and confidence using the Django admin interface to inspect and manage your application’s data.

In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:

  • Introducing Django
  • Setting up Django
  • Django URL patterns and routing
  • Django models
  • Django views and templates
  • Serving static files
  • Django admin interface
  • Django forms
  • Django settings and configuration
  • Error handling and debugging
  • Authentication and authorization

Suggested chatbot prompts with example responses for this chapter can be found at the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/prompts/ch09-django/readme.md

Introducing Django

Django is a high-level Python web framework for building websites that store and retrieve data. Its core idea is that most web applications share the same fundamental problems, so the framework should solve those problems once, in a consistent way, instead of forcing every developer to reinvent them. As a result, Django provides routing, database access, HTML templating, authentication, forms, security protections, and an admin interface out of the box.

MVT pattern

Architecturally, Django follows what it calls the MVT pattern : Model, View, Template . This is closely related to the more widely known MVC pattern : Model, View, Controller , but with slightly different naming that reflects Django’s specific way of dividing responsibilities:

  • Django’s Models represent the data layer. They define your database schema using Python classes, and Django handles translating those definitions into SQL and database tables.
  • Django’s Templates are responsible for presentation. They generate HTML by combining static markup with dynamic data, while keeping most application logic out of the template itself.
  • Django’s Views coordinate the request. A view receives a Hypertext Transfer Protocol ( HTTP ) request, interacts with models if needed, and returns an HTTP response, often by rendering a template with some context data.

If you are used to MVC, Django’s View roughly corresponds to a Controller, and Django’s URL configuration and request handling cover work that some frameworks would put in a controller layer. Uniform Resource Locator ( URL ) configuration maps incoming requests to view functions or classes, which keeps request handling explicit and easy to follow. This separation of concerns makes Django applications easier to understand as they grow, because models hold data rules, views handle requests, and templates render HTML.

A summary comparison of the components of Django’s MVT and MVC patterns is shown in Table 9.1 :

Concept

MVT

MVC

Incoming request handled by:

URL configuration

Route

Logic executed by:

View

Controller

Data structure defined by:

Model

Model

Web page response generated by:

Template

View

Table 9.1: Comparing MVT and MVC design patterns

Prompt : Please explain Django’s MVT architecture again, but this time trace a single HTTP request step by step from browser to database and back.

Opinionated and convention-driven

Django is popular partly because it gives you working features early. It is opinionated and convention-driven: follow Django’s structure, and you get routing, database access, forms, authentication, and admin tools with little setup.

For example, defining a model automatically gives you database tables, a Python API for querying data, and an admin interface for managing records.

Common tasks like form validation, user authentication, and protection against common security issues are already solved, so you can spend time building features instead of infrastructure.

Django is especially well-suited to projects where correctness, maintainability, and development speed matter more than optimizing every performance detail from day one. Its design choices favor clarity and explicitness, which is why it is widely used for content-driven sites, internal tools, APIs, and data-heavy applications.

Prompt : What are the most common Django conventions that beginners try to fight, and why is it usually better to follow them?

Django projects versus Django apps

A useful concept to understand early is the difference between a Django project and a Django app:

  • A Django project represents the entire website or system you are building.
  • A Django app is a self-contained unit of functionality within that project. For example, a blog, a user accounts system, or a comments feature could each be separate apps.

A single Django project is made up of one or more apps, even if you only create one app to begin with. This structure encourages modular design and makes it easier to reuse or reorganize functionality as a project grows.

Prompt : Please show me a simple diagram of how Django projects and apps relate to each other in a real-world application.

What does batteries included mean?

Django is often described as “batteries included”, and that phrase is worth unpacking. Django deliberately ships with solutions for common web development problems rather than leaving them as optional add-ons. Database migrations, authentication, form handling, security protections, and an administrative interface are all part of the core framework.

A database migration is a set of instructions that tells your database how to change its structure. Instead of directly editing the database, you write changes like adding a new column called date_of_birth , renaming that column, or creating a new table. Each of these changes is saved as a small file, usually in your project.

Where other web frameworks leave those features to additional layers on top of their framework, like a content management system ( CMS ), Django includes them.

This means Django projects tend to look similar to each other, which makes them easier to understand, maintain, and hand over to other developers.

The trade-off is that Django expects you to follow its conventions, but in return, you get routing, forms, authentication, migrations, static-file handling, and admin tools with little setup.

Request-response lifecycle

At a high level, Django applications follow a clear request–response lifecycle:

  1. A browser sends an HTTP request to your web server.
  2. Django matches that request against a set of URL patterns defined by path() to decide which view should handle it.
  3. The view runs Python code, optionally queries the database through models like Post.objects.filter() , and produces an HTTP response. In many cases, that response is HTML generated by rendering a template, but it could also be JavaScript Object Notation (JSON), a redirect, or an error page.
  4. This response is returned to the web browser to display to the user, or to the client app that made the request if it is just data.

Keeping this flow in mind makes it much easier to understand how the different Django components cooperate.

Django is a useful test of how well you understand a web application. An AI assistant can write a path() call or a Post.objects.filter() query quickly. The part you still have to judge is where that code belongs. Should this check live in the view, the model, the form, or middleware? What should happen if the post is missing, unpublished, or requested by the wrong user?

That is why Django is worth learning as a system, not as a pile of snippets. URLs choose views. Views make decisions. Models define and protect data. Templates render HTML. Middleware handles site-wide behavior. Settings describe the environment. When those pieces are clear in your head, generated code is much easier to review, debug, and reject when it puts logic in the wrong place.

Middleware

Before your view ever sees a request, Django runs it through a stack of middleware , which acts like a pipeline of processing steps. Each layer gets a chance to inspect or modify the request on the way in, and the response on the way out. This is how Django handles behavior that applies across the whole site without cluttering your view code.

Middleware is responsible for things that apply across your entire application, not just a single page. This includes session handling, security checks like cross-site request forgery ( CSRF ) protection, and user authentication. For example, when you access request.user in a view, that value has already been attached by Django’s authentication middleware earlier in the pipeline.

This design keeps your views focused on your app’s logic, while middleware handles the site-wide behavior around it. You are unlikely to write your own middleware at the start of learning Django, but understanding that it sits between the browser and your view helps explain how Django can provide so much functionality automatically, before your code even runs.

Beginner-friendly, but not only for small projects

Although Django is approachable for beginners, it is not a toy framework. It is designed to scale from small personal projects to large, long-lived applications. Many real-world systems start as simple Django projects and grow over time without changing frameworks.

Django’s emphasis on explicit structure, clear separation of responsibilities, and predictable conventions helps keep complexity under control as applications evolve.

Django releases

Django has a very regular cadence for releases:

  • Feature releases every eight months or so
  • Every few releases, one is designated long-term support ( LTS )
  • LTS releases receive security and data-loss fixes for much longer than non-LTS releases

An LTS release is designed to be boring in the best sense. Many professional Django teams standardize on LTS releases only. If you want to target an LTS release, the latest at the time of publishing is Django 5.2, which will be supported until April 2028. Many professional Django teams standardize on LTS releases for that reason.

This book targets Django 6.0, which is a non-LTS release. It is supported until April 2027. Later versions will exist by the time you read this book, but the concepts and code shown here remain valid. For example, you should be able to target 6.1 when it releases in August 2026, or 6.2 in April 2027, which is expected to be the next LTS release and will be supported until April 2030.

You can learn more about the current supported versions of Django at the following link: https://www.djangoproject.com/download/#supported-versions

Alternatives to Django

Although I chose Django for this book, it is not the only web framework for Python.

Flask is probably the most well-known alternative. It is much lighter than Django and gives you just the basics for handling HTTP requests and routing. You add other components yourself as needed. This makes Flask more flexible, but also means you need to make more decisions. You can learn more about Flask at the following link: https://flask.palletsprojects.com/

FastAPI is a newer framework that has become very popular for building APIs. It focuses on performance, modern Python features like type hints, and automatic documentation generation. It is widely used for backend services and AI-related applications. You can learn more about FastAPI at the following link: https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/

Pyramid sits somewhere in between Django and Flask. It allows you to start small and scale up in complexity, but it is less commonly used today than Flask or FastAPI. You can learn more about Pyramid at the following link: https://docs.pylonsproject.org/projects/pyramid/

In practice, most developers choose between three main options:

  • Django for full-featured web applications
  • Flask for simple or flexible projects
  • FastAPI for APIs and high-performance services

For this book, Django is a sensible choice. It gives new web developers a structured environment with fewer decisions to make, which aligns well with your goal of teaching concepts rather than forcing readers to assemble a stack from scratch.

Expectations for this chapter

The focus in this chapter is on Django’s core ideas: defining models, handling requests, rendering templates, and using the admin interface.

Django includes many other features, such as authentication systems and API tooling for building web services, but those build on the same foundations you will learn here.

Once you understand these basics, the rest of the framework becomes much easier to approach. With those ideas in place, you are ready to move on to creating your first Django project and seeing these ideas in action.

Setting up Django

Before writing any Django code, you need a working Python environment and a clean project setup. Django runs anywhere Python runs, so the steps are broadly the same on Windows, macOS, and Linux. The main differences are command syntax and file paths, which will be pointed out where relevant.

Creating and activating a virtual environment

Next, we will create a virtual environment for your Django project. This isolates your project’s dependencies from the rest of your system and avoids version conflicts later.

Create a folder named Chapter09 . Inside that folder, run the virtual environment command:

  • On Windows, run: python -m venv .venv
  • On macOS and Linux, run: python3 -m venv .venv

This creates a .venv folder containing a private Python installation for this project.

Now activate the virtual environment:

  • On Windows, run: .venv\Scripts\activate
  • On macOS and Linux, run: source .venv/bin/activate

When activation succeeds, your terminal prompt will usually change to show the virtual environment name: 

(.venv) C:\web-dev-ai\Code\Chapter09>

From this point on, any Python packages you install will be limited to this project.

pip install django

Good practice : A Django project contains generated files, local settings, cache folders, and sometimes secrets. When you use source control systems like Git, you should be careful not to blindly add everything in a Django project to the repository. For example, directories like .venv and __pycache__ , database files like db.sqlite3 , and secrets like passwords should be excluded.
