10

Bash/Shell – Command-Line Skills for Developers

Scripting with Bash or a similar shell may seem separate from web development, but it is never far away. Whether you are creating a new project, installing dependencies, running a development server, managing files, or deploying code, you will repeatedly find yourself typing commands into a terminal.

Shells like Bourne Again Shell ( Bash ) and Z Shell ( Zsh ) let you turn one-off commands into repeatable steps that you can save, edit, and run again later.

Remember that in Stack Overflow’s 2025 survey of 31,771 developers, 48.7% said they have done extensive development work with Bash/Shell. That makes shell scripting worth learning even if you mainly think of yourself as a web developer.

Bash is the default shell on most Linux systems and has long been central to macOS and server environments. Even on Windows, modern development environments expose Bash through tools like Windows Subsystem for Linux and Git Bash. As a result, Bash has become a common language across platforms.

Since macOS Catalina in 2019, the default shell on Macs is Zsh, not Bash. The basic commands in this chapter work identically in both shells. macOS also ships with a rather old version of Bash. To install an updated Bash on macOS, use the following Homebrew command: brew install bash . Alternatively, you can use Zsh because the differences won’t matter for this chapter’s content.

This chapter deliberately keeps Bash grounded in everyday developer tasks rather than treating it as a full programming language to be mastered in isolation. You will learn what Bash is and how it fits into the wider idea of a shell, practice the core commands used to navigate and manipulate files and then write a small script that automates a real task. You should finish the chapter feeling comfortable reading and adapting shell commands, even if you never write complex scripts entirely on your own.

Because the command line can feel unforgiving, we will also look at how AI tools can help you check your understanding. Used well, they can explain unfamiliar commands, suggest safer alternatives, and help you understand why something failed rather than just pasting in a fix you do not understand.

By the end of this chapter, you will understand what Bash does, navigate the file system, run common commands, write a simple Bash script, and use AI tools to check unfamiliar commands before you run them.

In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:

  • Introducing Bash
  • Setting up Bash on Windows
  • Basic commands
  • Writing a simple script
  • Automating your Django development
  • Using AI for shell help

Suggested chatbot prompts with example responses for this chapter can be found at the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/prompts/ch10-bash/readme.md

Introducing Bash

Bash stands for Bourne Again Shell , and it is both a Unix shell and a command language. In simple terms, Bash is the program that sits between you and the operating system, reading the commands you type and turning them into actions.

When you open a terminal window and type something like python manage.py runserver or npm install , you are not talking directly to Python or Node. You are talking to Bash, and Bash is responsible for launching those programs, passing arguments to them, and handling their output.

Prompt : Please explain the difference between Bash, a shell, and a terminal, with concrete examples.

Shell scripting

A shell is a user interface for the operating system, just not a graphical one. Instead of clicking icons or menus, you issue text commands. Unix systems have always treated this text-based interface as a normal way of working, which is why shells like Bash became so scriptable and expressive. Over time, Bash also became a programming language, with variables, conditionals, loops, and functions. This allows you to move beyond individual commands and start automating sequences of tasks.

Bash is especially useful in development because so many tools are designed around it. Running a local development server, starting and stopping background processes, cleaning build directories, or chaining together multiple tools are all straightforward in Bash.

Deployment scripts are almost always written as shell scripts. Continuous integration systems execute Bash commands to build, test, and deploy applications. Dockerfiles rely heavily on shell commands to assemble images. Even when you are using other development tools, Bash is often the glue holding everything together.

Script portability

Another reason Bash matters is portability. A Bash script written on your machine will usually run unchanged on a Linux server in the cloud. This shared environment is one of the reasons cloud infrastructure, DevOps practices, and containerization took off so quickly. When documentation says run the following commands , it is almost always assuming a Bash-like shell, even if it does not say so explicitly.

Terminals and shells

It is also worth separating Bash from the terminal itself. The terminal is just the window or application that displays text and accepts input. Bash is the program running inside that terminal. Other shells exist, such as zsh or fish , but Bash remains the common baseline. Even if your system uses a different default shell, Bash is usually installed and widely supported, which is why it is still taught and referenced so often.

At the outermost layer is the terminal window. This is just a user interface. On Windows, it might be Windows Terminal , on macOS Terminal.app , and on Linux, one of many terminal emulators. Its job is simple: display text and send your keystrokes somewhere. The terminal does not understand commands.

Running inside the terminal is the shell, in this case, Bash. Bash is a program. It reads the text you type, interprets it, keeps track of state such as the current directory and environment variables, and decides what to do next. When you press Enter , Bash parses the command line, expands variables, applies quoting rules, and resolves what should be executed.

When Bash recognizes a command like ls , python , or docker , it then launches an external program. These programs are separate executables provided by the operating system or installed tools. Bash starts them as child processes, passes arguments to them, and waits for them to finish. Their output flows back through Bash and is displayed by the terminal.

So, the flow is always: 

You type text → the terminal sends it to Bash → Bash interprets it → Bash runs programs → output flows back up to the terminal.

This flow explains several beginner confusions:

  • Why changing shells does not change the terminal window
  • Why Bash scripts can run Python, Docker, Git, or any other tool
  • Why errors often come from the program you launched, not from Bash itself
  • Why the same Bash command behaves the same on macOS, Linux, WSL, and servers

Bash gives you direct, scriptable control over your development environment. You do not need to know everything it can do, but understanding the basics will make many everyday tasks faster, clearer, and less mysterious.

To summarize:

  • Terminal : window (just input/output)
  • Shell (Bash) : interpreter (understands commands)
  • Programs : actual tools ( ls , python , docker )

    Prompt : Why is Bash still widely used when alternative shells like zsh and fish exist?

Common syntax across commands

Bash commands usually follow a predictable shape: a command name , followed by options (sometimes called flags), followed by arguments. Making this clear early helps you recognize patterns without needing to memorize everything.

For example: 

ls -l src
  • ls is the command (to list files)
  • -l is an option (to use long, detailed format)
  • src is an argument (the name of a folder to list) 
docker run -p 8000:8000 image-name
  • docker is the command (to use Docker)
  • run is a subcommand (what you want Docker to do)
  • -p is an option (publish a port)
  • 8000:8000 is an argument (map local port to container port)
  • image-name is an argument (the name of an image to run)

You do not need to memorize all the options yet. Focus on recognizing this space-delimited structure, as it will make new commands much easier to understand later.

Prompt : Please explain the general structure of a Bash command: command name, options, and arguments.

Stateful commands

Bash is stateful, meaning that when you type commands, Bash maintains context. Your current working directory, environment variables, and command history all persist from one command to the next.

This is why cd (change directory) matters, why a command can work one moment and fail the next, and why restarting a terminal sometimes fixes things. New developers often assume each command runs in isolation. It does not.

Prompt : What does it mean that Bash is stateful, and how does that affect scripts?

Command history and editing

One useful result of Bash being stateful is that it remembers what you have done. Every command you type is stored in your command history, which means you rarely need to retype long or complex commands.

Repeat previous commands

Press the ↑ (up arrow) key to cycle backward through previous commands: 

docker run -p 8000:8000 my-image

If you just ran this command and want to run it again, press ↑ and press Enter . This is especially helpful when working with long commands or when you are experimenting and need to retry something.

Search your command history

Instead of scrolling back line by line, you can search your command history:

  1. Press Ctrl + R
  2. Start typing part of a previous command, for example docker
  3. Bash will show the most recent matching command

Press Enter to run it, or keep pressing Ctrl + R to cycle through matches.

Edit commands before running them

When you recall a command using ↑ or Ctrl + R , you can edit it before pressing Enter . Developers do this constantly: 

docker run -p 8000:8000 my-image

You might change just the port: 

docker run -p 5000:5000 my-image

This is much faster and less error-prone than typing the whole command again.

Why this helps

Beginners often think they need to type every command from scratch. In practice, experienced developers rely heavily on command history to:

  • Retry commands after fixing an error
  • Make small adjustments to previous commands
  • Explore and experiment more quickly

This is another example of how Bash maintains state between commands. Your history, current directory, and environment all persist, which is why the terminal becomes more useful the longer you use it.

You do not need to memorize every command. Focus on understanding what commands do, and let the history feature help you reuse them efficiently.

Tab completion

Tab completion is a feature provided by the shell, not the terminal. When you press Tab , the shell tries to autocomplete what you’re typing, based on context:

  • File and folder names
  • Command names
  • Options and flags (for some tools)

With Bash, basic completion works out of the box (files, folders, commands), but more advanced completion (like Git branches, Docker options) depends on bash-completion being installed.

Zsh is much more full featured by default, with better suggestions, sometimes menu-style completion. Zsh is often enhanced further with frameworks like Oh My Zsh.

Across Bash, Zsh, and most environments, you can usually press Tab to complete file and folder names, and press Tab twice to show available options, and completion based on the current directory.

Splitting long commands across lines

Some commands can become long and difficult to read, especially when they include multiple options or arguments. Instead of writing everything on one line, you can split a command across multiple lines using a backslash ( \ ).

The backslash tells Bash that the command continues on the next line.

For example, instead of writing: 

docker run -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/app -e DEBUG=true my-image

You can write it like this: 

docker run \
  -p 8000:8000 \
  -v $(pwd):/app \
  -e DEBUG=true \
  my-image

This makes the command easier to read and modify, especially when copying from documentation or working with complex setups.

Important rules:

  • The backslash must be the very last character on the line
  • Do not add spaces after the backslash
  • Bash treats all lines as one continuous command

If you forget the backslash, Bash will try to run each line as a separate command, which usually leads to errors.

Many real-world commands, especially with tools like Docker, Git, or cloud CLIs, can become long and hard to manage. Splitting them across lines helps you:

  • Understand each part of the command
  • Avoid mistakes when editing
  • Copy and paste commands more safely

You will often see this style in documentation and scripts. Even though it looks like multiple lines, Bash still runs it as a single command.

Commands can be combined

Bash works especially well with text. Everything is text in and text out. Commands write to standard output, errors go to standard error, and those streams can be redirected or connected together. The pipe operator | sends one command’s output to another command’s input: 

ls -la | grep ".py"  # List only Python files
cat log.txt | wc -l  # Count lines in a file

Redirection using > or >> sends output to a file: 

echo "Hello" > file.txt   # Write (overwrites)
echo "World" >> file.txt  # Append

These two operators let small commands work together.

You do not need to learn pipes and redirection in depth yet, but keep in mind that commands can be chained together, which is why the shell feels composable rather than monolithic.

Creating shortcuts with aliases

As you start using the command line more often, you will notice that you type the same long commands repeatedly. Bash provides a simple way to create shortcuts for these commands using something called an alias.

An alias is just a short name that expands into a longer command.

In a Django project, you often run: 

python manage.py runserver

You can shorten this to a single word: 

alias serve="python manage.py runserver"

Now you can start the development server by typing: 

serve

This does the same thing as the full command, but it is faster to type and easier to remember.

When you type a command, Bash first checks:

  1. Is this an alias?
  2. If so, replace it with the full command
  3. Then execute the result

So: 

serve

becomes: 

python manage.py runserver

before anything is run.

Aliases are most helpful for long or repetitive commands and commands with flags you always use. For example: 

alias ll="ls -la"
alias migrate="python manage.py migrate"
alias test="python manage.py test"

Now your workflow becomes: 

serve
migrate
test

Temporary vs permanent aliases

If you define an alias in the terminal, it only lasts for that session. If you close the terminal, it disappears.

To make aliases permanent, add them to your shell configuration file:

  • Bash: ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile
  • Zsh: ~/.zshrc

For example, open your config file and add: 

alias serve="python manage.py runserver"

Then reload it: 

source ~/.bashrc

Now the alias will be available every time you open a new terminal.

Aliases are simple text replacements. They are great for shortcuts but limited because they cannot easily handle arguments, so they are not ideal for multi-step routines. They can also make commands less obvious to other developers because they are not standard.

If a shortcut becomes complex or needs logic, it is usually better to turn it into a script instead.

Aliases are one of the fastest ways to make the command line feel less repetitive. Think of aliases as quick shortcuts and scripts as repeatable processes.

Commands are unforgiving

Bash is powerful but not forgiving. A graphical file manager usually asks before deleting things. Bash often does exactly what you asked, immediately. The point is not to scare you, just to encourage a habit of reading commands carefully before pressing Enter , especially when copying from documentation or AI output.

Bash is not being introduced so you become a shell expert. It is being introduced so you can follow instructions, understand what tools are doing, and write small scripts when repetition becomes annoying.

Bash is a good place to slow down before accepting an AI-generated answer. A command such as rm , chmod , or docker run can change files, permissions, processes, or network access. Before running it, check what it will touch and whether it depends on your current directory.

Before you run a command, ask: Where am I in the file system? What files will this touch? Does it create something, delete something, change permissions, start a process, or send data over the network? That kind of thinking matters more than typing the command from memory. The command line rewards developers who understand behavior.

Many readers will be using Windows, which is a problem since Bash (or an alternative Bash-like shell like Zsh on Macs) is not a standard component of Windows. If you are using Windows and don’t have Bash or similar, in the next section you will learn how to install it. If you’re not using Windows, you can skip the next section and continue with the section titled Basic commands .

Setting up Bash on Windows

To use Bash on Windows, install Windows Subsystem for Linux ( WSL ).

WSL 2 is supported on Windows 11 and on Windows 10 version 1903 (build 18362) or later.

Install WSL from an elevated terminal

Open PowerShell as Administrator, then run: 

wsl --install

Alternatively, to install a specific Linux distribution like Ubuntu, run: wsl --install -d Ubuntu . To list available distributions, run: wsl --list --online

This installs WSL and typically installs a default Linux distribution (often Ubuntu) depending on your Windows version and configuration, as shown in the following output: 

Downloading: Ubuntu
[==========================53.5%                           ]

If you already have WSL installed, check what you have: 

wsl -l -v

This lists installed distributions and whether each is WSL 1 or WSL 2, as shown in the following output: 

  NAME              STATE           VERSION
* docker-desktop    Stopped         2
  Ubuntu            Running         2

Launch your Linux distribution and complete first-time setup

Open the Start menu, run your distro, for example, Ubuntu , and follow the prompts to create a Linux username and password. This is separate from your Windows login.

From now on, when you start Ubuntu , you should see the Bash prompt, as shown in Figure 10.1 :

Figure 10.1: Ubuntu Bash prompt and terminal window

Update packages inside Linux

In the WSL terminal, run: 

sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade -y

This keeps the environment current and avoids confusing install issues.

Good practice : sudo runs a command with administrator (root) privileges. When you use it, the system asks for your Linux password to confirm the action. This level of access should be used carefully and only for system-level tasks, such as installing software with apt . For everyday development commands like pip install , python , or npm , you should not need sudo . If those tools only work when run with elevated privileges, it usually means your environment or permissions are set up incorrectly and should be fixed rather than bypassed.

Confirm Bash is running

In the WSL terminal, run: 

echo "$SHELL"

You should see a path like /bin/bash (or similar).

In the WSL terminal, run: 

bash --version

You should see a version output (with copyright and license information): 

GNU bash, version 5.2.21(1)-release (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu)

Create a practice folder for the chapter

In the WSL terminal, run: 

mkdir -p ~/bash-chapter
cd ~/bash-chapter

In the WSL terminal, check where you are: 

pwd

You should see that you are in home , then your username like mine markjprice , and then the new directory that you just created: 

/home/markjprice/bash-chapter

In the WSL terminal, run: 

ls -la

If you are done with Bash, in the WSL terminal, you can run: 

exit

In Windows File Explorer, you can use the Linux node to view your WSL installations, as shown in Figure 10.2 :

Figure 10.2: Windows File Explorer and its WSL integration

These commands behave exactly as described in the chapter.

Now let’s put this background into practice by learning some common basic commands.

Basic commands

Before writing scripts or automating anything, you need a small vocabulary of everyday commands. These are the commands you will use constantly when working on projects, following tutorials, or debugging issues from the terminal. You do not need to memorize every option. Knowing what each command is for is far more important than knowing every flag it supports.

The core commands we will use in this chapter are:

  • pwd – prints the current working directory
  • ls – lists files and directories
  • cd – changes the current directory
  • mkdir – creates a new directory
  • touch – creates an empty file
  • cp – copies files and directories
  • mv – moves or renames files and directories
  • rm – deletes files and directories
  • cat – prints the contents of a file
  • echo – outputs text to the terminal

Navigation commands

Let’s start by focusing on just pwd , ls , and cd first. The rest will make more sense once navigation feels natural.

pwd – print working directory

pwd tells you where you are in the file system. This matters because most commands operate relative to the current directory: 

pwd

Typical output would be something like: 

/Users/mark/projects/my-site

Whenever a command fails with file not found , pwd is often the first thing to check. Many problems turn out to be caused by running a command in the wrong directory.

ls – list directory contents

ls shows you what files and folders exist in the current directory. Common options include -l for a detailed listing and -a to show hidden files: 

ls -la

Prompt : What happens step by step when I type a command like ls -la into a terminal?

Hidden files often start with a dot, such as .git or .env , and are common in development projects.

Prompt : What are hidden files in Unix systems, and why do they start with a dot?

cd – change directory

cd changes your current working directory. For example, to move into a folder called src : 

cd src

To go up one level, use: 

cd ..

To return to your home directory: 

cd ~

Getting comfortable with cd is essential, because almost everything else depends on being in the right place.

Prompt : Please explain relative vs absolute paths in Bash using a directory tree example.

Creating things

Now let’s see two commands to make a directory or a file.

mkdir – make directory

mkdir creates a new directory: 

mkdir scripts

You can create nested directories in one step using -p : 

mkdir -p app/static/css

This is common when setting up project structures.

touch – create a file

touch creates an empty file if it does not already exist: 

touch app.py

If the file already exists, touch simply updates its timestamp. Developers often use it to quickly create placeholder files.

Moving, copying, and deleting

You often need to move, copy, or delete filesystem items.

cp – copy files and directories

cp copies files from one location to another: 

cp settings.example.json settings.json

To copy a directory and its contents, use the -r (recursive) option: 

cp -r templates templates_backup

mv – move or rename files

mv moves files or directories. It is also used for renaming: 

mv old_name.py new_name.py

or: 

mv build/ dist/

There is no separate rename command. Renaming is just a move within the same directory.

rm – remove files and directories

rm deletes files: 

rm debug.log

To remove a directory and everything inside it, use -r : 

rm -r temp/

This command does not send files to a recycle bin. Once deleted, they are usually gone. This is one of the reasons developers treat rm -r with respect.

Prompt : Why does rm not ask for confirmation by default, and how do experienced developers stay safe?

Showing text

Lastly, let’s see how to output a file or a string to the console.

cat – display file contents

cat prints the contents of a file to the terminal: 

cat README.md

It is useful for quickly inspecting small text files, configuration files, or logs without opening an editor.

echo – print text

echo outputs text to the terminal: 

echo "Hello, Bash"

It is often used in scripts to show progress messages or to test variables and command output.

These commands form the foundation of almost everything you will do in Bash. Once they feel familiar, reading shell-based instructions becomes much easier, and writing simple scripts starts to feel natural.

Working with web resources

Now let’s see some network commands.

curl – transfer data from or to a server

curl is used to make HTTP requests from the command line. It is commonly used to download data, test APIs, or interact with web services: 

curl https://example.com

This fetches the content of the URL and prints it to the terminal.

To save the response to a file, use the -o option: 

curl -o index.html https://example.com

You can also send data, for example when working with APIs: 

curl -X POST -d "name=Mark" https://example.com/api

Developers often use curl to debug APIs, check responses, or automate requests in scripts.

wget – download files from the web

wget is designed for downloading files from the internet. It is especially useful for saving files directly to disk: 

wget https://example.com/file.zip

This downloads the file and saves it with its original name.

To save it with a different name, use -O : 

wget -O archive.zip https://example.com/file.zip

Unlike curl , wget is focused on downloading and can resume interrupted downloads, which is useful for large files.

Let’s put it all together by writing a simple script.

Writing a simple script

So far, you have been typing one command at a time into the terminal. A Bash script is simply a way to save a sequence of commands into a file and run them together. This is useful whenever you notice yourself repeating the same steps over and over, or when you want to document a process in a form that the computer can execute.

For example, let’s say you’ve been working with Django and you find yourself repeating the same three commands in order, over and over again:

  1. Change to the project directory: 

    cd project

  2. Activate the virtual environment: 

    source .venv/bin/activate

  3. Run the web server: 

    python manage.py runserver

If you create a script file named run_dev.sh that contains these three commands, then three steps become one:

  • Run the script: 

    ./run_dev.sh

A script replaces repeated typing with a single command.

Script files

A Bash script is just a plain text file. By convention, it usually has a .sh extension, although the extension itself is not technically required. Let’s start with a minimal example.

Create a new file called run_dev.sh : 

touch run_dev.sh

Open it in VS Code and add the following commands: 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Starting development environment..."
python manage.py runserver

The first line is called the shebang . It tells the operating system which program should be used to run the file. In this case, it says use Bash . The env form is preferred because it works across different systems where Bash might live in slightly different locations.

The remaining lines are just normal Bash commands, exactly the same as if you had typed them into the terminal by hand.

Prompt : Please explain the shebang line in Bash scripts and why /usr/bin/env bash is recommended.

Making script file executable

Before you can run the script, you need to make it executable: 

chmod +x run_dev.sh

If you forget this step and try to run the script, you will typically see an error like: 

$ ./run_dev.sh
bash: ./run_dev.sh: Permission denied

This happens because the file exists, but the operating system does not have permission to execute it as a program. Adding the execute permission with chmod +x resolves this.

Now you can run it like this: 

./run_dev.sh

The ./ path prefix matters. It tells Bash to look for the script in the current directory rather than searching for a system command with the same name.

Prompt : What does chmod +x actually change at the operating system level?

At this point, you have already learned something important: scripts run in the same shell environment you have been using interactively. If your script fails, the commands inside it would probably fail if you typed them manually as well. This makes debugging much less mysterious.

Adding logic to scripts

You can add simple logic to make scripts more useful. For example, variables let you avoid hard-coding values, like setting a PORT variable to 8000 and then referencing it with $PORT in a command: 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
PORT=8000
echo "Starting server on port $PORT"
python manage.py runserver "$PORT"

On some systems, you may need to use python3 instead of python .

You can also stop a script when something goes wrong. The following line tells Bash to exit immediately if any command fails: 

set -e

Placed near the top of the script, this prevents later commands from running in a broken state, which is especially useful in build or deployment scripts.

For safer scripts, use the full safety preamble: 

set -euo pipefail

Note the following about the preceding command:

  • -e : Exit immediately if any command fails
  • -u : Exit if you use an undefined variable (this catches typos)
  • -o pipefail : A pipeline fails if any command in it fails

This combination prevents entire categories of subtle bugs. Place it near the top of every script.

Prompt : Why does my Bash script exit early when I use set -e ?

A simple but realistic script might combine several tasks: 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
echo "Cleaning old files..."
rm -rf dist/
echo "Running tests..."
python manage.py test
echo "Starting server..."
python manage.py runserver

Nothing here is complicated, but putting these steps into a script means they always run in the same order, the same way, every time. That consistency is the real value of shell scripts.

You do not need to turn Bash into your primary programming language. Think of scripts as glue. They connect tools, enforce routines, and save mental effort.

Always quote variables

Unquoted variables in Bash can cause bugs and security issues: 

# If NAME contains spaces:
NAME="John Smith"
echo Hello, $NAME     # Bash sees: echo Hello, John Smith (3 args)
echo "Hello, $NAME"   # Bash sees: echo "Hello, John Smith" (1 arg)

In Bash, $VAR without quotes is subject to word splitting. If the value contains spaces, Bash splits it into multiple arguments. Good practice is to use "$VAR" to prevent this: 

FILE="my document.txt"
rm "$FILE"    # Correct: deletes "my document.txt"
rm $FILE      # Bug: tries to delete "my" and "document.txt"

This is the single most common source of bugs in Bash scripts.

Script arguments

So far, the scripts you have seen do exactly one thing in exactly one way. Bash scripts become much more useful when they can accept input from the command line.

Arguments passed to a script are available as numbered variables. $1 refers to the first argument, $2 to the second, and so on.

Create a file called hello.sh : 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
NAME="$1"
echo "Hello, $NAME"

Make it executable and run it: 

chmod +x hello.sh
./hello.sh Mark

This pattern shows up everywhere, from small utility scripts to large deployment tools. It allows one script to handle many similar tasks without modification.

Relative and absolute paths

Paths inside a Bash script work the same way they do in the terminal. Relative paths are resolved from the current working directory, not from the location of the script itself.

This means the following script can behave differently depending on where it is run from: 

rm data/output.txt

If you want predictable behavior, either use absolute paths or explicitly change the directory at the start of the script: 

cd /Users/mark/projects/my-site

Understanding this early avoids a common class of bugs where scripts work for one person but fail for another.

Prompt : Why does running the same Bash command sometimes work in one directory but fail in another?

Comments in scripts

Bash scripts support comments using the # character. Anything after # on a line is ignored by Bash: 

# Clean old build files
rm -rf dist/

Comments explain intent, which is often more important than explaining syntax. A script you understand today may be confusing in six months without comments.

Bash as glue

Bash does not replace other languages or tools. It connects them.

A single script might call Git, Docker, Python, and a web server in sequence. Bash does not care what language a tool is written in. If it can be run from the command line, Bash can orchestrate it.

This is why Bash remains relevant even as new languages and frameworks appear. It sits at the boundary between tools and lets them work together.

A note on safety

Bash scripts can change or delete files, stop services, and deploy code. They usually do exactly what they are told, without asking for confirmation.

Before running a script that you did not write yourself, read it. This is especially important for scripts copied from the internet or generated by AI tools. Treat shell scripts with the same caution you would give to executable files from an unknown source.

Prompt : What are common beginner mistakes in Bash scripts, and how can I spot them?

Automating your Django development

So far, the examples have been small and focused. Now let’s connect Bash directly to something you have already done: running a Django project.

In the previous chapter, you repeatedly ran a sequence of commands:

  1. Create or activate a virtual environment
  2. Install dependencies
  3. Apply database migrations
  4. Start the development server

Typing these every time is repetitive and easy to get wrong. This is exactly the kind of task Bash scripts are meant to simplify.

The problem is repetition

A typical Django setup session might look like this: 

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py runserver

There is nothing complicated here. But you run this sequence often enough that it becomes friction.

The solution is a shell script

Create a new file in your Django project root: 

touch run_dev.sh

Open it in your code editor and add the following: 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
echo "Setting up Django development environment..."
# Create virtual environment if it does not exist
if [ ! -d ".venv" ]; then
  echo "Creating virtual environment..."
  python -m venv .venv
fi
# Activate virtual environment
echo "Activating virtual environment..."
source .venv/bin/activate
# Install dependencies
if [ -f "requirements.txt" ]; then
  echo "Installing dependencies..."
  pip install -r requirements.txt
else
  echo "No requirements.txt found, skipping install"
fi
# Apply database migrations
echo "Running migrations..."
python manage.py migrate
# Start development server
echo "Starting Django development server..."
python manage.py runserver

Make the script executable: 

chmod +x run_dev.sh

Now, instead of running five commands, you run one: 

./run_dev.sh

This script is not doing anything new. It is just making your routine explicit and repeatable:

  1. It checks if .venv exists before creating it
  2. It activates the environment
  3. It installs dependencies only if a requirements.txt file exists
  4. It applies migrations every time
  5. It starts the server

Each step is something you were already doing manually.

Why automation scripts matter

You are not writing code for its own sake. You are capturing a process: This is how this project should be started . That has a few benefits:

  • You do not forget the steps
  • You avoid subtle environment issues
  • You reduce typing and small mistakes
  • You make the workflow obvious to someone else reading the project

If someone else clones your repository, they do not need instructions like “run these five commands.” They can just run: 

./run_dev.sh

Adding a configurable port for the server

You can make the script slightly more flexible by accepting a port number: 

PORT="${1:-8000}"
echo "Starting server on port $PORT..."
python manage.py runserver "$PORT"

Now you can run: 

./run_dev.sh 5000

or fall back to the default: 

./run_dev.sh

This is a typical use for Bash in a project: take a setup routine you already know and save it as a script.

Good practice : This script assumes a Unix-like environment (Linux, macOS, or WSL on Windows). On native Windows without WSL, activation uses a different path ( .venv\Scripts\activate ). In real projects, teams often provide separate scripts or use tools that handle cross-platform differences.

Now, let’s see how AI can help you learn and use shell scripts.

Using AI for shell help

The command line has a reputation for being hostile, largely because error messages can be terse and documentation often assumes prior knowledge. AI tools can make the command line easier to learn. Used properly, they act like an on-demand explainer rather than a magical command generator.

A sensible way to use AI with Bash is to ask why something works or fails, not just what to type. For example, if you see a command in documentation that you do not understand, you can ask:

  • Please explain what this Bash command does, piece by piece: 

    docker run -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd):/app my-image

A good AI response will break the command into flags, arguments, and substitutions, helping you build intuition rather than encouraging blind copying.

Help with syntax

AI is also helpful for syntax reminders. Bash has many small rules that are easy to forget, such as spacing around brackets or how variables are expanded. Instead of searching through man pages, you can ask targeted questions like:

  • How do I loop over all .txt files in Bash and print their names?
  • What does set -e do in a Bash script, and when should I avoid it?

Help with errors

When a script fails at the command prompt, pasting the error message and a small, relevant snippet of the script often leads to useful explanations:

  • This Bash script exits immediately with permission denied . Why?
  • Here is my script and the error output. What is wrong with it?

This works particularly well because Bash errors are often indirect. The line that fails is not always the line that caused the problem, and AI tools are good at spotting those patterns.

If you’re trying out your scripts in a code editor like VS Code, then you don’t even have to copy and paste into your preferred chatbot. GitHub Copilot Chat will inspect your active terminal session automatically, as the terminal context is included as part of your conversation. It shows the last command, working directory, and exit code for each open terminal.

Prompt : Please explain common Bash error messages like permission denied or command not found .

Beware that AI has limited context

That said, there are limits. AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini that run in a web browser do not see your file system, environment variables, or installed software. If a suggested command deletes files or modifies system state, it will do so just as eagerly as if a human had written it. Treat AI output as advice, not authority.

VS Code with GitHub Copilot, Rider with its AI Assistant, and CLI tools like Claude Code and OpenAI Codex do have lots of tools to gather context so are much better at providing dynamic relevant help. You will work with these more in later chapters.

Before running an AI-suggested command, make sure you can say what it reads, what it writes, and what it might delete or change. If you cannot explain that much, ask the AI to break the command down first.

That makes AI most useful as a command explainer, not as a source of commands to paste blindly.

Prompt : How can I safely debug a Bash script step by step?

In this section, you will be tested on what you’ve learned in this chapter and be provided with useful links to reference materials and resources.

Check your understanding

Answer the following questions that are deliberately conceptual rather than rote, encouraging explanation over memorization:

  1. What role does Bash play between you and the operating system?
  2. Why is Bash described as stateful, and how does that affect everyday command usage?
  3. Explain the difference between a terminal application and the Bash shell.
  4. Why might a command work in one directory but fail in another?
  5. What problem does a Bash script solve that typing commands manually does not?
  6. What is the purpose of the shebang line at the top of a script?
  7. Why must a script be marked as executable before it can be run?
  8. What risks are associated with rm -r , and how can developers reduce them?
  9. How does allowing scripts to accept arguments make them more flexible?
  10. What are the benefits and limitations of using AI tools for Bash help?

Answers can be found in Appendix A: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/docs/appendix_a.pdf

Practical exercise

Write a Bash script that creates a directory, creates a file inside it, writes a line of text to the file, and prints the file contents to the terminal. Then explain each line in your own words.

References

Bash has been around for decades, and its documentation reflects that maturity. Some resources are reference-heavy, others are more tutorial-oriented. It is useful to know which to reach for depending on whether you are learning or troubleshooting.

GNU Bash Reference Manual

The authoritative source is the GNU Bash Reference Manual. This is the specification-level documentation for Bash and is maintained as part of the GNU Project. You can read it online at the following link:

https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/bash.html

This manual is exhaustive. It explains Bash syntax, built-in commands, variables, quoting rules, redirection, job control, and scripting features in precise terms. You would not normally read it cover to cover, but it is excellent when you need to understand exactly how something behaves.

Bash man page

Closely related is the Bash man page, which is what you see when you type: 

man bash

This is more concise and is often quicker when you just need a reminder about syntax or options. For man pages on specific commands, enter man <command> , for example: 

man ls
man cd
man rm

The preceding commands will give you detailed, authoritative information about individual commands. These man pages are not always friendly, but they are accurate and ubiquitous.

The Bash Guide for Beginners

This guide focuses on fundamentals and common patterns, making it a good complement to the reference manual:

https://tldp.org/LDP/Bash-Beginners-Guide/html/

Advanced Bash-Scripting Guide

Despite the name, this is widely used as a reference for real-world scripting patterns. It is opinionated in places, but extremely thorough:

https://tldp.org/LDP/abs/html/

Explainshell

This tool lets you paste a shell command and see each part explained inline. It is particularly helpful when reading unfamiliar commands in documentation or CI logs: https://explainshell.com/

ShellCheck

ShellCheck is a static analysis tool for shell scripts. It highlights common mistakes, unsafe patterns, and portability issues. Even experienced shell users rely on it:

https://www.shellcheck.net/

Summary

In this chapter, you learned how Bash fits into a developer’s daily routine. Specifically:

  • What Bash is, and how it functions as a Unix shell and command language
  • How to navigate the file system from the command line using core commands such as cd , ls , and pwd
  • How to create, copy, move, and delete files and directories safely from the terminal
  • How to inspect file contents and produce output using commands like cat and echo
  • How to write a simple Bash script to automate a sequence of commands
  • How to use variables and command-line arguments inside Bash scripts
  • How to use AI tools to understand shell commands and debug scripts rather than blindly copying them

The main lesson is that Bash gives you a way to control your development environment. The commands matter, but what matters more is knowing what they will do before you run them.

In the next chapter, you will use these command-line skills to set up a complete web development project and the environment needed to work on it.

Setting Up Your Project Environment

The last part of this book shifts from learning individual technologies for frontend and backend web development to applying them in one realistic project. Rather than isolated examples, you will design and build a complete web application named TallyApp , a small survey and polling application.

This project is deliberately scoped to be small enough to understand end to end, but rich enough to feel like something you could plausibly extend or deploy. In this chapter, we kick off the TallyApp project by installing and configuring your development tools.

As a noun, a tally is a running count or record of items, events, or votes. It often refers to the total reached by incrementing the count step by step. For example, the final tally of votes means the completed count. As a verb, to tally means to count or to add items to a running total. It can also mean to agree or correspond. For example, the numbers do not tally means they do not match.

By the end of this chapter, you will have configured your development environment with GitHub Copilot, set up a consistent and repeatable environment using Docker, and learned how to place code under version control using Git so you are ready to start building features with confidence.

This chapter is about knowing which tool solves which problem. Copilot helps while you write and review code. Docker gives everyone the same runtime. Git records the history of the project so you can try changes without fear. You will use all three before adding TallyApp features.

Introducing TallyApp

TallyApp is a survey and polling application with three clear areas of functionality.

  1. First, it allows an authenticated user to design and publish surveys. This includes defining different types of questions, such as multiple choice and free-text responses, and generating a public link that can be shared with respondents.
  2. Second, it provides a clean, focused experience for people taking a survey, where they can follow a link, answer questions, and submit their responses without needing an account.
  3. Third, it gives the survey creator tools to analyze results, using charts and structured data views to explore trends and individual answers.

Across the upcoming chapters, you will incrementally set up your development environment with an AI coding assistant, and then specify, build, and refine TallyApp. Just as importantly, these chapters model how real web projects are developed. You will make design decisions, revisit earlier choices, and see how backend logic, frontend presentation, and data analysis fit together.

By the end of the TallyApp project, you will not just have learned individual features of web frameworks and languages. You will have built and understood a complete, working web application, and you will be in a much better position to design one of your own.

A warning about leaning on AI

A warning comes from Anthropic in their article, How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills : https://www.anthropic.com/research/AI-assistance-coding-skills .

Anthropic researchers conducted a randomized controlled trial involving 52 software developers.

All participants had regular experience with Python but were unfamiliar with a specific async library called Trio. They were randomly assigned to two groups:

  • AI-assisted group : Participants could use an AI coding assistant during the task.
  • Control group : Participants did not have AI assistance but could use documentation and web search.

Each participant completed two feature-building tasks using Trio. After finishing, they all took a quiz designed to measure mastery of the concepts they had just worked with. The quiz covered debugging, code reading, code writing, and conceptual understanding.

Here is what the study found:

  • On average, developers who used AI scored significantly lower on the post-task quiz (about 50 percent) compared to those who coded without AI (about 67 percent). This represented a 17 percent gap, roughly equivalent to two letter grades in a typical academic setting.
  • The biggest differences were observed on debugging and conceptual understanding questions, indicating that AI use was associated with weaker mastery of those skills.
  • The AI-assisted group finished the coding tasks only slightly faster, but this time difference was not statistically significant.
  • Qualitative analysis showed that some participants spent substantial time composing AI prompts (up to 30 percent of total time in some cases), which ate into potential efficiency gains.

The researchers concluded that:

  • AI assistance can undermine learning when people are acquiring a new, unfamiliar skill. Relying on the assistant to generate and debug code appears to reduce the cognitive effort that builds deep understanding.
  • Not all AI use is the same. Some participants who used AI mainly to ask conceptual questions or request explanations alongside generated code performed much closer to the control group. Those who offloaded thinking and delegated work to the AI tended to score lowest.
  • The study suggests that AI does not automatically speed learning, especially on unfamiliar tasks, and may even impede skill formation if developers use it as a shortcut rather than as a learning tool.

The study’s warning is simple: AI can help you finish a task without helping you learn the material. The way you use the assistant matters. Asking for explanations is different from letting it do the work.

Good practice : Always ask the AI to explain the code it writes while you are learning a new topic. Ask conceptual questions or request explanations alongside generated code. Avoid delegating work to the AI; stay in control.

Prompt : Please explain the risks of over-relying on AI during early learning. Design a learning plan that balances AI use with deep skill formation.

Chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, or Grok focus mainly on natural language interaction. They handle writing, summarizing, general research, and can also support coding queries, but coding assistance is just one of many tasks. They are best used as code and framework learning mentors.

AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot, Codex, or Cursor are optimized for developer workflows. They integrate with code editors and IDEs, suggest completions, generate project-specific code, and can assist with debugging and tests.

GitHub Copilot lets you choose between multiple coding AI models. For example, Copilot itself, Anthropic’s Claude, and OpenAI’s Codex. This means you’re not locked into a single model; you can pick whichever agent best fits your task.

Ollama and similar local LLM frameworks let you run a wide variety of LLMs on local desktop or server hardware. Models like Qwen3-Coder , StarCode2 , Codestral , Devastral , and so on are open source and optimized for coding tasks. You can run them locally through Ollama without ever sending data to the cloud.

If you care about data privacy, offline use, full control, and avoiding cloud APIs, then you want local LLM frameworks like Ollama with open-source coding models. Bring Your Own Key ( BYOK ) model support is a fast-moving feature set, and some capabilities may differ between chat, inline chat, and completions.

If you want the easiest start, use Copilot Free (cloud). You get a monthly allowance without configuring any keys.

If you want the best quality and do not mind API spend, keep Copilot models for day-to-day coding and optionally add your OpenAI API key so you can use specific provider models when needed.

If you want to avoid per-request costs and keep data local, run Ollama and select it via VS Code’s model management so Copilot Chat can use a local model for many tasks.

I have written an online-only article to cover use of local models in detail: https://github.com/markjprice/markjprice/blob/main/with-ai/local-models.md

Local setups are better in specific areas:

  • Privacy : No code leaves your machine. Useful for proprietary or sensitive work
  • Cost (long-term) : No per-token billing. Heavy usage becomes cheaper over time
  • Latency : Instant response for small models. No network dependency
  • Control : You can fine-tune. You can customize behavior

A practical setup is to use both cloud and local models, but for different jobs:

  • Use cloud models when you need stronger reasoning, larger context, or help comparing design options
  • Use local models when the task is small, private, or repetitive: explaining syntax, drafting a helper function, refactoring one file, or sketching tests

    Good practice : If the task requires judgment, not just generation, use a cloud model.

Configuring GitHub Copilot

At the end of this section, you will have GitHub Copilot running in VS Code for inline completions and chat. You will also have a second path configured so Copilot Chat can use either:

  • The built-in Copilot models (including the free plan if you qualify)
  • Your own model provider, including a local Ollama model, to avoid per-request API costs

VS Code’s BYOK model support is part of how Copilot Chat can be powered by third-party providers (including Ollama for local models).

Prerequisites are:

  • VS Code installed
  • A GitHub account you can sign into from VS Code. You can sign up at the following link: https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/start-your-journey/creating-an-account-on-github
  • Pick one of the following options:
    • GitHub Copilot Free plan (no API key required)
    • An OpenAI API key or another supported provider key for BYOK
    • A local model runtime like Ollama for local inference

      Warning! GitHub Copilot inline suggestions (the autocomplete you accept with Tab ) are not the same thing as Copilot Chat . VS Code’s BYOK model system is primarily about powering chat and editing experiences with different model providers. Some BYOK capabilities may not apply to completions in the same way. Treat local-model support as a chat-first (and edit-first) path, not a guaranteed replacement for every Copilot feature.

Install and sign in to Copilot in VS Code:

  1. Open VS Code and trigger Copilot setup by clicking the Copilot icon in the status bar.
  2. Sign in with GitHub. Follow the sign-in prompts. If your GitHub account already has Copilot access, VS Code uses it. If you do not have a subscription, VS Code can enroll you into the Copilot Free plan (with monthly usage limits).
  3. Verify Copilot is active. Open any code file, type a few characters, and pause. If Copilot is active, you should see gray ghost text suggestions you can accept (usually Tab ).

Figure 11.1: Selecting a model in GitHub Copilot Chat

If you’re using Copilot Free, expect monthly caps such as a limit on inline suggestions and a smaller number of premium requests (used by newer or more expensive models). For current limits, see Copilot plans at the following link: https://github.com/features/copilot/plans
