GitHub Copilot tips

Here are some tips to improve your experience with GitHub Copilot:

  • Use the model picker intentionally in Chat. Copilot supports multiple models, and the model you pick affects latency, accuracy, and cost multipliers (premium requests). For quick Q&A or lightweight edits, a faster model is often enough. For complex refactors or reasoning-heavy debugging, switch to a stronger model when you need it.
  • Know what burns premium requests. On plans that include premium requests, the newest frontier models often cost more per request (Copilot documents this as multipliers). If you’re on Free, be conservative: do exploration with cheaper models, then spend premium calls on the final do it right pass.
  • Ask for structured outputs to reduce token churn. Copilot Chat gets better (and cheaper) when you constrain it. Examples:
    • “List three approaches and recommend one.”
    • “Give a patch-style diff for these two files.”
    • “Only change the methods touched by this failing test.”
  • Watch your privacy knobs in VS Code. If you’re writing proprietary code, review Copilot settings in VS Code and tighten anything you are not comfortable with.

Ensure you have an OpenAI API key available

This section is for readers who want to use their own provider key from OpenAI or another supported provider to power chat and coding experiences in VS Code:

  1. Create and store your OpenAI API key. Create an API key in your OpenAI account and store it in a password manager. Do not hardcode it into source control.
  2. Open VS Code’s language model management UI by running the command to manage models. For example, in the Command Palette, select the menu item Chat: Manage Language Models .
  3. Add your provider key like OpenAI. Choose Bring your own language model key . Select OpenAI or another provider and then paste the key.

    Warning! VS Code’s BYOK is not available for Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise accounts (it is for individual plans like Free/Pro/Pro+).

  1. Select the provider-backed model in Copilot Chat. In Copilot Chat, use the model picker to choose the model you just added.

  2. Do a quick smoke test: 

    Summarize this file and suggest two refactoring steps.

Now that you’ve configured VS Code and GitHub Copilot to be your coding assistant, let’s see how Docker is useful for making a consistent development setup.

Docker for consistent server setup

Docker is a way to package an application and everything it needs including runtime, OS libraries, dependencies, and configuration defaults into a repeatable unit called an image . You then run that image as a container .

The practical benefit for TallyApp is consistency: developers on Windows, macOS, and Linux can run the same Django stack with the same versions and the same behavior, without spending hours fighting local setup differences.

Important concepts

Here are the important concepts that you need to know about Docker:

  • Images : A built, immutable template. You typically build one for your Django app. Prebuilt images are used for common services like database engines and management software.
  • Containers : A running instance of an image. Containers can be started, stopped, and replaced easily.
  • Dockerfile : A text file describing how to build an image. It contains layer-by-layer instructions to choose the base image, install dependencies, copy code, and how to start the process.
  • Docker Compose : A way to define and run a multi-container application with a single command. For example, the web container might be your Django project, a db container might host the PostgreSQL database engine, and so on.
  • Volumes : Persistent storage managed by Docker. This matters most for databases. If you do not use a volume for PostgreSQL, your data disappears when the database container is replaced.
  • Networks : Compose automatically creates a private network so containers can talk to each other by service name. For example, the Django container can reach the database at hostname db .
  • Ports : The doorways you expose to your host machine. You might map container port 8000 to host port 8000 so you can open the site in your browser.

    Prompt : What is the difference between Docker volumes and bind mounts? Please explain why bind mounts are ideal for development but risky in production.

Downloading and installing Docker

Even if you deploy TallyApp with SQLite first, it is still useful to learn Docker using PostgreSQL because it demonstrates a realistic multi-service setup. It also provides a clean upgrade path for you when you want fewer SQLite concurrency limits later.

Prompt : Please explain the concurrency limitations of SQLite in Django applications. What isolation levels does PostgreSQL use and how do they compare to SQLite? When should a Django project move from SQLite to PostgreSQL?

To use Docker, you will need the following:

  • Docker Desktop on Windows or Mac or Docker Engine on Linux
  • A Django project with a manage.py

Install Docker for your operating system from the following link: https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/ .

Setting up a basic TallyApp project

Now we can build the simplest Django project before containerizing it:

  1. Create a folder named Chapter11 . Inside that folder, run the virtual environment command that will create a .venv folder containing a private Python installation for this project:
    • On Windows, run: python -m venv .venv
    • On macOS and Linux, run: python3 -m venv .venv
  2. Activate the virtual environment:
    • On Windows, run: .venv\Scripts\activate
    • On macOS and Linux, run: source .venv/bin/activate

  3. When activation succeeds, your terminal prompt will usually change to show the virtual environment name: 

    (.venv) C:\web-dev-ai\Chapter11>

  4. With the virtual environment active, install Django using pip: 

    pip install django

  5. Verify the installation: 

    django-admin --version
  6. You should see the Django version number like 6.0.2 . If so, Django is ready to use.

  7. At the command prompt or terminal, create a Django project and name it tallyapp : 

    django-admin startproject tallyapp

  8. Change to the tallyapp project directory: 

    cd tallyapp

  9. Apply migrations to the local SQLite database: 

    python manage.py migrate

  10. Create an administrator account and then follow the prompts to set a username, email address, and password: 

    python manage.py createsuperuser

  11. Run the Django development server: 

    python manage.py runserver
  12. Start your preferred browser and navigate to http://127.0.0.1:8000/ .

You can Ctrl + Click the link in the output rather than typing the URL manually. If you see the Django welcome page, your setup is correct.

To view the admin site, navigate to http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/ .

Setting up Docker to host the project

Now we can create files to configure this project to be hosted in a Docker container and talk to PostgreSQL in another container to use as its database.

You will create three files:

  • Dockerfile defines how to build one container for the Django project web app and is about creation
  • .dockerignore defines what files and folders to exclude from the image
  • docker-compose.yml defines how to run multiple containers together and is about coordination between containers

Creating a Dockerfile

We will start by defining a Dockerfile that tells Docker how to build an image for a container. You can think of the Dockerfile as a recipe. It answers the following questions:

  • What base system do we start from?
  • What dependencies do we install?
  • What code do we copy in?
  • What command runs when the container starts?

For the TallyApp project, the Dockerfile will:

  • Start from python:3.12-slim because it is a stable, lightweight official Python base image that works well for a Django 6 project, but it is not the newest Python image available
  • Install dependencies from requirements.txt
  • Copy your TallyApp Django project into /app
  • Run python manage.py runserver

The Dockerfile produces a reusable image like tallyapp-web-image . That image will be a self-contained unit, and you can run it anywhere.

In the Chapter11\tallyapp folder, create a file named Dockerfile with the following content: 

# Use an official Python image as the base
FROM python:3.12-slim
# Prevents Python from writing .pyc files and 
# buffers to stdout/stderr
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# Set a working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app
# System deps (optional but common): build tools 
# for some Python packages
RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends build-essential \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# Install Python dependencies first
# (for better layer caching)
COPY requirements.txt /app/
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
# Copy the rest of the project
COPY . /app/
# Default command for the container (development-friendly)
CMD ["python", "manage.py", "runserver", "0.0.0.0:8000"]

Note the following about the preceding code:

  • We start the image with python:3.12-slim to get a stable, widely supported Python runtime with a minimal base system, avoiding the unpredictability of latest while keeping images small and reproducible.

    Prompt : Is python:3.12-slim the latest and best Python image for a Docker container?

  • It installs dependencies from requirements.txt .
  • It copies your code into the image.

    Prompt : Why is COPY requirements.txt done before COPY .. ?

  • It runs Django’s development server bound to 0.0.0.0 so it is reachable from outside the container.

    Warning! For a production container you must replace runserver with Gunicorn , but for now, this is a clear first step. You will learn about Gunicorn in Chapter 13 , Specifying and Building the Initial Project .

Creating a Docker Ignore file

When you build a Docker image, Docker sends the entire project folder (called the build context) to the Docker daemon. By default, that means everything in your project directory is included, even files you do not want in your image. This is where a .dockerignore file helps.

Just like .gitignore tells Git which files to skip (you will see this in the next section), .dockerignore tells Docker which files to exclude from the image build process. This keeps your images smaller, faster to build, and avoids accidentally including sensitive or unnecessary files.

Create a file named .dockerignore in the same folder as your Dockerfile, and add the following: 

# .dockerignore
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.git/
.gitignore
db.sqlite3
.env
*.sqlite3
docker-compose.yml
Dockerfile
.DS_Store

The benefits include:

  • Smaller images : Virtual environments, cache files, and local databases can be large. Excluding them reduces image size significantly.
  • Faster builds : Docker uploads the build context before building. Fewer files means faster builds, especially as your project grows.
  • Stronger security : Files like .env may contain secrets such as API keys or database passwords. If included in an image layer, they can be very difficult to remove later.
  • Cleaner environments : Your container should contain only what it needs to run. Development artifacts like .venv or .git are irrelevant inside the container.

Even though the Dockerfile uses COPY . /app/ , the .dockerignore file ensures that excluded files are never copied in the first place. This keeps your image clean without needing complex COPY rules.

Good practice : Keep your .dockerignore file aligned with your .gitignore file, but do not assume they should be identical. Docker cares about build context and image contents, while Git cares about version control. Some files, like Dockerfile or docker-compose.yml , are tracked by Git but usually do not belong inside the final image.

Creating a Docker Compose file

Next, we will define a docker-compose.yml file. While a Dockerfile defines how to build a single image, and a .dockerignore file excludes files and folders from an image, a docker-compose.yml file defines how to run multiple containers together.

You could run your Django container manually with docker run, but it would get messy fast. You would need to start PostgreSQL separately, link containers manually, pass environment variables by hand, and manage ports and volumes yourself. Docker Compose replaces all of that with one command and a single config file.

The docker-compose.yml file is orchestration . It answers:

  • What containers do we need?
  • How do they connect?
  • What environment variables do they use?
  • What ports are exposed?
  • What volumes persist data?

For our TallyApp project, Docker Compose will define two services:

  • web is the Django app container (built from the Dockerfile )
  • db is a PostgreSQL container

It will also:

  • Connect the two containers via a network
  • Map ports ( 8000 , 5432 )
  • Set environment variables for the Django project
  • Create a volume for database persistence

Running a single command, docker compose up , will start the entire system, not just one container.

In the Chapter11\tallyapp folder, create a docker-compose.yml file for Django and PostgreSQL: 

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: tallyapp
      POSTGRES_USER: tallyapp
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: tallyapp_password_change_me
    volumes:
      - tallyapp_postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U tallyapp -d tallyapp"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
  web:
    build:
      context: .
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      # Django will read these to build DATABASES config (you wire this up in settings.py)
      DJANGO_DB_NAME: tallyapp
      DJANGO_DB_USER: tallyapp
      DJANGO_DB_PASSWORD: tallyapp_password_change_me
      DJANGO_DB_HOST: db
      DJANGO_DB_PORT: "5432"
      DJANGO_SECRET_KEY: dev-only-change-me
      DJANGO_DEBUG: "1"
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    volumes:
      - .:/app
volumes:
  tallyapp_postgres_data:

Note the following about the preceding code:

  • db uses the official PostgreSQL image and initializes a database using environment variables documented for that image.
  • db has a healthcheck , and web depends on db being service_healthy , not merely started.
  • The tallyapp_postgres_data volume is what keeps database data persistent across container restarts.
  • The web service builds from your Dockerfile
  • The volumes: - .:/app bind-mount means code changes on the host instantly appear inside the container, which is ideal for a Docker-based dev environment.
  • depends_on starts the database container before the web container, but by itself it does not guarantee that PostgreSQL is ready to accept connections. To make startup more reliable, we defined a PostgreSQL healthcheck and set depends_on to wait for condition: service_healthy . Then Docker Compose waits until the database reports that it is ready before starting Django.

Switching from SQLite to PostgreSQL

Now we can configure project files like the Python dependencies and Django project settings so that the project uses PostgreSQL instead of SQLite:

  1. In the Chapter11\tallyapp folder, create a requirements.txt file to configure Django 6 to use PostgreSQL in Docker: 

    Django>=6.0,<7.0
psycopg[binary]>=3.1

  2. In settings.py , you can switch database config based on environment variables. A simple pattern is:

    • If DJANGO_DB_HOST is set, use PostgreSQL
    • Otherwise, fall back to SQLite for local non-Docker runs 
    import os
DJANGO_DB_HOST = os.environ.get("DJANGO_DB_HOST")
if DJANGO_DB_HOST:
    # PostgreSQL configuration
    DATABASES = {
        "default": {
            "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.postgresql",
            "NAME": os.environ.get("DJANGO_DB_NAME", "tallyapp"),
            "USER": os.environ.get("DJANGO_DB_USER", "tallyapp"),
            "PASSWORD": os.environ.get("DJANGO_DB_PASSWORD", ""),
            "HOST": DJANGO_DB_HOST,
            "PORT": os.environ.get("DJANGO_DB_PORT", "5432"),
            "CONN_MAX_AGE": 60,  # persistent connections (good for production)
        }
    }
else:
    # SQLite fallback (default for local development)
    DATABASES = {
        "default": {
            "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3",
            "NAME": BASE_DIR / "db.sqlite3",
            "OPTIONS": {
                "timeout": 20,  # helps reduce "database is locked" errors
            },
        }
    }

Build and run the Docker system

Now we can build the Docker image and start the containers using Docker Compose:

  1. Build images: 

    docker compose build

  2. Start containers: 

    docker compose up
  3. At this point PostgreSQL is running in one container, and Django is running in another container, exposed on http://localhost:8000 , as shown in Figure 11.2 :

Figure 11.2: Two containers running in Docker Compose

Prompt : What actually happens under the hood when I run docker compose up ?

  1. In Docker Desktop , expand the tallyapp entry to see its two containers for the PostgreSQL database and the tallyapp-web Django host, as shown in Figure 11.3 :

Figure 11.3: Two containers running in Docker Desktop

  1. In a new terminal window, run migrations and create an admin user inside the web container: 

    docker compose exec web python manage.py migrate
docker compose exec web python manage.py createsuperuser

Docker changes where you run commands and where you look for errors. You usually do not SSH into a server. You run commands inside the container that already has your app and dependencies. You also read the container logs, because that is where the app is running.

  1. Start your preferred browser and navigate to the admin site: http://localhost:8000/admin/
  2. Log in with the administrator account that you previously created and view the list of users, as shown in Figure 11.4 :

Figure 11.4: Administrator accounts

  1. Close the browser.

  2. At the command prompt or terminal, stop the containers: 

    docker compose down

To stop containers and remove volumes (this wipes the database) use the -v switch: docker compose down -v . This reinforces why volumes matter. Without a volume, a database container is disposable, and so is its data.

Reducing image size with multi-stage builds

The Dockerfile shown earlier is simple and easy to understand, but it includes tools that are only needed during installation, such as compilers. These tools increase the size of the final image and are not required when the application is running.

The current Docker image includes compilers ( gcc , make ), package manager cache, and build dependencies. Those are not needed at runtime and increase both the image size and potential attack surface.

A more advanced technique called a multi-stage build separates the build environment from the runtime environment. The first stage installs dependencies, and the second stage copies only the results into a clean image.

A multi-stage build separates:

  1. Build stage : Install dependencies, compile anything needed
  2. Runtime stage : Copy only what is needed to run the app

This avoids shipping unnecessary tools like compilers into your final image.

Here is a rewritten version of your Dockerfile using a multi-stage build: 

# ---- Stage 1: Build dependencies ----
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends build-essential \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --upgrade pip \
 && pip install --prefix=/install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
# ---- Stage 2: Runtime image ----
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# Copy installed packages from builder
COPY --from=builder /install /usr/local
# Copy project code
COPY . /app/
CMD ["python", "manage.py", "runserver", "0.0.0.0:8000"]

This produces smaller images, faster downloads, and a reduced attack surface. The final image only contains a Python runtime, your dependencies, and your app. Multi-stage builds are common in production setups, but optional for learning projects.

Viewing logs to debug container issues

When something goes wrong in a Docker-based setup, the first place to look is the container logs.

If you ran your containers with: 

docker compose up

You will already see logs in that terminal window.

However, if you run containers in the background or open a new terminal, you can view logs using: 

docker compose logs

This shows the combined output of all services, including your Django app and PostgreSQL database. For example, you might see Django startup messages, database connection errors, migration warnings, and Python exceptions.

You can focus on just one container: 

docker compose logs web

Or: 

docker compose logs db

This is useful when you want to separate Django errors from database output.

To watch logs as they happen: 

docker compose logs -f

This is like running docker compose up , but works even if the containers are already running in the background.

Viewing logs is important because Docker changes how you debug problems. You are no longer running everything directly on your machine. Your app runs inside containers, so errors show up there, not in your editor or terminal history.

If the app fails to start, or cannot connect to the database, the logs will usually tell you why.

For example:

  • “could not connect to server” tells you that PostgreSQL is not ready
  • “no such table” tells you that database migrations were not applied
  • Python traceback tells you that there is a bug in your code

Common mistakes and quick fixes

If Django starts before PostgreSQL is accepting connections, you might see connection errors on first startup. The simplest fix for a learning project is to rerun docker compose up or retry migrations. In more advanced setups you add a wait for DB script.

Prompt : Please show me a wait-for-database script for Django containers.

Docker reduces works on my machine problems by giving everyone the same Dockerfile and Compose services. That is why teams use it.

During learning, keep credentials clearly marked as development-only when using secrets in compose files. In real deployments, you would use environment injection, secret managers, or Docker secrets rather than committing passwords.

Prompt : Please explain the difference between environment variables, .env files, and Docker secrets. What are best practices for managing secrets in Docker Compose?

Where this fits in TallyApp’s overall deployment story

This Docker setup is primarily a development environment, but it teaches patterns that carry into production: immutable builds, multi-service composition, and persistent data via volumes.

It also sets up an easy database upgrade path: you can develop locally with PostgreSQL in containers, then later deploy with PostgreSQL on a VPS or managed PostgreSQL without changing your application logic, only its configuration.

While Docker focuses on packaging applications into consistent, portable environments, it does not address how code itself is tracked, shared, and evolved over time. That is where Git comes in. If Docker ensures that software runs the same way everywhere, Git ensures that teams (including human and AI programmers) can collaborate on that software without losing track of changes or overwriting each other’s work. Together, Docker and Git form a natural pairing in web development workflows, but before combining them, it is important to understand how Git manages version control so each change can be saved, reviewed, and, if necessary, undone.

Source code version control using Git

Before you add features to TallyApp, you need protection against your own mistakes. Git gives you a complete history of your project, lets you experiment safely, and makes collaboration and deployment straightforward.

This section teaches a focused, practical subset of Git using VS Code’s built-in Git integration. You will learn how to initialize a repository, make meaningful commits, create branches, connect to a remote, and recover from common mistakes.

What Git does

Git is a distributed version control system. It records snapshots of your project over time.

A few terms matter, as summarized in Table 11.2 :

Term

Definition

Repository

A folder that Git tracks. It contains a hidden .git directory that stores the project history.

Commit

A saved snapshot of your project at a specific moment, along with a message explaining the change.

Working branch

The files you are currently editing.

Staging area

The set of changes you intend to include in the next commit.

Branch

A parallel line of development. You can experiment on a branch without affecting main .

Remote

A hosted copy of your repository, typically on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket.

Table 11.2: Common Git terms

Git runs locally on your machine. Services such as GitHub host a remote copy so you can back up and share your work.

Initializing Git for TallyApp in VS Code

After creating your TallyApp Django project, initialize Git immediately:

  1. Open the TallyApp folder in VS Code.
  2. Click the Source Control icon in the left sidebar.
  3. Click Initialize Repository , as shown in Figure 11.5 :

Figure 11.5: VS Code Source Control view

  1. You now have a local Git repository, as shown in Figure 11.6 :

Figure 11.6: VS Code Source Control view

Creating a .gitignore for Django

A Django project generates files that should not be committed. You want to track source code, not machine-specific artifacts or secrets.

Create a file named .gitignore at the root of your project and add: 

.venv/
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*.sqlite3
.env
.DS_Store

This ignores virtual environments, Python bytecode, SQLite databases, environment variable files, and operating system clutter.

Good practice : If you use SQLite for development, ignoring db.sqlite3 is recommended. Your database state should be reproducible from migrations, not committed as a binary file.

You should now see that fewer files will be committed, as shown in Figure 11.7 .

Warning! Do not ignore *.md files. Markdown files are often used for documentation, README files, architecture notes, and even AI prompts. In many projects, they are part of the source of truth, not generated output. Ignoring them would mean losing important context and documentation from your repository. A good rule of thumb is this: only ignore files that can be recreated automatically (like virtual environments, caches, or compiled files). If a file contains human-written knowledge, it should almost always be committed.

Making Your First Commit

Once Git is initialized:

  1. Navigate to Source Control where you will see a list of untracked files.
  2. Click the + icon next to Changes to stage everything, as shown in Figure 11.7 :

Figure 11.7: Stage All Files

  1. Enter a commit message like: Initial TallyApp project scaffolding , and then click Commit , as shown in Figure 11.8 :

Figure 11.8: Source Control panel showing 0 Changes, 10 Staged Changes, and the commit message box

Good practice : A commit should describe intent, not mechanics. Good messages explain what changed and why. Examples for TallyApp: Add Survey model and admin registration, Create survey CRUD views and templates, Add login protection to survey pages, Improve styling of survey list.

The daily Git workflow

As you build TallyApp, follow this loop:

  1. Make sure you have no changed files.
  2. Make a small change.
  3. Run the app and verify it works.
  4. Stage all files.
  5. Write a clear commit message.
  6. Commit.

This discipline makes your history readable and makes debugging easier later.

In Source Control:

  • Files under Changes are modified but not staged
  • Files under Staged Changes will be included in the next commit

You can stage individual files using the + icon.

Creating a branch for a feature

Branches let you experiment without risking the main branch.

To create a branch:

  1. Click the branch name in the bottom-left of VS Code, usually main , as shown in Figure 11.9 :

Figure 11.9: Creating a new Git branch

  1. Select Create new branch , and type a name like: feature/home-page , and then press Enter .

  2. At the command prompt or terminal, create a new feature: 

    python manage.py startapp homepage

  3. In tallyapp/settings.py , add the app, as shown highlighted in the following code: 

    INSTALLED_APPS = [
    'django.contrib.admin',
    'django.contrib.auth',
    'django.contrib.contenttypes',
    'django.contrib.sessions',
    'django.contrib.messages',
    'django.contrib.staticfiles',
    "homepage",
]

  4. In homepage/views.py , add statements to import some types, and define two functions, as shown highlighted in the following code: 

    from django.contrib.auth.decorators import login_required
from django.contrib.sessions.models import Session
from django.shortcuts import render
from django.utils import timezone
# Create your views here.
def _active_authenticated_user_count() -> int:
    """
    Approximation: count non-expired sessions that have an authenticated user id.
    This counts sessions, not unique users. One user on two devices counts twice.
    """
    now = timezone.now()
    active_sessions = Session.objects.filter(expire_date__gt=now)
    count = 0
    for s in active_sessions:
        data = s.get_decoded()
        if data.get("_auth_user_id"):
            count += 1
    return count
def home(request):
    context = {
        "active_user_count": _active_authenticated_user_count(),
    }
    return render(request, "homepage/home.html", context)

What this signed-in users number really means: It counts users with a valid, unexpired session. It does not guarantee they are actively using the site this second. It may count the same person multiple times (phone + laptop). It can stay non-zero for a while even if people close the browser, because sessions often expire hours or days later. This approach loads all sessions from the database, which works fine for a small project but would be too slow for a production site with thousands of sessions. The leading underscore in the function name _active_authenticated_user_count is a Python convention that signals that this function is an internal helper, not part of the public API.

  1. In the homepage folder, create a urls.py file: 

    from django.urls import path
from .views import home
urlpatterns = [
    path("", home, name="home"),
]

  2. In tallyapp\urls.py , add a reference to the new feature, as shown highlighted in the following code: 

    from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include
urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path("", include("homepage.urls")),
]

  3. Create templates/base.html : 

    <!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>{% block title %}My Django Site{% endblock %}</title>
</head>
<body>
    <header>
        <h1>My Django Site</h1>
    </header>
    <main>
        {% block content %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
</body>
</html>

  4. Create templates/homepage/home.html : 

    {% extends "base.html" %}
{% block title %}Home · TallyApp{% endblock %}
{% block content %}
<div class="card">
  {% if user.is_authenticated %}
    <p class="muted">Hi {{ user.username }}. You're signed in.</p>
  {% else %}
    <p class="muted">You're not signed in yet. Log in to admin.</p>
    <div class="card-actions">
      <a class="btn primary" href="/admin">Log in</a>
    </div>
  {% endif %}
  <hr style="border:0;border-top:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.14); margin:16px 0;">
  <p class="muted">
    Signed-in users right now (approx): <strong>{{ active_user_count }}</strong>
  </p>
</div>
{% endblock %}
  5. Now commit as before.

Your work on the home-page feature is isolated and you can switch between it and the main branch at will.

Merging a branch

To merge back into main :

  1. Switch back to main .
  2. 2. Open the Command Palette and choose Git: Merge Branch .
  3. Select your feature branch.

If no conflicts exist, Git creates a merge commit.

A remote Git server provides backup and enables collaboration:

  • Use Commit to save locally
  • Use Sync Changes to push to GitHub

Working with pull requests and code review

So far, you have created branches and merged them locally. That works when you are working alone, but most real projects use a slightly different process.

Instead of merging directly into the main branch, developers open a pull request.

A pull request is a way to propose a change, review it, and discuss it before merging.

Here is the standard process used by most teams:

  1. Create a feature branch: 

    git checkout -b feature/home-page

  2. Make changes and commit them: 

    git add .
git commit -m "Add home page view and template"

  3. Push the branch to GitHub: 

    git push origin feature/home-page
  4. Open a pull request in GitHub:
    • Compare your branch to main
    • Add a description of what changed and why
  5. Review the changes:
    • You (and others) can comment on specific lines
    • You can suggest improvements or fixes

  6. Make updates if needed: 

    git add .
git commit -m "Fix feedback from review"
git push
  7. Once approved, merge the pull request into main .

A pull request is not just a button in GitHub. It serves three important purposes:

  • Review : someone checks the code before it becomes part of the main project
  • Discussion : design decisions can be questioned and improved
  • History : the project records not just what changed, but why

Even if you are working alone, opening a pull request for your own work is useful. It gives you a chance to review your changes before merging. The pull request step slows you down slightly, but that is the point. It forces you to think before code becomes permanent.

This is especially important when using AI-generated code. It is easy to accept code that “looks right” but has subtle issues. A pull request creates a natural checkpoint for review. AI makes it easier to produce code quickly. Pull requests are where you apply human judgment to decide whether that code is actually good.

Many teams protect the main branch so it cannot be changed directly. All changes must go through a pull request. This prevents accidental mistakes and ensures every change is reviewed.

Pulling changes and handling conflicts

If you work on multiple machines or collaborate, you will need to pull changes:

  1. Click Sync Changes or run Pull .

If conflicts occur, VS Code opens a merge editor.

  1. Choose one of: Accept Current Change , Accept Incoming Change , or Accept Both Changes .
  2. Edit if necessary. What should be edited is entirely dependent on the specific conflict scenario.
  3. Save, stage, and commit the resolved file.

A conflict does not mean corruption. It means Git needs help deciding between two edits.

Undoing common mistakes

You only need three recovery tools at this stage.

  • Discard local edits : Right-click a modified file in Source Control and choose Discard Changes .
  • Unstage a file : Right-click a staged file and choose Unstage Changes .
  • Amend the last commit : If you forgot a file:
    1. Stage the file.
    2. Open the Source Control menu ... .
    3. Choose Commit | Amend Commit .

Amend rewrites the last commit. Only use it if you have not pushed yet.

From this point onward:

  • Every meaningful change to TallyApp should be committed
  • Each new feature should live on a branch
  • Each chapter section should end with a commit

By the time you deploy TallyApp, committing, branching, and reviewing changes should feel like the normal rhythm of the project.

12

Unit, Integration, and End-to-End Testing

Do not leave testing until the end. It is how you turn a working prototype into dependable software. In a real project like TallyApp, features interact, users do things you did not expect, and small changes break code that looked unrelated. A good test suite lets you refactor, extend, and deploy with fewer nasty surprises.

A view might return the wrong survey. A permission check might let one user edit another user’s data. A form might accept invalid input. A JavaScript or template change might make a button disappear. You might fix one bug and accidentally reintroduce an older one.

Tests are how you make those risks visible. A good test suite does not prove your application is perfect. It gives you fast, repeatable feedback about the behavior you care about most.

This chapter explores testing at three different levels:

  • Small, fast unit tests that validate isolated pieces of logic
  • Broader integration and user interface tests that verify components work together
  • Using AI tools to draft, review, and improve tests

You will see how these layers catch different kinds of mistakes. When combined thoughtfully, they give you a safety net, so you can change code without guessing whether the project still works.

You will start with unit tests for small pieces of logic, then move into Django integration tests that exercise views, Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), authentication, forms, and the database. After that, you will use Playwright to automate a few browser-level user journeys. You will also learn how to manage test data, run tests in continuous integration, and use AI tools without letting them generate shallow tests that only look useful.

The main habit to build is simple: before you ask whether the code works, ask what behavior the system is supposed to guarantee.

By the end of this chapter, you will have designed and implemented a layered testing strategy for TallyApp, written meaningful unit and integration tests in Django, automated real browser interactions with end-to-end tests, and learned how to use AI tools to accelerate test creation without handing over engineering judgment.

In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:

  • The testing pyramid and testing philosophy
  • Unit testing Python and Django
  • Integration testing Django applications
  • End-to-end web user interface testing
  • Managing test data and fixtures
  • Continuous integration and automated test pipelines
  • Asking an AI to write tests
