13

Specifying and Building the Initial Project

A good software project starts before anyone writes code. It starts with understanding the goal. What are you building? Who is it for? What problem is it meant to solve? And just as important, what are you choosing not to build?

In this chapter, we move from isolated examples to the first working version of TallyApp. It is realistic enough to teach planning, structure, data modeling, permissions, forms, and testing, but still small enough to finish.

TallyApp is a survey platform. Approved users can create and publish surveys. Members of the public can complete them anonymously. Survey creators can review both individual responses and aggregated results. This type of website is familiar, practical, and large enough to force real design decisions without overwhelming you with unnecessary complexity or turning into a product you could spend a year building.

This chapter is about thinking before building. You will define the scope before implementation. You will set constraints before you let the tools lead you. You will use a lightweight, AI-assisted planning process to translate a structured project brief into a working Django application. Along the way, you will see how a clear brief reduces guessing, limits feature creep, and makes technical decisions less arbitrary.

Those questions matter more than the first lines of code. If you ask an AI assistant to build the project before you define the main decisions, you will probably get a pile of code that looks impressive but makes assumptions you did not choose. So, before building, you will write a short project brief. The brief describes the goal, users, features, non-goals, constraints, and definition of done.

This is a simplified version of how real projects work. You will build an extensible survey system with authentication, permissions, data modeling, testing, and a clean user interface.

By the end of this chapter, you will have defined a clear project brief for TallyApp, translated that brief into an actionable development plan, scaffolded a Django 6 project with appropriate apps and models, implemented core authentication and survey functionality, and established a small project that you can extend in the next chapter.

In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:

  • Defining the scope and goals of the project
  • Creating the TallyApp project
  • Reviewing the AI-created project
  • Using the Codex App for interactive development

    Suggested chatbot prompts with example responses for this chapter can be found at the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/prompts/ch13-project/readme.md

Defining the scope and goals of the project

Before installing anything or writing code, be explicit about what you are building and, just as importantly, what you are not. A clear scope makes technical decisions easier and keeps the project focused as it grows.

The project you will build is a web project called TallyApp. At a high level, TallyApp allows people to create surveys, share them publicly, collect responses, and analyze the results. This is similar to many real-world applications and gives us plenty of opportunities to explore backend logic, frontend presentation, data modeling, and visualization without drifting into unnecessary complexity.

User journeys

TallyApp supports three main user journeys.

User journey 1: Create and publish a survey

An authenticated user can create a survey with a title and description, add questions, and choose different question types such as multiple choice and free-form text answers. Once the survey is ready, it can be published and given a public link that can be shared with others. This part teaches data modelling, forms, validation, and permissions.

User journey 2: Take a survey

Anyone with the public link can view the survey and submit responses without needing an account. The interface is intentionally simple and task-focused. Respondents answer questions and submit the form, and their responses are stored reliably. This part of the project highlights URL design, templates, form handling, and protecting against invalid or duplicate submissions.

User journey 3: View and analyze results

The survey creator can view aggregated results, such as counts and percentages for multiple-choice questions, as well as individual responses for free-text questions. Results are presented using tables and charts, so patterns are easy to spot. This part of the application introduces reporting queries, basic analytics, and data visualization.

Project limits

It is also important to define boundaries. TallyApp is not a full enterprise survey platform. We are not building user billing, team collaboration, advanced permissions, or complex branching logic between questions. These omissions are deliberate. They keep the focus on learning how to design and build a complete web application rather than chasing more features or building something we can monetize.

Why a survey project?

The best way to learn web development is to work on real projects that you would use yourself or that at least spark an interest in you.

If you are a student or a professional developer who has no choice over the projects or technologies that you implement, how can you work on a real project that needs the technologies you are interested in learning about?

Attributes of a good learning project

To help us learn all the different technologies that web developers need to know these days, we need a project that:

  • Genuinely needs a mix of technologies and skills.
  • Is cool, fun, and practical, so it will stretch our skills both from an engineering perspective as well as creatively.
  • Is as real as possible, and that we would use ourselves.
  • Has already been implemented by others with public products that we can draw inspiration from, preferably with some open-source examples so we can review code implementations. Even if not, a product with feature screenshots would help us draft a product requirements document ( PRD ).

A PRD lists the features for a product to allow someone to understand what it should do. It does not say how it should do it. That would be defined in a functional specification that is more detailed.

  • Has a small enough minimum viable product (MVP) that we have an achievable short-term goal to aim for.
  • Has a large enough potential that it stretches to something much more complex long-term.

When you’re struggling with a bug, you need to stay motivated. The best way to stay motivated is to work on a project that you will use yourself. Eat your own dog food, as they say.

Prompt : Please explain the difference between a product requirements document and a functional specification with examples from a Django web app.

Features of survey and polling tools

Personally, I have used survey and polling software to gain insight into my students and readers. For example, the most popular survey product is probably Google Forms, although there are dozens of alternatives, as shown in the following list:

  • Google Forms: https://workspace.google.com/forms/about/
  • Microsoft Forms: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/online-surveys-polls-quizzes
  • Poll Everywhere: https://www.polleverywhere.com/
  • TechRadar’s best list: https://www.techradar.com/best/best-survey-tools

Most survey tools have a free tier, so you can try them out. We are looking at these products for inspiration, not trying to copy them.

After exploring the core features that define survey and polling tools, the next step is to look more closely at the building blocks of any survey: the different types of questions you can ask and how each one shapes the data you collect.

Question types

There are dozens of question types, from multiple choice to scale selection via matrix and freeform text, as shown in Figure 13.1 :

Figure 13.1: Types of survey questions in Google Forms

Some of these question types should be easy enough to implement, like the plain text response or selecting one option from many. Others are likely to be harder to implement once you think about all the potential possibilities.

Polling and quizzes

Survey tools have similar features to other tools, like live polling and quiz builders. They all need some way to build the survey, poll, and quiz, and some way to take it, and finally, ways to analyze the results.

I often deliver live training sessions and webinars. It is useful to ask the audience a bit about themselves, like where in the world they are, what their current experience is, and what they expect to get out of the session. The main difference between a survey and a live poll is the duration that question items are available to answer. The main difference with a quiz is the concept of a correct answer and scoring at the end.

Quizzes also share a lot of similarities. The main difference is the breadth of question item types. You can imagine that a quiz builder for learning mathematics or physics could have some quite elaborate components with complex implementations.

Analyzing the responses

Another major feature of survey tools is the ability to analyze the results using everything from basic charts to complex machine learning algorithms to spot unusual patterns.

What are the product requirements?

A product requirements document is the result of analyzing a business problem. It defines a set of suggested features that solve the problems that the software is supposed to address.

Minimal requirements overview

A minimal viable product for a survey tool would include:

  • A website to take a survey anonymously
  • A website to view the survey results
  • Data storage for the survey question items and responses

Minimal website requirements

To take a survey, the solution should provide a website. This is to make the surveys accessible to as many people as possible. Every device has a web browser, so a website will have the broadest reach. We can also easily share surveys using hyperlinks.

The website should respond to a request to take a survey identified by a unique value, as shown in the following link:

https://www.tallyapp.net/123456

The website should allow anonymous visitors, present the question items to them, and record their responses. To keep it simple, there could be no restrictions on taking the survey multiple times. There would be no user registration required or authentication checks.

Prompt : What security risks exist in anonymous survey submissions? What other vulnerabilities should I watch for in a survey web application?

Minimal question item types

The website should support the following question types:

  • Single line plain text
  • Multi-line plain text
  • Rating (1-10)
  • Multiple choice (one selection). Shows radio buttons

Each item type should allow a plain text question.

Minimal data storage requirements

How should a survey and its responses be stored? It needs to be simple At first, it is tempting to think a document database would be simpler because a survey looks like a nested document: survey, questions, choices, responses. But TallyApp also needs permissions, reporting, filtering, and aggregation. For this book, a relational database is the better teaching choice because it makes those relationships explicit.

Minimal analysis app requirements

The analysis app should show a list of all surveys and their status, for example, if they are active, if they are complete, how many have taken them, the details of their answers, and summaries of the results. Numeric results should appear as tabular data as well as charts.

Prompt : What mistakes do beginners make when defining the scope for their first web app?

Ideas for extended requirements

One of my favorite aspects of a survey tool is that there are many areas where you can choose to extend the minimal product:

  • A website that a visitor can register with and track the surveys they have completed
  • Dozens of different question types
  • Dozens of ways to analyze the results
  • Multiple ways to store the questions and results, from a fully normalized database to document-based cloud storages
  • Multiple ways to process the results and provide a service layer above the data stores

I have put more ideas for extending a survey project online. You can read them at the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/docs/extending-ideas.md

Now let’s create the TallyApp project.

Creating the TallyApp project

This section creates the first working version of TallyApp. It is deliberately small: one Survey model, plus create, edit, and delete screens restricted to logged-in users. It also includes register, log in, and log out. The UI uses clean, simple styling with plain CSS, and includes SVG assets for a logo and a survey sketch illustration used on editing pages.

Assumptions for this section:

  • Django 6
  • Python 3.14
  • A local virtual environment
  • SQLite database (we can swap to PostgreSQL later)

Practical AI-assisted project planning

Formal spec-driven development that you will learn about in the next chapter can be useful, but for a beginner-friendly process, it is often excessive. Full spec systems involve structured requirement documents, traceability, staged refinement loops, and sometimes dedicated command sets or multi-agent AI workflows. That is valuable in large teams building regulated or mission-critical systems. It is not necessary for learning how to design and build a clean Django application.

Instead, you can use a lightweight approach. The idea is to write a short, structured project brief in Markdown, then use a carefully written one-shot prompt to guide the AI.

Prompt : Show me an example of a bad one-shot prompt for TallyApp and how to improve it.

For example, before building TallyApp, create a file named project-brief.md with clearly defined sections such as:

  • Goal
  • Target users
  • Core features
  • Non-goals
  • Technical constraints
  • Definition of done

This forces you to define scope before writing code. Including a Non-goals section prevents accidental feature creep, which is one of the most common problems in both human-led and AI-assisted development.

Once the brief is written, you can prompt your AI assistant along the following lines: 

I am building a Django 6 project called TallyApp. The attached Markdown file describes the requirements. Please:
- Break the project into implementation phases.
- Propose Django models and relationships.
- Suggest URL patterns and app structure.
- Provide initial scaffolding for models, views, and templates.
- Restate the requirements in your own words before generating code and identify any ambiguities.

That final instruction is important because it forces the AI to review the requirements before coding. This reduces hallucinations and makes assumptions visible. It also models a good professional habit to clarify before you implement.

This is why the brief matters. Codex or Claude Code can create Django files in seconds, but they will still make product decisions unless you make them first. Should TallyApp allow someone to submit the same survey twice? Should a survey become locked after it is published? Should results be stored for easy reporting later, or only for simple display now? Those are not coding questions. They are design decisions. Write them down before asking the AI to build anything. The better your brief, the better the code has a chance of being.

Prompt : Why does asking the AI to restate requirements before generating code reduce hallucinations? Please explain the psychology behind structured prompting and why it improves code quality.

Review the AI’s work before running it

After receiving the output, you do not blindly paste it into your editor. You review it. Here’s a checklist:

  • Review the model relationships.
  • Confirm the field data types.
  • Look out for unnecessary complexity.
  • Run database migrations and tests.

It is particularly important to look out for security issues:

  • Every form template should include {% csrf_token %}
  • Protected views should use @login_required or LoginRequiredMixin
  • Watch out for raw SQL queries that could allow SQL injection attacks so the code should use the Django object-relational mapper (ORM) exclusively
  • User input should never be rendered unescaped, for example {{ variable }} will automatically escape the output
  • Make sure that SECRET_KEY is not hardcoded in any committed file
  • Survey submission views should validate ownership and permissions

The AI produces a draft, but you remain the software engineer who applies human judgment to the generated code.

This approach captures many of the benefits of spec-driven thinking:

  • Explicit scope
  • Defined constraints
  • Clear success criteria
  • Reduced ambiguity
  • Structured planning before coding

But it avoids the overhead of formal specification frameworks.

As your skills grow and your projects become more complex, you can adopt more formal spec-driven approaches, as you will see in the next chapter. But for building TallyApp and mastering web development fundamentals, a clear project brief plus a well-crafted prompt is the right balance of structure and simplicity.

Prompt : Compare one-shot prompting with iterative refinement prompting for building a Django project.

Choosing a Django version

Although Django 5.2 is the only active Long-Term Support (LTS) release (supported until April 2028), we will target Django 6.0 because the 6 versions will have an LTS version 6.2 starting in April 2027 during the expected lifetime of this book, as shown in Figure 13.2 and at the following link: https://www.djangoproject.com/download/

Figure 13.2: Django supported releases

Now that we’ve chosen to target Django 6.0 or later, let’s write the project brief.

AI project brief for TallyApp

Create a file named project-brief.md in the root of your project containing the following Markdown code:

This project brief can be downloaded from the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/Code/TallyProject/project-brief.md 

# TallyApp – Project Brief
## 1. Overview
### Project Goal
TallyApp is a web application that allows approved users to create surveys and publish them publicly. Members of the public can take surveys without registering. Survey creators can view both individual responses and aggregated results.
### Problem It Solves
TallyApp allows individuals or organizations to quickly gather structured feedback using multiple types of survey questions without building custom software.
---
## 2. Target Users
### Survey Creators
- Must register for an account with a valid email address.
- Must be approved by an administrator before creating surveys.
- Can create, publish, and end surveys.
- Can view results (individual and aggregated).
### Survey Takers
- Do not need to register.
- Can submit responses anonymously.
### Home Page for Target Users
- Describes functionality of website.
- Two large buttons to:
    1. Create a Survey (Register or Log In)
    2. Take a Survey
---
## 3. Core Features (Version 1 Scope)
### Authentication & Authorization
- Define a custom group named SurveyCreators whose membership authorizes survey creation functionality.
- Survey Creator registration.
- Admin approval required before users can create surveys; users are added to SurveyCreators group when approved.
- Login and logout.
- Only members of SurveyCreators group can create surveys.
### Survey Creation
- Create or edit a survey with:
  - Title
  - Description
  - Start date
  - Optional end date
  - Publish status
  - "Show on homepage" flag (default: true)
- Unpublished surveys do not have results.
- Surveys cannot be edited after publishing.
- Surveys cannot be unpublished.
- Surveys can be ended early. This cannot be reversed.
- Surveys may be open-ended (no end date).
- Once ended a survey cannot be taken by users.
- Surveys consist of zero, one or more question items that can be added, edited, or removed via the survey edit page.
- Surveys each have a unique public URL shown on the survey edit page as soon as they are created.
- Published survey with start_date in future cannot be taken and show a warning page with the start date shown.
### Question Types
Each survey can contain multiple questions of the following types:
1. Multiple choice – single answer
2. Multiple choice – multiple answers
3. Text input (free-form)
4. Matrix ratings with range of ratings e.g. 1 to 5 for one or more items
Question/choice authoring UI must be fully implemented.
- Dynamic form handling for mixed question types.
### Public Survey Access
- Public homepage lists published surveys (if "Show on homepage" is true) with a public URL to take the survey.
- Surveys support pagination on list views.
- Public users can submit responses.
- Surveys may display results "to date."
### Results
Survey creators can:
- View aggregated results.
- View individual responses.
- View responses even while survey is still open.
- View pie and bar charts for suitable results.
- View report of any duplicate submissions per email/IP/session.
### Graphics, styling and branding
- SVG assets for a logo and a survey sketch illustration used on editing pages.
- The UI uses CSS and SVG files to give TallyApp a subtle brand: gradient header or navbar, colorful logo SVG, light tinted background sections.
### Data Storage
- SQLite database.
- Relational model with clear foreign key relationships.
### Testing
- Basic unit tests for:
  - Model behavior
  - Permissions
  - Publishing rules
  - Survey response submission
- End-to-end tests using Playwright for:
  - Each user story.
---
## 4. Non-Goals (Out of Scope)
- No payments.
- No social authentication.
- No real-time updates (no WebSockets).
- No advanced analytics.
- No export to CSV.
- No REST API.
- No role system beyond admin approval and standard user.
---
## 5. User Stories
1. As a user, I want to register so that I can create surveys.
2. As an admin, I want to approve users before they create surveys.
3. As an approved user, I want to create and publish a survey.
4. As a survey creator, I want to end a survey early.
5. As a public visitor, I want to complete a survey without registering.
6. As a survey creator, I want to see both aggregated results and individual responses.
---
## 6. Data Model (High-Level)
### User
- Extends Django's built-in User model.
- Has a custom group named SurveyCreators whose membership gives access to create, edit and delete survey features.
### Survey
- Creator (ForeignKey to User)
- Title
- Description
- Start date
- Optional end date
- Published flag
- Show on homepage flag
- Created timestamp
- Ended early flag (optional)
### Question
- Survey (ForeignKey)
- Text
- Question type (single choice, multiple choice, text)
- Order field
### Choice
- Question (ForeignKey)
- Text
- Order field
### Response
- Survey (ForeignKey)
- Optional email identifier
- Submitted timestamp
### Answer
- Response (ForeignKey)
- Question (ForeignKey)
- Selected choice(s) (ManyToMany or intermediate model as appropriate)
- Text answer (for text questions)
---
## 7. Technical Constraints
- Python 3.14
- Django 6.x
- SQLite database
- Clean, modern, mobile-friendly responsive UI
- Server-rendered templates
- No JavaScript frameworks required
---
## 8. Security & Permissions
- Only approved users can create surveys.
- Only survey creators (and administrators) can view the results of their own surveys.
- Public users can submit responses.
- Surveys cannot be modified after publishing.
- Only admins can approve users to create surveys.
---
## 9. Definition of Done
- Users can register and log in.
- Admin can approve users.
- Approved users can create and publish surveys.
- Public users can submit responses.
- Survey creators can view results.
- Pagination works.
- Basic unit tests pass.
- Application runs locally using SQLite without errors.
---
## 10. Future Enhancements (Not Version 1)
- CSV export
- Charts and visual analytics
- Survey scheduling automation
- Email invitations
- API endpoints
- Role-based permissions beyond basic approval

A blank project brief template can be downloaded from the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/Code/TallyProject/project-brief-template.md

Reviewing the full steps

Before we ask an AI to generate code, it helps to see the full steps from idea to working application. The prompt is only one step in that process, as shown in Figure 13.3 :

Figure 13.3: From idea to working project with AI assistance

A project brief guides the AI, but human review and iteration are what turn generated code into a usable application. Human judgment is the difference. AI writes code. You decide what should be built.

To summarize: Think clearly  Write a solid brief  Guide the AI  Review everything  Fix what is wrong  Iterate. Good results come from a good brief and careful review, not from a magic prompt.

Improving your project briefs

Before asking an AI to build a new project by following your project brief, it’s good practice to ask your AI to review it. For example: 

Read project-brief.md and act as a senior engineer reviewing a new project before implementation.
Your job is to find everything that is missing, unclear, or risky.
Work in phases:
# Phase 1: Gap analysis
Identify missing or weak areas across:
- Requirements clarity and scope boundaries
- User journeys and edge cases
- Data model assumptions
- Permissions and security
- Validation and error handling
- Performance and scalability risks
- Testing strategy
- Operational concerns (deployment, configuration, secrets)
Do not suggest solutions yet. Just list gaps and ambiguities.
# Phase 2: Targeted interview
Ask me focused questions to resolve those gaps.
- Skip obvious or already well-defined areas
- Prioritize high-impact uncertainties
- Ask one topic at a time, not a long list
- Push for concrete decisions, not vague preferences
Continue until there are no meaningful unknowns left.
# Phase 3: Trade-offs and assumptions
For any remaining open decisions, propose 2–3 options with clear trade-offs.
# Phase 4: Update the brief
Produce an improved version of the file named project-brief-ai-enhanced.md that:
- Preserves all correct existing content
- Clarifies ambiguous sections
- Adds missing constraints and edge cases
- Makes assumptions explicit
Show the updated file in full. Do not remove sections unless clearly incorrect.
Be concise, direct, and practical. Avoid generic advice.

This will enhance your project brief because doing a gap analysis stops the AI from immediately asking weak questions like: Who are your users? Instead, it has to think first, then ask.

This makes the AI slow down and inspect the brief before jumping into code. That is closer to how an experienced developer reviews a feature request before implementation.

If you prefer a more compact version of the prompt: 

Read project-brief.md and review it like a senior engineer before implementation.
1. List missing or unclear areas (requirements, edge cases, data model, permissions, validation, performance, testing).
2. Interview me with focused questions to resolve the most important gaps. Ask one topic at a time.
3. For unresolved decisions, propose options with trade-offs.
4. Produce an improved version of the brief, preserving correct content and making assumptions explicit.
Skip obvious points. Be direct and practical.

Prompt : What are the risks of blindly trusting AI-generated scaffolding code?

Now let’s look at the visual design of a website.

Guiding AI with a design.md

The project brief defines what the system should do. It only briefly defines how the system should look, feel, or behave from a user interface perspective. If you skip that step, the AI will make those decisions for you. Often, you need to be more specific, especially when creating a public website for an organization with a strong brand.

A simple way to avoid this is to create a second document alongside your project brief: design.md .

This file captures your design decisions in plain language so that both you and your AI assistant follow the same rules.

Why a separate design document?

Separating design from the project brief keeps concerns clear:

  • The project brief defines behavior, features, and constraints
  • The design document defines layout, interaction, and visual consistency

This mirrors how real projects are often structured. Product and engineering define behavior. Design defines how that behavior is presented.

For a learning project like TallyApp, pixel-perfect design is unnecessary. Consistency is enough.

What goes into design.md?

A useful design.md does not need to be long; it should answer a few practical questions:

  1. Layout and structure : Describe the overall page structure:

    • Header with navigation ( Home , My Surveys , Login/Register )
    • Main content area with a fixed-width container
    • Footer (optional) 
    Pages use a simple layout: a top navigation bar, a centered content column, and minimal distractions. Avoid complex multi-column layouts.

  2. Navigation and flow : Explain how users move through the app:

    • Where users land after login
    • How they access survey creation
    • How they return to previous pages 
    After logging in, users are redirected to "My Surveys." Primary actions should be visible without scrolling.

  3. Forms and interaction patterns : Define how forms behave:

    • Labels above inputs
    • Clear validation messages
    • Submit buttons at the bottom 
    All forms use server-side validation with clear error messages shown above each field. Avoid JavaScript-heavy form logic.

  4. Styling approach : Set constraints on styling:

    • Use plain CSS
    • Avoid heavy frameworks unless needed
    • Prefer simple color palette 
    Use a minimal CSS approach. No CSS frameworks. Keep colors neutral with one accent color for actions.

  5. Components and reuse . Encourage consistency:

    • Buttons look the same everywhere
    • Tables follow a consistent structure
    • Messages use a shared style 
    Use reusable CSS classes for buttons, alerts, and tables. Do not redefine styles per page.

  6. Accessibility and clarity . Even at a basic level:

    • Use semantic HTML
    • Ensure readable text
    • Avoid hidden interactions 
    Prefer semantic HTML elements. Buttons should be <button>, not clickable <div> elements.

Using a design file with AI tools

Once you have both project-brief.md and design.md , you can include both in your prompt: 

The project-brief.md file defines functionality. The design.md file defines layout, styling, and interaction rules. Follow both.

This reduces a common problem where AI-generated code mixes styling approaches or creates inconsistent UI patterns.

Some tools are starting to formalize this idea. For example, Anthropic’s Claude Design encourages separating design intent from implementation so the model can generate more consistent user interfaces.

Introducing Claude Design by Anthropic Labs: https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-design-anthropic-labs

You do not need a special tool like Claude Design to apply the same idea. A simple design.md file achieves most of the benefit.

Good practice : Do not turn design.md into a full design system. For TallyApp, a single page of guidelines is enough. The purpose is not to design a production UI. The purpose is to stop the AI from inventing one.

The more clearly you define behavior and design upfront, the less time you spend fixing code later.

Now let’s move into the step where most people jump too early: writing the prompt.

A one-shot prompt for applying your project brief

You can paste the following into your AI assistant after attaching or pasting the project brief: 

I am building a Django 6 web application called TallyApp.
The project-brief.md file in the current directory contains the full project brief. The design.md file defines layout, styling, and interaction rules. Follow both.
Before generating any code:
1. Restate the project requirements in your own words.
2. Identify any ambiguities or design decisions that need clarification.
3. List assumptions you will make.
4. Highlight potential complexity risks.
Then:
5. Break the implementation into logical development phases.
6. Propose a Django app structure.
7. Design the data models with fields and relationships.
8. Suggest URL patterns.
9. Outline views and their responsibilities.
10. Define permission rules and enforcement strategy.
11. Explain how surveys become immutable after publishing.
12. Explain aggregation logic for multi-select answers.
Only after completing the above analysis, generate beginner-friendly scaffolding code for:
- models.py
- basic forms
- views
- urls.py
- minimal templates
- static files including CSS and SVG
- basic unit tests
- E2E tests using Playwright
Keep the implementation simple.
Avoid advanced patterns unless clearly justified.
Explain why you choose particular modeling decisions, especially for multiple-choice answers and text responses.

Prompt : How would you modify the TallyApp one-shot prompt to enforce stricter architectural constraints?

Since we are using this simple technique, a Markdown file for the spec and a single prompt, we don’t need the interactivity of a tool like GitHub Copilot in a code editor or integrated development environment ( IDE ). We can use an AI command-line interface ( CLI ) like Codex or Claude Code. Since it is common for developers to switch between the two main competitors in this space due to model capability fluctuations and cost spikes, we will look at both CLI tools.

    codex

Figure 13.5: OpenAI Codex configured to use the gpt-5.5-codex model with medium thinking

  1. Copy and paste the one-shot prompt into the prompt.

  2. When you see the following response, press Enter to accept: 

    [Pasted Content 1207 chars]

  3. Note that Codex will start creating files and running checks. Let it work, but read what it says as it goes: 

    • I have the brief parsed and there's no existing code yet, so I'll scaffold a single Django app (surveys)
  with beginner-friendly function-based views, model-level safeguards, and templates/static/test files.
  Plan: (1) create models and forms that encode publish immutability + mixed-question responses, (2) wire
  views/URLs/templates for creator and public flows, (3) add CSS/SVG assets, (4) add unit + Playwright E2E
  scaffolds and summarize decisions.
• I'm starting file creation now, beginning with models.py and forms.py so the permission, immutability, and
  answer-shape rules are encoded before wiring the UI.
...
• I'm now wiring the core application flow (views.py, urls.py, templates, tests) around the models/forms
  already created, keeping everything function-based and explicit for beginner readability.

Avoiding AI usage limits

AI tools often impose usage limits, especially on free or lower-tier plans. A few habits reduce wasted prompts and help you avoid running out halfway through a task.

First, be deliberate with your prompts. Instead of sending multiple small, vague requests, combine them into a single, clear and well-structured prompt. This reduces back-and-forth and gets you closer to a useful result in one response. (In a distributed architecture, this principle is known as: Be chunky, not chatty .)

Second, iterate efficiently. Rather than restarting from scratch, refine previous prompts or ask the AI to improve its own answer. Building on existing context uses fewer requests and produces better results.

Third, avoid unnecessary experimentation when working on real tasks. It’s easy to burn through usage by trying many variations. When you have a clear goal, stay focused and direct.

Finally, switch tools or modes when appropriate. Some platforms offer different models, free tiers, or fallback options. Knowing when to use a lighter model versus a more advanced one can help you stay within limits.

The key idea is to treat AI interactions as a resource. Thoughtful, well-structured prompts not only improve quality but also help you stay productive without running into caps.

The most interesting design decision in TallyApp

If there is one part of TallyApp where database design really matters, it is how survey answers are modeled. Everything else in the system is fairly straightforward.

The difficulty comes from one simple fact: not all questions are the same.

TallyApp currently supports three question types:

  • Multiple choice, single answer
  • Multiple choice, multiple answers
  • Free-form text

At first glance, it might seem tempting to store everything in one flexible Answer model with a few nullable fields. For example:

  • A selected_choice field for single-answer questions
  • A selected_choices many-to-many field for multi-answer questions
  • A text_value field for text questions

That works, but it forces you to think carefully about data integrity. You must ensure:

  • Single-answer questions never store multiple choices
  • Multiple-answer questions can store multiple choices
  • Text questions never reference a choice
  • Choice-based questions never store free-form text in place of a choice

The model must encode rules that reflect the business logic of your application.

This is where the relational thinking that you learned about in Chapter 7 , SQL – Managing Data , becomes interesting. One common and clean approach is:

  • A Response model representing one user’s submission
  • An Answer model representing a response to a single question
  • A foreign key from Answer to Question
  • A foreign key from Answer to Response
  • A nullable foreign key to Choice for single-answer questions
  • A many-to-many relationship to Choice for multi-answer questions
  • A text field for text responses

Then you enforce rules at the form or model validation level based on question.question_type .

This design teaches three useful ideas:

  1. First, it shows how relational databases model variability. Instead of creating three separate tables for three question types, you create one flexible structure and constrain it logically.
  2. Second, it teaches normalization. A survey response is not a flat blob of JSON. It is a structured set of answers, each tied to a question. That makes aggregation, filtering, and reporting dramatically easier.
  3. Third, it highlights future extensibility. If you later decide to add rating-scale questions or numeric inputs, your model already has a clear extension point.

There is also an important architectural lesson here. The data model defines what is possible. If you or your AI model answers carelessly, you will struggle later when implementing features like aggregated counts, filtering by question, validation rules, export features, and performance optimization.

In fact, many real-world systems that outgrow themselves do so because their early data models were too simplistic.

Using the Codex App for interactive development

So far in this chapter, you have used a one-shot prompt to generate a complete project scaffold. That technique is efficient but it is still mostly text-based. You describe what you want, the AI generates code, and then you review it.

The Codex App introduces a different way of working. Instead of only describing the system in text, you can interact with a running application and give feedback directly against what you see.

This is especially useful once TallyApp is running locally and you move from build the structure to refine the behavior and interface .

You can learn more about the Codex App at the official documentation: https://developers.openai.com/codex/app

What the Codex App adds

The Codex App is a graphical interface for working with AI-assisted development. It sits alongside your editor and local development environment and allows you to:

  • Chat with a model about your codebase
  • Run commands and inspect outputs
  • Work with files and generated code
  • Interact with a live preview of your application

The key difference from earlier workflows in this chapter is that the AI is no longer working from descriptions alone. It can be guided using the actual running UI.

This reduces a common problem with AI-assisted development: vague instructions such as make this look better or fix the layout , which often produce inconsistent results.

Browser-based interaction for UI work

One of the most useful features of the Codex App is its ability to interact directly with a running web application through a built-in browser panel. This turns web UI work into something much closer to pointing at the screen and saying, “Change this.”

Once your Django development server is running, you can connect the Codex App to your local site:

  1. Start a chat with your preferred model
  2. Start your Django dev server (for example, python manage.py runserver )
  3. Open the browser panel in the Codex App
  4. Navigate to your local site (for example, http://127.0.0.1:8000 )
  5. Use the browser tools to inspect and annotate the UI

The browser panel includes features such as:

  • Taking screenshots of the current page
  • Adding annotations to specific UI elements
  • Sending those annotated screenshots directly into the chat

When you click on a button, form, or layout element and attach a comment, the model receives both the visual context (screenshot) and your instruction tied to a specific part of the UI.

For example: 

This button is too small and blends into the background. Make it more prominent and consistent with the primary action style.

This is far more precise than describing the problem in text alone.

In earlier sections, you saw how important it is to define behavior and structure before generating code. UI refinement has a similar challenge: describing visual issues in words is often imprecise.

The browser interaction feature improves this in three ways:

  1. Shared context : The AI sees exactly what you see, instead of inferring layout from templates and CSS.
  2. Targeted changes : Feedback is attached to a specific element, not a vague description of a page.
  3. Faster iteration : You can quickly try changes, review them, and refine again without rewriting long prompts.

This saves you from describing layout problems from memory.

Example steps with TallyApp

Once your TallyApp project is running locally, you might use these steps:

  1. Open the homepage in the Codex browser panel.
  2. Click the Create a Survey button.

  3. Add an annotation, as shown in Figure 13.15 : 

    This should be the primary action. Increase contrast and add more padding.
  4. Let Codex propose changes to your CSS and templates.
  5. Review the changes before applying them.
  6. Reload and repeat.

Figure 13.15: Annotating the TallyApp home page with a comment using Codex App

You can follow a similar process for form layouts, navigation structure, error messages, spacing, and alignment issues.

Limitations and good habits

This feature is useful, but it should still be used with the same discipline as the rest of your workflow.

Keep these points in mind:

  • Do not accept UI changes blindly. Always review generated CSS and templates.
  • Keep your design.md in sync with changes, so you do not drift into inconsistent styles.
  • Avoid making many small, uncoordinated tweaks. Prefer grouped, intentional changes.
  • Use this for refinement, not initial architecture.

Also note that interaction is currently element-by-element. If you want to change multiple components consistently, you should describe the pattern, not just individual elements.

Use the Codex browser interaction when:

  • The application is already running
  • You are refining layout, styling, or usability
  • You can point to specific issues on the screen

Do not rely on it for:

  • Initial project design
  • Data modeling decisions
  • Security or permission logic

Those still belong in your project brief and design thinking earlier in the chapter.
