Adding Project Features Using Spec-Driven Development

In the previous chapter, you used a large prompt and a product requirements document to generate the first working version of TallyApp. That approach demonstrated how AI tools can scaffold an entire project quickly. However, real software projects rarely stop after the first implementation. New features are added, behavior is refined, and edge cases are discovered as the system evolves.

For the next feature, do not start by asking the AI to “add something useful.” Start by writing down the feature. Say what it should do, who can use it, what should happen when it fails, and how you will check that it works.

This style of working is often called Spec-Driven Development . The specification becomes the agreed description of the feature, and the code becomes its implementation. When AI coding assistants are involved, this discipline is particularly important because they tend to fill in missing details by inventing behavior based on unvalidated assumptions. A clear specification leaves fewer gaps for the AI to fill and gives the AI less room to invent behavior you did not ask for.

In this chapter, you will apply this approach to the existing TallyApp Django project. Instead of generating a brand new application, you will extend the current codebase by designing and implementing a small but realistic feature.

By the end of this chapter, you will have written a structured feature specification, used an AI coding assistant to implement it inside an existing Django project, and verified that the implementation satisfies clearly defined acceptance criteria.

In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:

  • Spec-driven development
  • Using Spec Kit to structure specifications
  • Adding a URL shortener feature to TallyApp
  • Ideas for extending TallyApp

Suggested chatbot prompts with example responses for this chapter can be found at the following link: https://github.com/markjprice/web-dev-ai/blob/main/prompts/ch14-spec/readme.md

Spec-driven development

In Spec-Driven Development, you begin with a written description of what the system should do. Instead of starting with code and hoping the design sorts itself out, write down the feature first: the problem, what is in scope, what is out of scope, and what must be true when the work is finished. Then you implement.

This idea is not new. Good engineers have always written requirements, user stories, and acceptance criteria. What is new is the presence of AI coding assistants. Tools such as GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, and Claude Code can generate large amounts of code quickly. They can scaffold projects, refactor modules, and even propose architectural changes. That can help, but it also introduces risk. Without a clear specification, AI tools will confidently implement assumptions you did not intend. They will fill in gaps you did not know existed. They will optimize for plausibility rather than correctness. That is dangerous because plausible code is often harder to spot than obviously broken code.

Spec-Driven Development brings discipline to AI-assisted coding. The specification becomes the reference document. It defines the scope of the feature, the non-goals, the data model, the behavior of the user interface, and the error conditions. The AI is not asked to build an app . It is asked to satisfy explicit acceptance criteria. Each requirement must be traceable to code. Each behavior must be verifiable.

This is why the specification matters. Codex or Claude Code can write a lot of Django code, but it will not know whether a feature is finished unless you define finished. For the URL shortener, that means writing rules such as: who can create links, how codes are generated, what happens for an unknown code, and which tests must pass.

Prompt : Why do AI coding assistants tend to make incorrect assumptions when specifications are incomplete? Describe the risks of vague requirements when using AI coding assistants.

Tests turn a specification from a document into something enforceable. A spec that cannot be verified is simply documentation. A spec backed by automated tests becomes enforceable. In a Python web project, this usually means mapping acceptance criteria to unit tests with pytest and, where appropriate, browser-level tests. The test suite becomes the referee. When AI generates code, the tests decide whether that code is acceptable. If it fails, the implementation is wrong, regardless of how polished it looks.

What a good specification contains

A useful web feature spec should be short, but not vague. For TallyApp, a typical feature spec might include the following sections:

  • Goal : A short paragraph describing what this feature enables. Example: Allow authenticated users to create, edit, and delete surveys .
  • Non-Goals : List what you are deliberately not building. Example: No public survey sharing in this iteration .

    Prompt : Please explain why “non-goals” are important in software specifications and give examples from real-world projects.

  • User Stories : Write the main interactions from the user’s perspective:
    • As a logged-in user, I can create a new survey
    • As a logged-in user, I can edit the title of an existing survey
    • As a logged-in user, I can delete my own survey
  • Acceptance Criteria : These are precise, testable conditions. Acceptance criteria should be written so they can become tests without reinterpretation. Avoid vague statements like the UI should be clean . They should be observable facts:
    • When a valid survey form is submitted, the survey is saved in the database
    • When an invalid form is submitted, validation errors are displayed
    • A user cannot edit another user’s survey
    • After deletion, the survey no longer appears in the list view

      Prompt : Please show me some examples of poorly written acceptance criteria and how to rewrite them into clear, testable requirements.

  • Data model changes : Define fields, relationships, and constraints. For example:
    • Survey: id (primary key), owner (foreign key to user), title (string, max length 200), created_at (timestamp). If a field has constraints, write them down. If a relationship has cascading behavior, specify it.
  • Error handling and edge cases :
    • What happens if a user attempts to edit a survey that does not exist?
    • What happens if required data is missing?
    • What HTTP status codes should be returned for forbidden access?

      Prompt : Please give examples of edge cases developers often forget when writing specifications. Please explain how to identify hidden assumptions in a software specification.

  • Verification commands : Write down how you will check the feature later:
    • Run unit tests
    • Run integration tests
    • Start the development server and confirm behavior manually if needed

      Prompt : Please explain how spec-driven development differs from test-driven development ( TDD ) and behavior-driven development ( BDD ). Include a side-by-side comparison of spec-driven development, TDD, and BDD, including strengths and weaknesses of each approach.

Tools for Spec-Driven Development

There is not one standard way to do spec-driven work. Different teams structure their specifications differently, use different terminology, and automate different parts of the process. Some developers prefer lightweight Markdown documents stored alongside the source code. Others use structured templates that resemble traditional requirements documents. Some processes emphasize automated tests as the executable form of the specification, while others focus on planning artifacts that guide AI tools through staged implementation.

A small ecosystem of tools has begun to appear to support this style of development. One example is Spec Kit , an open-source project from GitHub that provides templates and commands for writing specifications, generating implementation plans, and breaking features into tasks. Another tool is OpenSpec , which aims to standardize machine-readable software specifications that can be interpreted by AI agents. Some developers are also experimenting with specification-first workflows built into AI coding environments such as Cursor, Continue, and Claude Code, where structured prompts and planning steps guide the model through feature development.

Warning! Because GitHub Spec Kit, OpenAI Codex, Anthropic Claude Code, and other AI tools are evolving quickly, treat exact prompts and small setup details as likely to drift over time.

Now that you’ve been introduced to some spec-driven development tools, let’s look in more detail at one practical option.

Using Spec Kit to structure specifications

One practical tool that supports Spec-Driven Development is Spec Kit , an open-source project published by GitHub. It provides a structured workflow and templates for writing specifications, planning implementations, and coordinating AI-assisted development.

Spec Kit is not a framework or library. Instead, it is a lightweight system that helps developers organize their specifications so that both humans and AI assistants can understand them clearly.

The Spec Kit workflow

Spec Kit organizes development into a sequence of stages. Each stage produces a document that clarifies the system before moving on to the next step.

A typical workflow looks like this:

1. Project principles, also called the constitution

A document that defines the high-level rules and philosophy of the project. These might include conventions such as coding standards, architectural constraints, or testing requirements.

Example questions addressed in this stage:

  • Should the system prioritize simplicity or extensibility?
  • What testing practices are required?
  • What technologies are allowed or forbidden?

This document sets the rules the AI should follow when it changes the project.

2. Feature specification

The specification describes the feature that will be built.

It typically includes:

  • The goal of the feature
  • Non-goals and constraints
  • User stories
  • Acceptance criteria
  • Data model changes
  • Error handling and edge cases

This is the stage where you define exactly what the feature must do.

3. Implementation plan

Once the specification is approved, the next document describes how the feature will be implemented.

The plan usually includes:

  • Architecture changes
  • New modules or services
  • Database migrations
  • Testing strategy
  • Deployment considerations

AI tools are particularly useful in this stage because they can suggest implementation approaches based on the specification.

4. Task breakdown

The implementation plan is then converted into a list of concrete development tasks.

For example:

  • Create ShortLink Django model
  • Add redirect view
  • Create form for generating short links
  • Write unit tests

These tasks can be executed sequentially, often with AI assistance.

5. Implementation

Only after the specification, plan, and tasks are defined does the actual coding begin.

At this stage, the AI assistant is given clear instructions and constraints. Instead of inventing behavior, it simply implements what has already been described.

Prompt : Please explain how tools like Spec Kit and OpenSpec help prevent AI coding assistants from introducing unintended features.

Structure helps, but it has a cost. Before using Spec Kit for every change, it is worth knowing when a lighter approach is enough.

When is Spec Kit overkill?

Spec Kit can help keep AI-generated work on track, but it can be too much for small changes. You are trading some coding time for more planning and review time.

Let’s understand when Spec Kit is likely overkill or unnecessary.

When a lighter prompt is enough

If you are in the exploratory phase, for example, prototyping a UI or testing a basic concept, Spec Kit’s rigid flow ( /constitution  /specify  /plan  /tasks ) can slow you down.

Small projects often benefit from vibe coding, where you give a high-level prompt and iterate on the code directly. Setting up a Constitution for a weekend hobby project is overkill.

High context-to-code ratio

Spec Kit can generate hundreds of lines of Markdown for a single feature. For a small project (like a basic URL shortener with two views), the documentation can be longer than the code. The exception is when learning because a smaller project is easier to understand.

The risk is that you spend more time reading and correcting the AI’s plans and specs than it would take to simply write the code or review a single-shot AI output.

Minor tweaks and one-off bug fixes

If you’re just changing a button color, updating a regex, or fixing a simple logic error, just prompt your AI coding tool directly. Running a full /specify and /plan cycle for a 5-line change is inefficient and adds unnecessary files to your repository.

Token cost and speed

Each step in the Spec Kit workflow involves significant back-and-forth with the LLM, consuming thousands of tokens and taking several minutes of processing time.

For a small project, you want the result in 10 seconds. Spec Kit makes you wait for the AI to think through the architecture, which is often unnecessary for well-trodden paths (like a basic Django app).

Birgitta Böckeler’s taxonomy

Spec-Driven Development is best understood as a spectrum. At one end, you might write a short prompt that captures intent. At the other, you might produce a full specification with acceptance criteria and validation steps. Birgitta Böckeler describes spec-driven work as a spectrum rather than a single rigid process.

Birgitta Böckeler’s taxonomy of Spec-Driven Development is not a formal standard like a published specification. It is a practical way of describing how it shows up at different levels of rigor when working with AI.

Lightweight

You still think before you code, but the spec is minimal. It might be a short paragraph, a checklist, or even a well-crafted prompt. Typical characteristics:

  • A brief description of the goal
  • Maybe a couple of constraints or edge cases
  • Often embedded directly in the AI prompt
  • Little or no separate artifact

Use this for small features, bug fixes, and exploratory work where you are iterating quickly. The key idea is that you are guiding the AI, but not formalizing everything. This still counts as SDD because you describe the change before coding.

Structured

This is closer to what we will see in this chapter. Typical characteristics:

  • A clearly written specification
  • Defined behavior and user interactions
  • Data model considerations
  • Acceptance criteria or test cases
  • Separate from the implementation step

Use this for medium-sized features, changes with multiple moving parts, and where correctness matters more than speed. The key idea is that the spec becomes a reference point.

Formal or end-to-end

This is the full version, often associated with frameworks like Spec Kit. Typical characteristics:

  • Multiple structured artifacts (spec, plan, tasks, validation steps)
  • Traceability from requirements to implementation
  • Iterative refinement of the spec itself
  • Strong alignment between humans and AI over longer workflows

Use this for large features or systems, high-risk or high-complexity work, and team environments where coordination matters. The key idea is that the specification drives the entire lifecycle, not just the initial prompt.

You can learn more about Birgitta Böckeler and watch some of her conference talks at the following link: https://gotopia.tech/experts/1305/birgitta-boeckeler

Alternatives to Spec Kit

Structured AI development workflows are not one-size-fits-all. Heavier frameworks, such as Spec Kit, can work well when you need strong guardrails, explicit planning, and traceable handoffs across a larger or riskier project.

For smaller features or solo work, a lighter approach such as OpenSpec may be a better fit because it preserves the habit of writing down intent without turning the process into a document factory. The goal is to give the AI enough clear context to produce better code.

For readers exploring spec-driven AI workflows, there is a spectrum. Spec Kit is more structured and stage-oriented. OpenSpec is lighter and less stage-oriented. Beginners should be wary of any method that produces lots of planning documents without clearly improving implementation, testing, or review.

You can learn more about OpenSpec as an alternative to Spec Kit at the following link: https://github.com/Fission-AI/OpenSpec

Spec Kit commands

Spec Kit includes helper scripts that automate parts of this process. After initializing the project, you can run commands that guide the development process:

  1. /speckit.constitution – define project principles
  2. /speckit.specify – create a baseline specification
  3. /speckit.plan – generate an implementation plan
  4. /speckit.tasks – break the plan into tasks
  5. /speckit.implement – execute the implementation

Additional commands help refine the specification or check consistency between artifacts.

Warning! GitHub’s current Spec Kit README notes that most agents expose /speckit.* slash commands, but Codex CLI in skills mode uses $speckit-* instead. Skills mode is behind a feature flag, so if you didn’t explicitly enable it, you’re not using it. To enable skills mode, you should have started Codex like this: codex --enable skills . If you didn’t pass that flag (or configure it in your setup), then skills are off.

These commands do not generate production code themselves. Instead, they structure the conversation with the AI so that each step builds on the previous one.

AI coding tools are good at filling gaps. That is useful when the gap is obvious, but risky when the missing detail is a product decision. If the spec does not say whether short links are public, private, expiring, or trackable, the tool may choose for you.

Spec Kit reduces this problem by making the specification explicit and structured. Because the specification, plan, and tasks all live in the repository, they can be reviewed, versioned, and improved over time.

For teams experimenting with AI-assisted development, this approach provides a useful balance: the speed of AI-generated code combined with the discipline of traditional software engineering.

Install the Specify CLI

For this chapter, install the GitHub SpecKit Specify CLI with uv , as shown in the following command: 

uv tool install specify-cli --from git+https://github.com/github/spec-kit.git

uv is a fast Python package manager from Astral. We use it here because Spec Kit’s installation from a Git repository works more reliably with uv tool install. If you prefer, you can also clone the repository and install with pip install -e .

If uv is not installed yet, install uv first, then run the command above. You can install uv from the following link: https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/ .

After installation, confirm that the Specify CLI and its dependencies are available: 

specify check

With the process in place, let’s apply it to a small feature that fits naturally into a survey application.

Adding a URL shortener feature to TallyApp

A useful way to learn how to do Spec-Driven Development is to add a feature to an existing system. In this section, you will add a URL shortener to TallyApp.

Why a URL shortener?

A URL shortener might seem unrelated to surveys. But survey creators often want to share their survey links in emails, presentations, or printed materials. A long URL such as https://tallyapp.example.com/surveys/8e5a4c39-2f4d-4b9e-bbfa-2c10a96d21fd/take/ is inconvenient to share. A short link such as https://tallyapp.example.com/s/abc123 is easier to remember and distribute.

The goal of this feature is to allow survey creators to generate a short link that redirects to their survey.

Prompt : Please explain how URL shorteners work internally. Describe the algorithms commonly used to generate short URL codes and compare random code generation with hash-based URL shortening.

Writing the feature specification

Before writing any code, define the behavior of the feature.

A typical feature specification includes the following sections.

Goal

Allow authenticated users to create short URLs that redirect to longer links inside TallyApp.

The most common use case will be generating short links for surveys.

Non-Goals

To keep the feature small and focused, we explicitly exclude several capabilities:

  • No analytics tracking in the first version
  • No expiration dates for links
  • No custom aliases (users cannot choose the short code)
  • Only authenticated users can create short links

These restrictions prevent the feature from expanding into a full commercial-style service.

User stories

Describe the interactions from the user’s perspective:

  • As a logged-in user, I can create a short link for a survey URL
  • As a logged-in user, I can view a list of the short links I created
  • As any visitor, I can visit a short URL and be redirected to the target page

Figure 14.1 shows what happens when someone visits a short link like /s/abc123 :

Figure 14.1: URL shortener request flow

The URL shortener request flow:

  1. The browser requests the short URL from your site.
  2. Django matches the /s/<code>/ pattern and calls the view redirect_short .
  3. The view looks up the code in the ShortLink table.
  4. Django returns an HTTP 302 redirect to the original survey URL for the browser to request.
  5. Django returns a 404 Not Found response if the code does not exist.

Acceptance criteria

These criteria define observable behavior:

  • When a valid URL is submitted, a short code is generated
  • The short code is unique
  • Visiting /s/<code> redirects to the stored target URL
  • A user can only see short links they created
  • If a short code does not exist, a 404 Not Found response is returned

These conditions are specific enough to be turned into automated tests.

Data model

Add a new Django model named ShortLink . Its fields are shown in Table 14.1 :

Field

Type

Description

id

primary key

internal identifier

owner

ForeignKey(User)

creator of the short link

target_url

URLField

the original URL

code

CharField(10)

unique short identifier

created_at

DateTimeField

timestamp

Table 14.1: Fields for the ShortLink model

Model constraints are:

  • code values must be unique and have a maximum of ten characters
  • code values should be randomly generated from URL-safe characters

Verification steps

The feature can be verified by:

  1. Running unit tests
  2. Visiting a generated short link in the browser
  3. Confirming the redirect behavior

Ask the AI to generate an implementation plan

Once the specification exists, you can give it to an AI coding assistant and ask for a plan.

Example prompt: 

You are helping extend an existing Django project named TallyApp.
Implement the following feature according to the specification below.
[Paste spec]
First generate an implementation plan. Do not write code yet.

A good plan should suggest steps like these:

  1. Create a new Django app named shortlinks
  2. Define the ShortLink model
  3. Add migrations
  4. Create views for:
    • creating short links
    • redirecting short links
  5. Add URL routes
  6. Create a basic HTML form
  7. Add unit tests

Review the plan before asking the AI to implement it.

Plan and implement the URL shortener feature using Specify and Codex

First, a note on the moving parts. GitHub’s Spec Kit and its Specify CLI can initialize an existing project, install templates, and generate agent-specific command files. Spec Kit supports Codex CLI as a first-class agent option, and it specifically documents specify init . --ai codex and specify init --here --ai codex for existing projects.

OpenAI’s current Codex setup flow is: sign in, select the folder or repository you want Codex to work on, and then start a task.

Let’s use SpecKit with Codex step-by-step:

  1. Start in the root folder of your existing Django project, the same folder that contains manage.py and your app folders.

  2. Initialize Spec Kit in the current folder instead of creating a new folder: 

    specify init . --ai codex

Spec Kit also supports --script ps if you want PowerShell-oriented scripts, which is a sensible choice on Windows: specify init . --ai codex --script ps

  1. You will be warned about existing files, as shown in Figure 14.2 :

Figure 14.2: Initializing Specify in a project folder

  1. Press Y to continue.
  2. Select if you want Bash/shell or PowerShell scripts. Either will work on Windows as long as you have installed Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 ( WSL2 ). On Mac or Linux, select Bash.

    Prompt : Please explain how GitHub Spec Kit works internally and what files it generates in a project repository. Show the directory structure created by Spec Kit and explain the purpose of each file.

  1. Set an environment variable for Codex configuration for this project: 

    setx CODEX_HOME "C:\web-dev-ai\TallyProject\.codex"

  2. Start Codex with the latest GPT model, for example, 5.5 in April 2026: 

    codex --model gpt-5.5

    At the time of writing in April 2026, OpenAI also says GPT-5.5 is now available in Codex and is the recommended choice for most Codex tasks; in the CLI you can start a session with codex --model gpt-5.5 . You can check the latest OpenAI Codex model at the following link: https://developers.openai.com/codex/models

  1. In Codex, create a constitution file, as shown in Figure 14.3 and the following output: 

    /speckit.constitution 
This is an existing Django project named TallyApp.
Project principles:
1. Keep the architecture simple and beginner-friendly.
2. Prefer Django built-ins over third-party packages unless there is a strong reason.
3. Write code that is readable for learners new to Django.
4. Use pytest or Django tests to verify acceptance criteria.
5. Add small, incremental features instead of broad architectural rewrites.
6. Preserve existing behavior unless the spec explicitly changes it.
7. Use server-rendered Django templates unless a richer client-side experience is clearly justified.
8. Avoid over-engineering.

Figure 14.3: Creating a constitution file

Create the URL shortener specification

Next, run the Spec Kit specification step. The documented command is /speckit.specify .

In Codex, run: 

/speckit.specify

Then paste a focused prompt like this: 

Create a feature specification for adding a URL shortener to the existing TallyApp Django project.
Goal:
Allow authenticated users to create short URLs that redirect to longer links inside TallyApp. The main use case is generating short links for surveys so they are easier to share.
Non-goals:
- No click analytics in this version
- No expiration dates
- No custom aliases
- Only authenticated users can create short links
User stories:
- As a logged-in user, I can create a short link for a survey URL
- As a logged-in user, I can view a list of short links I created
- As any visitor, I can visit a short URL and be redirected to the target page
Acceptance criteria:
- When a valid URL is submitted, a short code is generated
- The short code is unique
- Visiting /s/<code> redirects to the stored target URL
- A user can only see short links they created
- If a short code does not exist, return 404 Not Found
Data model:
ShortLink
- owner: ForeignKey(User)
- target_url: URLField
- code: CharField(max_length=10, unique=True)
- created_at: DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
Constraints:
- code must be unique
- codes should be randomly generated
- deleting the owning user deletes the link
Please generate a spec that matches the existing Django codebase and keeps the implementation small and teachable.

When Codex generates the spec, read it carefully. This is the point where you should correct anything too clever, too broad, or inconsistent with the existing TallyApp design.

It is fine to make changes to any of the files that Specify creates for you.

Should Spec Kit files be committed to Git?

In most teaching and team projects, yes: commit the specification artifacts that explain the feature, especially the specs/ folder and files such as spec.md , plan.md , tasks.md , and quickstart.md . These files are part of the project’s design history. They explain what you asked the AI to build, what was accepted, and how the feature should be verified.

Treat the .specify/ folder more carefully. It can contain project-level Spec Kit configuration, templates, scripts, and agent command files. For a team project, commit it if you want everyone to use the same Spec Kit workflow. For a solo experiment, you can keep it local if it only contains generated helper files that can be recreated.

Do not blindly commit everything. Before committing, run git status and inspect the changed files. Do not commit secrets, personal machine paths, API keys, temporary output, caches, __pycache__/ , virtual environments, or agent logs. If Spec Kit creates files that define the shared workflow, commit them. If files are only the local tool state, ignore them.

Here’s a small .gitignore example: 

# Python
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
.venv/
.env
# Local tool output
out/
*.log
# Keep Markdown specs and project documentation tracked.
# Do not ignore *.md.

Generating the spec is not the same as approving it. This is the first point where your judgment matters more than the AI’s fluency.

Review the generated spec file

Spec Kit stores specs as repository artifacts. For example, a feature folder under specs/ containing spec.md and related planning documents.

Open the new spec file and check for five things:

  • The goal is clear.
  • Non-goals really limit scope.
  • Acceptance criteria are testable.
  • The data model is small and fits Django.
  • The feature does not add extras like dashboards, analytics, Quick Response ( QR ) codes, or admin processes you did not request.

This review matters because the rest of the steps will build on this file.

Ask Codex to produce the implementation plan

Once the specification looks right, move to the planning phase with: 

/speckit.plan

Use a prompt like this: 

Create an implementation plan for the URL shortener feature in TallyApp.
Constraints:
- Existing Django project
- Keep the code simple and suitable for a teaching project
- Prefer one new app named shortlinks unless there is a compelling reason not to
- Use Django templates and standard views
- Include tests for redirect behavior, permissions, and 404 handling
- Do not introduce background jobs, analytics, or external services

Then inspect the plan. A good plan should mention creating the app, model, migration, form, views, routes, template, and tests, without wandering into unnecessary abstractions.

Prompt : How should developers structure prompts when asking AI to generate an implementation plan?

Ask Codex to break the plan into tasks

Next, run: 

/speckit.tasks

Prompt it like this: 

Break the URL shortener implementation plan into a sequence of small, reviewable tasks.
Each task should be concrete and produce a visible result.
Include tasks for:
- model creation
- migrations
- creation form
- list page for a user's links
- redirect route
- tests
- brief documentation update

Keep the work small at this stage. If Codex creates a giant single task called Implement URL shortener , push back and ask it to split the work more finely.

Have Codex implement the feature

Now run: 

/speckit.implement

Give Codex a strict prompt such as: 

Implement the URL shortener feature according to the approved specification, plan, and task list.
Requirements:
- Follow the project principles
- Keep the implementation minimal and readable
- Do not add features not in the spec
- Update URLs, templates, models, and tests as needed
- Run the test suite and report any failures clearly
- Show me the diff or summarize changed files before any large refactor

OpenAI Codex is a coding agent that works on project folders and repositories, and GitHub Spec Kit is designed to supply the staged artifacts Codex can act on. That combination is exactly what you want here: the spec constrains the agent, and the agent writes the code.

Codex will output a summary: 

Implemented the URL shortener feature and kept it within the approved scope: one new shortlinks app, standard Django views/templates, no analytics, no background jobs, no external services.
  What Changed
  Core feature:
  - Added shortlinks/models.py, shortlinks/forms.py, shortlinks/views.py, shortlinks/urls.py, shortlinks/admin.py, and shortlinks/migrations/0001_initial.py.
  - Added the create/list templates at shortlinks/templates/shortlinks/shortlink_form.html and shortlinks/
    templates/shortlinks/shortlink_list.html.
  - Wired the app into tallyapp/settings.py and tallyapp/urls.py.
  - Added a simple navigation entry in surveys/templates/surveys/base.html and a dashboard button in surveys/
    templates/surveys/dashboard.html.
  Verification and docs:
  - Added feature tests in shortlinks/tests.py and a regression check in surveys/tests.py.
  - Updated project-brief.md, quickstart.md, and marked all tasks complete in tasks.md.
  - Added a minimal .gitignore for Python/Django and local Node artifacts.
Tests
  Ran python manage.py test shortlinks surveys
  Result: 17 tests run, all passed.
  Notes
  All URL shortener tasks are now marked complete. The working tree also contains pre-existing planning/spec changes under .specify/ plus generated __pycache__ updates from test execution; I did not revert those automatically.

According to the output, all URL shortener tasks are now marked complete, so the next step is to review the implementation and then if we are happy, to accept it. Passing tests are encouraging, but they are not permission to stop thinking.

Review the implementation before accepting it

Do not trust the first pass blindly. Read every changed file. I would specifically inspect:

  • shortlinks/models.py
  • shortlinks/views.py
  • shortlinks/forms.py if one was added
  • shortlinks/urls.py
  • The project urls.py
  • Templates for create/list pages
  • Test files
  • Any migration files

Pay attention to whether Codex followed the spec literally. AI coding agents can produce working code, but they still have a habit of adding helpful things nobody asked for.

Prompt : Please explain how developers can review AI-generated code effectively.

Run Django locally and verify the feature manually

From the TallyApp root, run the usual Django commands:

  1. Codex may already have created the migration, but this command is harmless if there are no model changes. Make the migrations: 

    python manage.py makemigrations

  2. Perform the migrations: 

    python manage.py migrate

  3. Run the tests: 

    python manage.py test

  4. Start the web project: 

    python manage.py runserver
  5. Then manually verify the acceptance criteria in the browser:
    • create a short link as a logged-in user
    • confirm the code is generated
    • visit /s/<code> and confirm redirect behavior
    • try a non-existent code and confirm 404
    • confirm one user cannot see another user’s short links

This manual pass is still worth doing even when the tests are green.

Optional refinement pass

A good final Codex prompt is: 

Review the implemented URL shortener feature against the specification and acceptance criteria.
Identify:
- any missing behavior
- any unnecessary complexity
- any code that should be simplified for teaching purposes
- any tests that are missing

The preceding review prompt is where the workflow often pays off. It asks Codex to review the code against the agreed spec.

So we’ve now added a new feature, reviewed it, and if needed, refined it. The URL shortener is only one example. The same steps become more useful as the feature becomes more ambiguous or touches more parts of the system.

For the last section of this chapter, let’s think of some other features that could extend the capabilities of our project.

Ideas for extending TallyApp

At this point, the TallyApp project has authentication, survey creation, response collection, analytics, testing infrastructure, and now an additional feature built using Spec-Driven Development.

However, many interesting directions remain for expanding the application.

The best way to practice spec-driven workflows is to keep adding small, clearly defined features.

Here are several ideas that would make engaging exercises.

Interactive map location questions

Instead of selecting a country from a dropdown list, respondents could choose their location on a map.

Imagine a question such as: Where are you participating from?

The interface could display a globe or world map where users click their location.

The response would store latitude and longitude coordinates. Survey analytics could then display responses geographically, showing clusters of participation across different regions.

Prompt : Design a specification for geographic survey responses using a map interface.

Drag-and-drop ranking questions

Some surveys ask users to rank items in order of preference.

For example: Rank these programming languages by how much you enjoy using them.

A drag-and-drop interface could allow respondents to reorder items visually:

  1. Python
  2. JavaScript
  3. Go
  4. Rust

The result would store the ranking order in the database.

This kind of question type introduces interesting data modeling challenges.

Prompt : Design a specification for drag-and-drop ranking questions in a survey app and explain the data modeling challenges involved in ranking questions.

Survey branching logic

More advanced surveys show different questions depending on earlier answers.

Example: Do you own a car?

Yes  show questions about driving habits

No  skip to public transport questions

This feature introduces conditional logic in the survey engine and forces you to think carefully about how questions and responses are structured.

Prompt : Design a specification for adding branching logic to a survey system.

Real-time response dashboards

Survey creators might want to see responses updating live while participants are answering.

This could be implemented using WebSockets, Django Channels, or live updating charts.

Watching responses accumulate in real time makes the application feel much more dynamic.

Prompt : Explain how WebSockets could be used to create real-time survey response dashboards.

Survey themes and styling

Another visual improvement would allow survey creators to customize the appearance of their surveys.

Possible features include:

  • Color themes
  • Custom logos
  • Light and dark modes

This would give you a reason to practice CSS custom properties, theme classes, and light/dark styling.

Prompt : Please show me how to add theming support to a Django web application.

Practice, references, and resources

In this section, you will be tested on what you’ve learned in this chapter and be provided with useful links to reference materials and resources.

Check your understanding

Answer the following questions:

  1. What is Spec-Driven Development, and why is it useful when working with AI coding assistants?
  2. Why is writing a specification before coding more important when using AI tools than when coding manually?
  3. What are the key sections of a good feature specification?
  4. Why are non-goals an important part of a specification?
  5. What makes acceptance criteria effective?
  6. How do tests turn a specification into an executable contract?
  7. What is the role of Spec Kit in this workflow?
  8. What are the main stages in the Spec Kit workflow?
  9. Why can Spec-Driven Development be considered overkill for small changes?
  10. Why should you review AI-generated code even after tests pass?
  11. You ask an AI tool to “add a useful feature” without a specification. The result includes extra functionality you did not want. Why did this happen?
  12. You write a specification but skip the non-goals section. The implementation becomes overly complex. What went wrong?
  13. Your acceptance criteria say “the UI should be user-friendly.” Why is this a problem?
  14. A task list contains one large item: “Implement URL shortener.” Why is this a problem?
  15. You run /speckit.implement without reviewing the spec or plan. What is the likely outcome?
  16. You complete the implementation and tests pass, but you skip manual testing. What risk remains?

Summary

In this chapter, you used Spec-Driven Development to add a new feature to an existing Django project. You saw how a written specification gives an AI coding assistant clearer boundaries, especially when the feature affects models, views, routes, templates, and tests.

You learned how to define goals, non-goals, user stories, acceptance criteria, data model changes, and verification steps. You also saw how tools such as Spec Kit can turn that specification into a staged process: project principles, feature spec, implementation plan, task list, implementation, review, and refinement.

Most importantly, you practiced the part of development that AI cannot do for you: deciding what behavior is wanted, what behavior is out of scope, and how you will prove that the system works.

Specifically, you learned the following:

  • What Spec-Driven Development is and why it is useful with AI coding assistants
  • How to structure a feature specification
  • How to extend an existing Django project using a written specification
  • How to add a URL shortener feature to TallyApp
  • How to verify that an implementation satisfies defined acceptance criteria
  • How small, well-defined features make large systems easier to evolve

In the next chapter, you will learn how to deploy your web project to a host server so that it becomes available publicly, so other people can reach it.

Deploying to Public Servers

In the previous chapters, you built TallyApp as a local Django project. That was enough while you were designing features, writing tests, and learning how the pieces fit together. But a web application is not really finished until someone else can use it.

In this chapter, you will deploy TallyApp to a server so other people can use it over the internet. That means moving from a development setup on your own machine to a production-style setup that keeps running, accepts requests from the internet, protects user data, serves static files, stores a real database, and rebuilding the server by hand each time.

This chapter gives you a working deployment path for a small Django app. You will see each major piece, configure it yourself, and keep the setup simple enough to understand.

We will use a deliberately simple stack: a small Virtual Private Server ( VPS ), Ubuntu, Nginx, Gunicorn, Django, and SQLite. This is not the only way to deploy Django, but it is a good learning setup because you can see every major part of the system. Later, the same architecture can grow by replacing SQLite with PostgreSQL, adding Cloudflare, using managed backups, or automating deployment with Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment ( CI/CD ).

By the end of this chapter, you will have deployed TallyApp to a publicly accessible server, understand how requests flow through a production Django stack, know how to preserve and back up user data across deployments, and understand which parts of the stack need to change as traffic grows.

In this chapter, we will cover the following topics:

  • Deployment options for a Django website
  • Protecting a Django website from common attacks
  • Deploying TallyApp
  • Final thoughts

Deployment options for a Django website

When you have been working locally, running the site just meant starting Django’s development server and opening a browser on your own machine. Deployment replaces that temporary setup with a system that keeps running, can accept requests from the public internet, and survive reboots and crashes.

In practical terms, deployment involves:

  • A server that is always on and reachable from the internet
  • A web server that listens on standard HTTP ports
  • An application server that runs Django as a long-lived process
  • A database that persists data independently of your code
  • A repeatable process for updating code and applying migrations

None of this is specific to TallyApp. These are the same building blocks used by Django sites of all sizes.

A production architecture for TallyApp

At a high level, TallyApp will run in production using a common, deliberately boring architecture, as shown in Figure 15.1 :

Figure 15.1: A simple production architecture for TallyApp

The components have clear responsibilities:

  • Nginx receives public web traffic, serves static files, and helps handle Transport Layer Security (TLS) , a cryptographic protocol that secures data sent over a network (TLS is often terminated by Nginx, Cloudflare, or both). When you visit a site using https:// , TLS ensures three things: (1) Encryption: data is unreadable to anyone intercepting it. (2) Authentication: the server proves it really is who it claims to be. (3) Integrity: data cannot be silently altered in transit.
  • Gunicorn runs Django as a production application server.
  • Django processes requests and talks to the database.
  • SQLite stores survey data on disk as a persistent file.

Keeping these jobs separate makes later changes less painful. You can move from SQLite to PostgreSQL, or put Cloudflare in front of Nginx, without rewriting your views and models.

Prompt : Please explain the difference between a web server, application server, and database in a Django deployment, with a real-world analogy.

Why a production Django site needs Gunicorn and Nginx

Django’s built-in development server is not designed for production use. Instead, Django applications are typically run behind a Web Server Gateway Interface ( WSGI ) server. WSGI is a specification, not a library. Gunicorn is one of the common WSGI implementations used with Django.

Gunicorn runs your Django project as a long-lived Python process. It does not listen directly on the public internet. Instead, it listens on a local socket and waits for Nginx to forward requests to it:

  1. A browser sends an HTTP request.
  2. Nginx receives it first.
  3. That server calls your Django application using the WSGI interface.
  4. Django returns a response object.
  5. The server sends the HTTP response back to the browser.

WSGI exists so that Django (and other web frameworks) do not need to know or care which web server is in front of them. As long as the server speaks WSGI, Django can run behind it.

Key points about WSGI:

  • It is synchronous and request–response based, meaning each request is handled in a blocking way. The server passes a request to your Django app, and that worker is tied up until the response is fully generated. If your code waits on something slow, like a database query or an API call, that worker just sits there waiting. It cannot do anything else in the meantime. Request–response based means a connection is not kept open to send multiple messages back and forth over time.
  • In practice, this means WSGI works very well for traditional web pages and APIs, but it is not designed for things like real-time updates, chat systems, or live notifications where long-lived connections are needed.
  • Django is a WSGI application, and Gunicorn is a WSGI server.

Gunicorn loads your Django project and calls it for each incoming request using the WSGI protocol.

Prompt : What is WSGI and how does it compare to ASGI in Python web apps? When would I choose ASGI (e.g. Daphne/Uvicorn) instead of Gunicorn?

Gunicorn configuration

For TallyApp, we will intentionally keep Gunicorn’s configuration conservative. It will have a single worker process and optionally a small number of threads. It will be managed by the operating system’s service manager, so it starts automatically on boot.

This configuration works particularly well with SQLite, which prefers limited write concurrency.

Using Nginx as a reverse proxy

A reverse proxy receives the public request and forwards it to another service behind the scenes. Nginx sits in front of Gunicorn and acts as the public-facing web server. Its responsibilities include:

  • Listening on ports 80 and 443
  • Serving static files such as CSS and images
  • Forwarding dynamic requests to Gunicorn

Nginx handles slow clients efficiently so your Django app does not have to.

This division of labor is one of the reasons Django applications perform well even on modest hardware.

Prompt : Please explain reverse proxies in simple terms and why Nginx is used in front of Gunicorn and include a request flow diagram showing how Nginx, Gunicorn, and Django interact.

Choosing between shared hosting, VPS, and cloud platforms

For this book, a VPS is the best place to start. A VPS gives you a full Linux machine with root access at a low monthly cost. You install exactly what you need and nothing more.

You should also note that other options exist:

  • Shared hosting is cheaper but usually unsuitable for Django deployments
  • Platform-as-a-service (PaaS) offerings handle more for you, but you learn less about the moving parts
  • Large cloud providers offer enormous flexibility, but also complexity that is unnecessary at this stage

A small VPS lets you see how the pieces fit together without overwhelming you.

The monthly cost mostly depends on the amount of CPU, memory, storage, and bandwidth you choose, as shown in Figure 15.2 :

Figure 15.2: Typical monthly costs for a VPS

You should be able to find a VPS hosting provider for about US$5-10 per month, which will be enough to have a proper web server to host your Django projects. But to get lower costs, you often have to commit to one or more years of hosting, so expect to pay $60-$120 for a year of hosting. Many readers may prefer just to host locally and never actually deploy to a public server.

Prompt : What are the trade-offs between VPS, PaaS, and serverless for a Django app?

SQLite as the database

People often say SQLite is not suitable for production, but that is too broad. SQLite is a file-based database that excels at simplicity and reliability, but it has limits around concurrent writes.

For TallyApp, SQLite is a reasonable choice if:

  • Traffic is modest
  • Database writes are short-lived
  • The application runs with a small number of worker processes
  • Write-ahead logging ( WAL ) is enabled

The database itself is just a file on disk. Django reads and writes it using the SQLite library. There is no database server to install or manage.

Prompt : Please explain write-ahead logging ( WAL ) in SQLite and why it matters for concurrency. At what point does SQLite become a bottleneck in a production Django app?

Database persistence and migrations

One of the most important deployment rules is this: never treat your database as disposable .

Your application code can be replaced at any time. Your database must survive deployments.

To achieve this:

  • Store the SQLite database file outside the application code directory
  • Update code separately from data
  • Use Django migrations to evolve the database schema

When you deploy a new version of TallyApp, you run migrations against the existing database. Data remains intact while the schema changes incrementally. This mirrors how migrations work with larger databases such as PostgreSQL. The commands are similar even though the database engine is different.

Backing up your data

Even for a learning project, backups matter. Users will assume their survey responses persist.

SQLite provides built-in mechanisms for creating consistent backups of a live database. A typical approach is:

  • Create a snapshot using SQLite’s backup facilities
  • Store the snapshot in a dated backup directory
  • Optionally copy it off the server

This can be automated with a daily scheduled task. The key idea is consistency. Always use SQLite’s own tools to create backups rather than copying the database file blindly, especially if the application may be running while the backup is taken.

Updating the site safely

A typical update cycle for TallyApp looks like this:

  1. Upload or pull the latest code
  2. Install or update dependencies
  3. Apply migrations
  4. Collect static files
  5. Restart the application service

Because data lives outside the code directory, updates are routine and low-risk. This is an important mental shift from local development, where deleting and recreating databases is common.

When to move to PostgreSQL

When traffic grows or writes become frequent and unpredictable, SQLite will start to show its limits. This is not a failure. It is simply the point at which the application has outgrown a file-based database.

The next step is usually PostgreSQL running on the same VPS. The architecture remains almost identical. Nginx and Gunicorn stay the same. Django stays the same. Only the database backend changes.

This is one of Django’s strengths. Database backends are swappable with minimal application changes if you have followed best practices.

Prompt : Please walk me through migrating a Django project from SQLite to PostgreSQL safely.

Scaling further with a managed database

Beyond a single VPS, databases are often moved to managed services. At that point:

  • Application servers can be scaled horizontally
  • Databases gain automated backups and replication
  • Operational complexity shifts from you to the provider

TallyApp does not need this level of infrastructure, but understanding the path matters. Your Django project can grow with your needs.

Summary of deployment options

Deploying TallyApp to the internet does not require exotic tools or complex cloud services. A small VPS, a conventional web stack, and a disciplined approach to data persistence are enough.

More importantly, this chapter establishes patterns that will serve you well beyond this project. The same principles apply whether you are deploying a learning app, a startup prototype, or a production service with real users and real expectations.

With a clear deployment approach in place, the next step is to ensure that your application remains secure and resilient once it is exposed to the unpredictable environment of the public internet.

Protecting a Django website from common attacks

Once your site is live on the public internet, it will start receiving traffic from sources you did not invite. Some will be legitimate users. Many will be automated bots scanning for weaknesses. This is normal.

For a beginner Django project like TallyApp, the goal is not to eliminate all risk. That is unrealistic. The goal is to avoid obvious mistakes, reduce the impact of common attacks, and make the site resilient enough that it keeps working even under nuisance traffic.

Django already includes many built-in protections, but they only help if you use them correctly and deploy your application with care.

You might make the following assumptions:

  • People will try to bring your site down : Partly true, but not in a targeted way. Most traffic will be automated bots. The architecture above handles that well.
  • A single server might be fragile : Correct. A single Droplet is a single point of failure. But for a demo site, that is acceptable if you have backups and can redeploy quickly.
  • You need strong protections from day one : Not really. You need basic Django settings and server protections, not heavy infrastructure. The combination of Django best practices + Cloudflare + basic server hardening covers most real risks.

Understanding the most common attacks

Most attacks against small web applications are not sophisticated. They are automated and repetitive, looking for easy wins.

The most relevant categories for a Django app are shown in Table 15.1 :

Name

Description

Cross-site scripting (XSS)

Attackers try to inject malicious JavaScript into pages viewed by other users. Django templates escape output by default, which blocks most simple cases. Problems usually arise when developers deliberately bypass escaping.

Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)

A user is tricked into submitting a request they did not intend, such as changing account details. Django includes CSRF protection middleware, but it must be enabled and used correctly in forms.

SQL injection

Malicious input attempts to alter database queries. Django’s object-relational mapper ( ORM ) protects against this by using parameterized queries, but unsafe raw SQL can reintroduce the risk.

Authentication abuse

Bots attempt to guess passwords or reuse leaked credentials. Login pages are a common target.

Security misconfiguration

This is one of the most common problems. Leaving DEBUG = True , exposing secrets, or failing to restrict allowed hosts can leak sensitive information or open the door to attacks.

File upload abuse

If your app allows uploads, attackers may try to upload malicious files or extremely large files to exhaust resources.

Denial of service (DoS)

Rather than hacking the site, attackers overwhelm it with traffic or expensive requests. For small apps, this is usually application-level abuse, not large-scale network flooding.

Table 15.1: Common types of website attack

The Open Worldwide Application Security Project ( OWASP ) Top 10 is a widely recognized list of the most common and impactful security risks affecting web applications. Maintained by a global community of security professionals, it highlights patterns seen in actual breaches. Rather than being an exhaustive list, it serves as a practical guide to the kinds of vulnerabilities developers are most likely to encounter, helping teams prioritize the issues that matter most when building and deploying secure applications.

The OWASP Top 10 continues to highlight issues like broken access control, injection, and misconfiguration as leading causes of vulnerabilities in web applications: https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/

Prompt : Please give some examples of XSS, CSRF, and SQL injection in Django apps.

A practical security baseline for beginners

You do not need expensive tools to protect a small Django application. A simple, well-configured setup goes a long way.

Start with Django’s deployment checklist:

  1. Set DEBUG = False
  2. Define ALLOWED_HOSTS
  3. Keep your SECRET_KEY private
  4. Run python manage.py check --deploy

Django explicitly warns that running with DEBUG = True in production can expose stack traces, settings, and sensitive internal details.

Prompt : What does Django’s check --deploy command actually validate internally?

Enforcing HTTPS and secure cookies

Django recommends enforcing HTTPS across the entire site, not just login pages, because session cookies are shared across requests. Always serve your site over HTTPS. This protects login sessions and user data.

In your Django settings you should enable the following options: 

if not DEBUG: # Only enabled in a production environment.
    SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
    SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
    CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
    SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000  # 1 year
    SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS = True
    X_FRAME_OPTIONS = "DENY"
    SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF = True

Note the following about the preceding settings:

  • SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True : Forces all HTTP requests to be redirected to HTTPS. If a user visits http://your-site.com , Django will automatically redirect them to https://your-site.com . This ensures all communication is encrypted. Without this, users might access your site over plain HTTP, which allows attackers to intercept or modify traffic (man-in-the-middle attacks).
  • SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True : Ensures that session cookies are only sent over HTTPS. Browsers will not include the session cookie in HTTP requests. Session cookies identify logged-in users. If sent over HTTP, they can be intercepted and used to hijack sessions.
  • CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True : Ensures that the CSRF protection cookie is only sent over HTTPS. Similar to session cookies, but specifically for CSRF tokens. CSRF protection depends on a secret token. If that token is exposed over HTTP, an attacker could potentially bypass CSRF protections.
  • SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000 (1 year in seconds): Enables HTTP Strict Transport Security ( HSTS ) and tells browsers to always use HTTPS for your site for the next year. After visiting your site once over HTTPS, the browser will refuse to connect over HTTP for the specified duration. It prevents downgrade attacks where an attacker tries to force a user back to HTTP.

    Warning! You should only enable this once you are confident HTTPS is working correctly everywhere.

  • SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS = True : Extends HSTS to all subdomains. For example: api.your-site.com, admin.your-site.com, and so on. Attackers often target weaker subdomains. This ensures the entire domain is HTTPS-only.
  • X_FRAME_OPTIONS = "DENY" : Prevents your site from being embedded inside an <iframe> . The browser will block any attempt to load your pages in a frame on another site. Protects against clickjacking attacks, where a malicious site tricks users into clicking hidden elements from your site.
  • SECURE_CONTENT_TYPE_NOSNIFF = True : This tells browsers not to guess (or “sniff”) the content type of a response. The browser must respect the Content-Type header sent by the server. Prevents certain attacks where a file is disguised as one type (e.g., text) but executed as another (e.g., JavaScript).

Taken as a group, these settings enforce HTTPS everywhere, protect sensitive cookies, prevent common browser-based attacks (clickjacking, MIME sniffing), and reduce the risk of interception and manipulation of traffic.

They are part of Django’s built-in secure by default in production approach, but they only work correctly when your app is properly deployed behind HTTPS (for example, using Nginx or a cloud platform that terminates TLS).

Warning! Do not enable these blindly in development because HTTPS is often not configured locally, and redirects and secure cookies can break your dev workflow.

Protecting against XSS and CSRF

Django helps here, but only if you follow its conventions:

  • Use Django templates rather than building HTML strings manually
  • Avoid marking user input as safe unless absolutely necessary

  • Ensure all forms include CSRF tokens, as shown in the following form: 

    <form method="post">
    {% csrf_token %}
    <!-- form fields -->
</form>

For additional protection, consider enabling a Content Security Policy ( CSP ), which restricts where scripts can be loaded from. Django 6 includes built-in support for CSP configuration, for example settings like SECURE_CSP , but earlier Django versions, like the current LTS version 5.2, do not.

A CSP is a browser-enforced security mechanism that controls which resources a web page is allowed to load and execute. It is defined by the server (usually via an HTTP response header) and tells the browser things like which domains JavaScript can be loaded from, whether inline scripts are allowed, and where images, stylesheets, fonts, and other assets can come from.

The goal is to reduce the impact of attacks such as cross-site scripting (XSS) . Even if an attacker manages to inject malicious code into your page, a well-configured CSP can prevent that code from running because it is not from an approved source.

A simple example might look like this: 

Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://trusted.cdn.com;

The preceding HTTP header tells the browser to only load resources from your own site by default, and only allow scripts from your site and a trusted Content Delivery Network ( CDN ).

CSP works best as an additional layer of defense. It does not replace secure coding practices, but it makes exploitation significantly harder when something goes wrong.

You can learn more about CSP at the following link: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CSP

Avoiding SQL injection

The safest approach is simple: use Django’s ORM: 

# Safe
User.objects.filter(username=username)

Avoid constructing SQL queries manually using string concatenation. If you must use raw SQL, use parameterized queries.

Django’s documentation emphasizes that its ORM protects against SQL injection by default, but only when used properly.

Securing authentication

Login endpoints are a favorite target for bots.

Basic protections include:

  • Enforce strong passwords
  • Add rate limiting to login attempts
  • Consider adding a human-verification challenge after repeated failures
  • Avoid exposing the Django admin at predictable URLs without additional protection

A simple rate-limiting approach can dramatically reduce brute-force attempts.

Handling file uploads safely

If your app allows file uploads:

  • Limit file size
  • Validate file types
  • Never execute uploaded files
  • Store uploads outside your main application domain

Django recommends serving uploaded files from a separate domain or storage system to reduce risk.

Defending against denial-of-service

For a small project, most DoS attempts are actually abusive usage patterns.

Common examples:

  • Repeated login attempts
  • Large file uploads
  • Expensive database queries
  • Aggressive crawling

Low-cost defenses include:

  • Rate limiting key endpoints
  • Limiting upload size
  • Using caching where appropriate
  • Moving static files to a CDN

Using a service like Cloudflare can provide free or low-cost protection, including basic Distributed Denial of Service ( DDoS ) mitigation and request filtering.

Prompt : Please show me how to implement rate limiting in Django using middleware or third-party packages. Please explain how Cloudflare protects a small website from bots and attacks.

Protecting secrets and configuration

Never store secrets in your source code repository.

Use environment variables instead: 

import os
SECRET_KEY = os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"]

Django’s deployment guidance stresses that sensitive settings must remain confidential.

Logging, monitoring, and backups

Security is not just about prevention. You must also detect and recover.

At a minimum:

  • Enable logging for errors and suspicious activity
  • Monitor failed login attempts
  • Keep regular database backups
  • Test restoring from backups

For example, add the following code to your settings.py : 

import os
LOG_DIR = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, "logs")
os.makedirs(LOG_DIR, exist_ok=True)
LOGGING = {
    "version": 1,
    "disable_existing_loggers": False,
    "formatters": {
        "verbose": {
            "format": "{asctime} {levelname} {name} {message}",
            "style": "{",
        },
    },
    "handlers": {
        "file": {
            "level": "WARNING",
            "class": "logging.FileHandler",
            "filename": os.path.join(LOG_DIR, "django.log"),
            "formatter": "verbose",
        },
    },
    "loggers": {
        "django": {
            "handlers": ["file"],
            "level": "WARNING",
            "propagate": True,
        },
    },
}

The preceding code:

  • Logs warnings, errors, and exceptions
  • Writes to logs/django.log
  • Captures suspicious activity like bad requests or errors

To check the server logs, use the following Bash/shell commands: 

sudo journalctl -u gunicorn -f
sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log

To log failed logins, add the following code to your login view: 

import logging
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
def login_view(request):
    if request.method == "POST":
        username = request.POST.get("username")
        password = request.POST.get("password")
        user = authenticate(request, username=username, password=password)
        if user is None:
            logger.warning(f"Failed login attempt for username: {username}")
        else:
            login(request, user)

OWASP highlights that failures in logging and monitoring can allow attacks to go unnoticed for long periods.

Use a ready-made package to track logins

To track failed login attempts, temporarily block brute-force attacks, and store attempts in the database, you can install a Django middleware package named Axes: 

pip install django-axes

Then enable the package in settings.py : 

INSTALLED_APPS += ["axes"]
MIDDLEWARE += ["axes.middleware.AxesMiddleware"]
AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS = [
    "axes.backends.AxesBackend",
    "django.contrib.auth.backends.ModelBackend",
]
AXES_FAILURE_LIMIT = 5
AXES_COOLOFF_TIME = 1  # hours

This package logs to permanent tables so you must then run database migrations: 

python manage.py migrate

It is reasonable to expect that a public demo site like TallyApp will receive unwanted traffic. However, this will mostly come from automated bots, not targeted human attackers.

Summary checklist

For a beginner-friendly deployment, aim for the following:

  • Disable debug mode
  • Enforce HTTPS everywhere
  • Use secure cookies
  • Configure ALLOWED_HOSTS
  • Keep secrets out of source control
  • Use Django’s ORM and built-in protections
  • Add rate limiting to login and public endpoints
  • Limit and validate file uploads
  • Put a CDN or proxy in front of your site
  • Enable logging and maintain backups

Each of the preceding points is covered in detail in either this chapter or Chapter 9 , Django – Web Development on the Backend .

This does not make your application invulnerable. It makes it robust enough for production use, which is exactly what you need for a public-facing example like TallyApp.

With these security fundamentals in place, we can now move on to deploying TallyApp to a public server, applying these practices in a real, working environment.

Deploying TallyApp

The first step is to pick a host server provider. This is the machine that will run your application continuously and make it accessible to users over the internet. Unlike your local development environment, this server must be reliable, reachable at all times, and capable of handling requests from unknown users and automated systems.

There are several categories of hosting to choose from, each with different trade-offs. Shared hosting is inexpensive but too restrictive for most Django applications. Platform-as-a-service options remove much of the operational burden, but they also hide how deployment actually works. At the other end of the spectrum, large cloud providers offer enormous flexibility, but can introduce unnecessary complexity for a small project. For a project like TallyApp, a VPS strikes the right balance. It gives you full control over a Linux machine at a low cost, while still being simple enough to understand how all the pieces fit together.

Choosing a VPS also aligns well with the architecture introduced earlier in this chapter. You will install and configure each component yourself: the web server, the application server, and the database. This might sound like extra work, but it is where much of the learning happens. Instead of relying on a black-box platform, you will see exactly how requests flow through your system and how your application behaves in a real environment.

In the next section, we will use DigitalOcean as our hosting provider. It offers a straightforward way to create and manage virtual servers, with predictable pricing and strong documentation. More importantly, it allows us to focus on understanding deployment rather than wrestling with infrastructure complexity.

Why DigitalOcean is a good fit for TallyApp

I chose to use DigitalOcean as my host provider because it sits in a useful middle ground between too abstract platforms that hide everything and hyperscale clouds that overwhelm beginners with options and pricing complexity.

For a project like TallyApp, it is arguably useful for learning because it forces you to understand what is happening during deployment, without drowning you in enterprise concerns.

The biggest advantage is simplicity. You can go from zero to a public server in minutes using a Droplet , which is just a virtual machine. That maps nicely to how Django is traditionally deployed, using tools like Gunicorn and Nginx.

The documentation is strong and beginner-friendly. DigitalOcean has spent years building tutorials specifically for common stacks like Django, including step-by-step guides for Ubuntu, Gunicorn, and Nginx. You can read the DigitalOcean documentation tutorials at the following link: https://www.digitalocean.com/community/tutorials .

DigitalOcean VPS also gives you full control. You will learn how web servers, reverse proxies, and application servers fit together, rather than relying on a black-box platform.

The downsides you should be aware of

The trade-off for simplicity is that you are responsible for more things yourself.

You are managing a server. That means:

  • Applying security updates
  • Configuring firewalls
  • Managing processes and services
  • Handling scaling manually

There is no automatic scaling. If your site suddenly gets popular or attacked, a single Droplet can become overwhelmed.

You still own application security because it is not fully managed. Unlike platforms such as Heroku or Vercel, DigitalOcean does not automatically handle many application-level protections. You need to configure them.

Backups and monitoring are optional add-ons. They are not fully integrated by default unless you enable them.

Is it suitable for a public demo like TallyApp?

Yes, with one condition: you must add a thin layer of protection in front of it. A single low-cost Droplet is perfectly capable of running a Django app with light to moderate traffic. For a book companion site, that is usually more than enough.

However, exposing a raw server directly to the internet is not ideal. Without additional protection, it will quickly receive:

  • Bot traffic scanning for vulnerabilities
  • Login brute-force attempts
  • Crawlers and scrapers
  • Occasional traffic spikes

This is where combining DigitalOcean with a proxy layer becomes important.

What protection DigitalOcean provides

DigitalOcean gives you infrastructure-level security, but not full application protection.

Included protections:

  • Basic network isolation through virtual private networking
  • Cloud firewalls to restrict inbound traffic by port and IP
  • Secure Shell (SSH) key authentication instead of passwords
  • Datacenter-level physical security
  • DDoS protection at the infrastructure level (limited and not deeply configurable)

These are useful server-level protections, but they do not protect against:

  • Application-layer attacks (for example, login abuse)
  • XSS or CSRF issues
  • Misconfigured Django settings
  • Bot traffic targeting your endpoints

Some useful features are available but require enabling or additional cost, as shown in Table 15.2 :

Feature

Description

Backups

Automatic backups typically cost around 20% of the Droplet price.

Monitoring and alerts

Basic monitoring is available, but you need to configure alerts yourself.

Load balancers

Start at around $12 per month. Useful if you scale beyond a single server.

Managed databases

More expensive than self-hosting PostgreSQL, but reduce operational risk.

Table 15.2: DigitalOcean features that can be enabled

The missing piece: edge protection

DigitalOcean gives you the server, but it does not filter every bad request before it reaches your app. This is where adding Cloudflare (or a similar service) in front of your Droplet enhances your protection.

With even a free Cloudflare plan, you get:

  • CDN caching for static content like CSS stylesheets and images
  • Basic DDoS protection
  • Bot filtering
  • TLS termination (HTTPS handled at the edge)

At a low cost, you can add:

  • Rate limiting (for login and forms)
  • Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules

When paired with a simple edge service like Cloudflare and good Django configuration, DigitalOcean plus Cloudflare and correct Django settings is enough for a small public TallyApp deployment.

Deploying step-by-step

You will benefit more from understanding deployment than from taking the shortest path to a working server.

We will standardize on the following target stack: a small Droplet for the app server, Ubuntu LTS, SQLite for database simplicity, Nginx as reverse proxy, Gunicorn for Django, Uncomplicated Firewall (UFW) , and optional backups. That is suitable for a public demo app with modest traffic.

Create a DigitalOcean Droplet

Now we can create a Droplet to host our website project:

  1. Register a DigitalOcean account at the following link: https://cloud.digitalocean.com/
  2. On your account’s Projects page, you will already have a default project, often named first-project . We can leave this as-is.
  3. Click Create , and then click Droplets , as shown in Figure 15.3 :

Figure 15.3: Creating a Droplet

  1. Select a region, either close to most of your expected visitors, or close to you. I chose New York .
  2. Select an image for your operating system. I chose Ubuntu 24.04 (LTS) x64 .
  3. Select the Droplet size. I chose:
    • Basic (shared CPU)
    • Regular SSD
    • $12 per month
    • 2 GB / 1 CPU
    • 50 GB SSD Disk
    • 2 TB transfer
  4. Optionally, enable an automated backup plan. I chose Daily Backups at a cost of $3.60 per month. Backups are kept for one week. For the time window, I chose midnight to 4 a.m. in the Eastern US time zone.
  5. Select an authentication method. I chose SSH . Click Add SSH Key and follow the instructions. You must name the SSH key (I used tallyapp-sshkey ) and it will create two files. The file without .pub is your private key. Keep it private. The .pub file is the public key you copy to DigitalOcean.

You can learn more about how to connect to Droplets using SSH at the following link: https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/how-to/connect-with-ssh/

  1. Click Create Droplet .
  2. Note the IP address assigned to your server, as shown in Figure 15.4 :

Figure 15.4: Your server’s IP address

  1. At the command prompt or terminal, enter the command to connect to your remote server using the private SSH key file you created earlier, the default root user account, and the IP address of the remote server: 

    ssh -i tallyapp-sshkey root@167.99.52.197

The default username on initial creation is root on most operating systems, like Ubuntu and CentOS. If you add another user, you can use that username instead.

  1. Enter the passphrase for the SSH key.

  2. You will now be connected to the remote server host, as shown in the following lightly edited output: 

    Welcome to Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (GNU/Linux 6.8.0-71-generic x86_64)
System information as of Tue Mar 24 16:46:12 UTC 2026
